source_claims.statement: C is a general-purpose language created in 1972 by Dennis Ritchie for relatively direct CPU architecture access.
C is used for operating systems, kernels, drivers, protocol stacks, supercomputers, microcontrollers and embedded systems.
C evolved from B/New B in the context of Unix development and reimplemented the Unix kernel.
C is static, weakly enforced/typed, manifest and nominal.
C provides static, automatic and dynamic storage with manual management.
C combines low-level access with portability through standardized semantics.
The preprocessor provides macros/inclusion/conditional compilation and libraries extend the small core.
Array and pointer semantics are tightly coupled; unchecked bounds are both powerful and risky.
C evolved from K&R through C89/C90/C95/C99/C11/C17/C23 and C2Y/C29.
Embedded C addresses fixed-point arithmetic, named address spaces and hardware I/O.
C is used in systems, games, servers, CGI history and computational libraries.
C interoperates with assembly and higher-level languages and implements other language runtimes.
C has memory, type-safety, runtime-checking, aliasing, ABI, preprocessing and error-handling limitations.
Coding standards, analysis tools and hardware capabilities mitigate subsets of C risks.
C influenced a broad family of programming and hardware-description languages.

value.filename: Campus network / Campus Area Network source supplied by user
value.note: Line ranges are normalized to the supplied article sections; the source itself contains Wikipedia-style inline references.

value.name: CAN composition
value.expression: CAN = interconnected LANs within a limited geographic area
value.meaning: Defines the CAN structurally and geographically.

value.name: Scale ordering
value.expression: LAN < CAN < MAN < WAN
value.meaning: Captures the source's explicit relative size hierarchy.

value.name: Campus ownership model
value.expression: Campus tenant/owner → networking equipment + transmission media
value.meaning: Models the source's statement that campus equipment and media are almost entirely owner-controlled.

value.name: University facility connectivity
value.expression: CAN → buildings/facilities
value.meaning: Represents campus-wide interconnection of administrative, academic, research, residential, recreational, and outlying structures.

value.name: Corporate campus backbone
value.expression: Buildings → high-speed Ethernet → optical fiber
value.meaning: Represents the source's described corporate-campus implementation pattern.

value.name: High-speed Ethernet examples
value.expression: High-speed Ethernet → Gigabit Ethernet / 10 Gigabit Ethernet
value.meaning: Captures the named examples of campus interconnection technologies.

value.name: CAN stated range
value.expression: 1 km ≤ CAN range ≤ 5 km
value.meaning: Represents the source's stated geographic range.

value.name: Same-domain building condition
value.expression: same domain + connected buildings → CAN (source-stated condition)
value.meaning: Captures the article's classification statement without extending it beyond the source.

value.name: LAN aggregation
value.expression: LAN₁ + LAN₂ + … + LANₙ → CAN
value.meaning: Shows how multiple local networks form the campus-scale network.

value.name: Campus physical infrastructure
value.expression: CAN → switches/routers → fiber/copper/Cat5
value.meaning: Maps logical campus networking scope to physical infrastructure named in the source.

value.name: Historical university examples
value.expression: Stanford → SUNet; MIT → Athena; CMU → Andrew
value.meaning: Associates early campus networking examples with institutions.

value.name: Corporate examples
value.expression: Googleplex / Microsoft campus → corporate campus network
value.meaning: Maps the named corporate campuses to the corporate CAN use case.

value.name: Network-scale taxonomy
value.expression: PAN → LAN → CAN → MAN → WAN → Internet
value.meaning: A simplified path through categories explicitly present in the source taxonomy; it is a conceptual ordering, not a claim that every listed category is strictly geographic scale.

value.name: Owner-operated infrastructure
value.expression: enterprise/university/government → owns → campus infrastructure
value.meaning: Captures the ownership relationship emphasized by the source.

value.distinction: CAN interconnects LANs across a limited campus area; LAN is one constituent local network.
The source places CAN below MAN in scale.
The source places CAN below WAN in scale.
The source presents these as alternative terms rather than distinct technologies.
Switches/routers are active networking equipment; fiber/copper/Cat5 are transmission media.
Both connect buildings, but the source gives different organizational contexts and examples.
Both are named CAN media; fiber is specifically associated with the high-speed Ethernet corporate pattern.
Both are examples of high-speed Ethernet; the source distinguishes them by named link speed.
The source provides both a numeric range and a domain/connectivity condition; these are different classification dimensions.
CAN is a campus network scope; backbone is a network type listed separately in the taxonomy.
The taxonomy mixes geographic scale categories with categories such as SAN, WLAN, VLAN, and LPWAN.
The source emphasizes campus ownership of infrastructure rather than an externally owned access network.

value.misconception: CAN is just a larger single LAN.
value.correction: The source defines CAN as an interconnection of LANs, so its defining structure is aggregation/interconnection of local networks.

value.misconception: CAN is larger than a MAN.
value.correction: The source explicitly states CAN is smaller than MAN.

value.misconception: CAN always means wireless networking.
value.correction: The source emphasizes switches, routers, optical fiber, copper plant, and Cat5 cabling; wireless is not required by this definition.

value.misconception: CAN equipment must be externally owned.
value.correction: The source says equipment and transmission media are almost entirely owned by the campus tenant/owner.

value.misconception: Only universities use CANs.
value.correction: The source explicitly includes enterprise, university, and government ownership/use contexts and discusses corporate campuses.

value.misconception: A CAN has to use fiber.
value.correction: Fiber is one named medium; copper plant and Cat5 are also explicitly named.

value.misconception: Every campus CAN must use 10 Gigabit Ethernet.
value.correction: 10 Gigabit Ethernet is one example of high-speed Ethernet, alongside Gigabit Ethernet.

value.misconception: The 1–5 km figure is an absolute universal standard.
value.correction: The source states this range but marks the associated statement with a citation-needed note; it should be treated as source-provided rather than a universal engineering rule.

value.misconception: Campus network and corporate area network are completely different technologies.
value.correction: The source presents campus network and corporate area network as alternative terminology for CAN.

value.misconception: A CAN is the same thing as the Internet.
value.correction: CAN is a limited-area network interconnecting LANs; the Internet is separately listed as a much broader network category.

value.name: CSS rule structure
value.expression: stylesheet → rule → selector(s) + declaration block → property:value
value.mechanism: Selectors determine targets; declarations assign values.

value.name: Cascade resolution
value.expression: matching declarations → priority/importance → specificity → source order → selected value
value.mechanism: The cascade resolves competing declarations using priority and tie-break rules.

value.name: Selector matching
value.expression: selector + DOM structure/attributes/state → matching elements
value.mechanism: Selectors can use element type, IDs, classes, attributes, relationships, pseudo-classes, and pseudo-elements.

value.name: Inheritance
value.expression: ancestor value → eligible descendant property
value.mechanism: Some properties inherit from ancestors when not overridden.

value.name: Box model
value.expression: content + padding + border + margin → box geometry
value.mechanism: Element dimensions and surrounding spacing determine layout geometry.

value.name: External stylesheet reuse
value.expression: HTML → link stylesheet → shared CSS → rules applied across pages
value.mechanism: A common stylesheet reduces repetition and can be cached.

value.name: Responsive presentation
value.expression: viewport/device/media → media query → selected rules → adapted layout
value.mechanism: Conditional styling changes presentation across screens, orientations, and output media.

value.name: Browser compatibility workflow
value.expression: feature → support data → cross-browser test → @supports/fallback → resilient output
value.mechanism: Compatibility information and fallbacks reduce browser-specific failures.

value.name: Preprocessor compilation
value.expression: Sass/Less/Stylus source → compiler → CSS → browser rendering
value.mechanism: Preprocessors provide authoring abstractions but the browser receives CSS.

value.name: Multi-medium presentation
value.expression: semantic markup → user/media-specific styles → screen/print/speech/Braille output
value.mechanism: Separation permits the same content to be presented in different forms.

value.name: Framework styling
value.expression: framework stylesheet → reusable patterns → page layout
value.mechanism: Frameworks accelerate common design tasks but may introduce unused CSS overhead.

value.name: Presentational markup migration
value.expression: repeated HTML formatting → shared CSS rules → simpler markup
value.mechanism: Moving style declarations out of markup reduces duplication and maintenance effort.

value.distinction: HTML defines structure/content; CSS defines presentation.
CSS controls styling/layout; JavaScript supplies behavior.
Selectors choose targets; declarations set property values.
Pseudo-classes describe state/context; pseudo-elements target generated or partial content.
An ID identifies a single document element; classes can be reused.
Cascade resolves competing declarations; inheritance passes eligible values from ancestors.
Specificity compares selector weights; source order is a tie-breaker.
Inline declarations attach to one element; external CSS centralizes reusable rules.
Absolute units use fixed reference measures; relative units depend on context.
Responsive styles adapt to viewport/device context.
CSS 3 is modular; the source rejects a single monolithic CSS 4 release.
Sass, Less, and Stylus add authoring abstractions and compile to CSS.
Frameworks speed development but can add unused features and overhead.
Prefixes historically targeted browser-specific behavior; @supports tests support conditions.
Separating presentation lets the same content be adapted to different media.
Some style-reuse limitations can be addressed by languages compiling to CSS.

value.misconception: CSS defines document structure.
value.correction: HTML defines structure; CSS specifies presentation.

value.misconception: A CSS class is itself a CSS subsystem feature.
value.correction: The class attribute belongs to the markup model; CSS selectors match its value.

value.misconception: Pseudo-classes and pseudo-elements are identical.
value.correction: Pseudo-classes match state/context; pseudo-elements target generated or partial content.

value.misconception: The last CSS rule always wins.
value.correction: Importance and specificity can take precedence over source order.

value.misconception: Specificity works like decimal arithmetic.
value.correction: Specificity components are compared as separate weights.

value.misconception: Every CSS property inherits automatically.
value.correction: Only properties that inherit by their rules receive ancestor values.

value.misconception: ID and class selectors are interchangeable.
value.correction: IDs identify a document element; classes can be reused.

value.misconception: CSS is only for screen visuals.
value.correction: CSS can tailor print and source-described speech/Braille contexts.

value.misconception: CSS 4 is one unified version after CSS 3.
value.correction: The source describes CSS 3 as modules rather than a monolithic CSS 4.

value.misconception: Vendor prefixes guarantee interoperability.
value.correction: Browser-specific prefixes do not eliminate testing or fallback needs.

value.misconception: Framework CSS is always smaller than handcrafted CSS.
value.correction: Frameworks may include unused styles and add download/maintenance overhead.

value.misconception: Preprocessors replace browser CSS.
value.correction: Sass, Less, and Stylus compile to CSS processed by browsers.

value.misconception: Inline styles are best for site-wide consistency.
value.correction: External stylesheets centralize reusable rules and can be cached.

value.misconception: Responsive design just shrinks content.
value.correction: Responsive styles adapt layout to device, viewport, and orientation.

value.misconception: JavaScript polyfills are native CSS.
value.correction: Polyfills are JavaScript code that may emulate unsupported Web behavior.

value.misconception: CSS has no limitations.
value.correction: The source lists scoping, rule naming/composition, hover-control, and text-targeting limitations.

formal_models.name: CSS rule structure
formal_models.expression: stylesheet → rule → selector(s) + declaration block → property:value
formal_models.mechanism: Selectors determine targets; declarations assign values.

formal_models.name: Cascade resolution
formal_models.expression: matching declarations → priority/importance → specificity → source order → selected value
formal_models.mechanism: The cascade resolves competing declarations using priority and tie-break rules.

formal_models.name: Selector matching
formal_models.mechanism: Selectors can use element type, IDs, classes, attributes, relationships, pseudo-classes, and pseudo-elements.

formal_models.name: Inheritance
formal_models.mechanism: Some properties inherit from ancestors when not overridden.

formal_models.name: Box model
formal_models.expression: content + padding + border + margin → box geometry
formal_models.mechanism: Element dimensions and surrounding spacing determine layout geometry.

formal_models.name: External stylesheet reuse
formal_models.expression: HTML → link stylesheet → shared CSS → rules applied across pages
formal_models.mechanism: A common stylesheet reduces repetition and can be cached.

formal_models.name: Responsive presentation
formal_models.expression: viewport/device/media → media query → selected rules → adapted layout
formal_models.mechanism: Conditional styling changes presentation across screens, orientations, and output media.

formal_models.name: Browser compatibility workflow
formal_models.expression: feature → support data → cross-browser test → @supports/fallback → resilient output
formal_models.mechanism: Compatibility information and fallbacks reduce browser-specific failures.

formal_models.name: Preprocessor compilation
formal_models.expression: Sass/Less/Stylus source → compiler → CSS → browser rendering
formal_models.mechanism: Preprocessors provide authoring abstractions but the browser receives CSS.

formal_models.name: Multi-medium presentation
formal_models.expression: semantic markup → user/media-specific styles → screen/print/speech/Braille output
formal_models.mechanism: Separation permits the same content to be presented in different forms.

formal_models.name: Framework styling
formal_models.expression: framework stylesheet → reusable patterns → page layout
formal_models.mechanism: Frameworks accelerate common design tasks but may introduce unused CSS overhead.

formal_models.name: Presentational markup migration
formal_models.expression: repeated HTML formatting → shared CSS rules → simpler markup
formal_models.mechanism: Moving style declarations out of markup reduces duplication and maintenance effort.

source_claims.claim: CSS specifies presentation of markup documents and is a core Web technology alongside HTML and JavaScript.
CSS separates content/structure from presentation, enabling reuse, maintainability, caching, accessibility, and alternate media.
CSS rules pair selectors with declaration blocks containing property-value declarations.
Selectors match elements by type, ID, class, attributes, relationships, state, and partial/generated content.
The cascade resolves competing declarations using priority, specificity, order, inheritance, and defaults.
CSS controls layout, dimensions, spacing, borders, typography, responsive design, and visual effects.
CSS can provide distinct presentation for screen, print, speech, Braille, and mobile contexts.
CSS originated in 1990s style-sheet proposals and CSS Level 1 was released in December 1996.
CSS 3 is developed as separate modules and summarized in periodic snapshots.
Browser differences are addressed with testing, feature queries, support tables, and fallbacks.
The source describes limitations involving scope, pseudo-class control, rule naming/composition, and arbitrary text targeting.
The ecosystem includes preprocessors, frameworks, extensions, and organization methodologies.

semantic_distinctions.distinction: HTML defines structure/content; CSS defines presentation.
CSS controls styling/layout; JavaScript supplies behavior.
Selectors choose targets; declarations set property values.
Pseudo-classes describe state/context; pseudo-elements target generated or partial content.
An ID identifies a single document element; classes can be reused.
Cascade resolves competing declarations; inheritance passes eligible values from ancestors.
Specificity compares selector weights; source order is a tie-breaker.
Inline declarations attach to one element; external CSS centralizes reusable rules.
Absolute units use fixed reference measures; relative units depend on context.
Responsive styles adapt to viewport/device context.
CSS 3 is modular; the source rejects a single monolithic CSS 4 release.
Sass, Less, and Stylus add authoring abstractions and compile to CSS.
Frameworks speed development but can add unused features and overhead.
Prefixes historically targeted browser-specific behavior; @supports tests support conditions.
Separating presentation lets the same content be adapted to different media.
Some style-reuse limitations can be addressed by languages compiling to CSS.

misconceptions.misconception: CSS defines document structure.
misconceptions.correction: HTML defines structure; CSS specifies presentation.

misconceptions.misconception: A CSS class is itself a CSS subsystem feature.
misconceptions.correction: The class attribute belongs to the markup model; CSS selectors match its value.

misconceptions.misconception: Pseudo-classes and pseudo-elements are identical.
misconceptions.correction: Pseudo-classes match state/context; pseudo-elements target generated or partial content.

misconceptions.misconception: The last CSS rule always wins.
misconceptions.correction: Importance and specificity can take precedence over source order.

misconceptions.misconception: Specificity works like decimal arithmetic.
misconceptions.correction: Specificity components are compared as separate weights.

misconceptions.misconception: Every CSS property inherits automatically.
misconceptions.correction: Only properties that inherit by their rules receive ancestor values.

misconceptions.misconception: ID and class selectors are interchangeable.
misconceptions.correction: IDs identify a document element; classes can be reused.

misconceptions.misconception: CSS is only for screen visuals.
misconceptions.correction: CSS can tailor print and source-described speech/Braille contexts.

misconceptions.misconception: CSS 4 is one unified version after CSS 3.
misconceptions.correction: The source describes CSS 3 as modules rather than a monolithic CSS 4.

misconceptions.misconception: Vendor prefixes guarantee interoperability.
misconceptions.correction: Browser-specific prefixes do not eliminate testing or fallback needs.

misconceptions.misconception: Framework CSS is always smaller than handcrafted CSS.
misconceptions.correction: Frameworks may include unused styles and add download/maintenance overhead.

misconceptions.misconception: Preprocessors replace browser CSS.
misconceptions.correction: Sass, Less, and Stylus compile to CSS processed by browsers.

misconceptions.misconception: Inline styles are best for site-wide consistency.
misconceptions.correction: External stylesheets centralize reusable rules and can be cached.

misconceptions.misconception: Responsive design just shrinks content.
misconceptions.correction: Responsive styles adapt layout to device, viewport, and orientation.

misconceptions.misconception: JavaScript polyfills are native CSS.
misconceptions.correction: Polyfills are JavaScript code that may emulate unsupported Web behavior.

misconceptions.misconception: CSS has no limitations.
misconceptions.correction: The source lists scoping, rule naming/composition, hover-control, and text-targeting limitations.

value.title: Cloud Computing — Full Relationship-Rich Semantic Knowledge Graph
value.purpose: A detailed graph of cloud-computing concepts, service models, architecture, dependencies, providers, economics, operations, security, privacy, standards, history, and legal context.
value.source_policy: The supplied Simple English Wikipedia extract is authoritative for source-derived claims. Modern provider and architecture concepts are marked as synthesis. No external web research was performed.
value.temporal_caveat: Provider/product examples in the article are historical. They are preserved as source-era examples, not as a current market ranking.
value.provenance_policy: Line numbers refer to the extracted source lines. Empty line lists identify concepts added as explanatory synthesis.

value.graph_design: Directed typed relationships express mechanisms, dependencies, roles, constraints, examples, and distinctions rather than generic related_to links.

value.name: Cloud service abstraction
value.description: Provider-operated infrastructure is abstracted through virtualization and service interfaces so consumers can use capabilities without managing every physical detail.

value.name: Service-model stack
value.description: IaaS exposes infrastructure; PaaS exposes a platform; SaaS exposes an application. Provider responsibility generally increases at higher abstraction levels.

value.name: Typical cloud application dependency graph
value.description: Illustrative modern dependency chain; not every component is explicitly discussed in the source.

value.name: Usage and cost
value.description: Measured consumption supports usage billing and cost visibility; total cost still depends on usage and pricing.

value.name: Reliability and recovery
value.description: Redundancy, replication, backups, failover, and tested recovery can reduce failure impact but do not guarantee zero downtime or data loss.

value.name: Cloud security responsibility
value.description: Provider and consumer responsibilities vary by service model; identity, access, encryption, and compliance remain key concerns.

value.name: Architecture and interoperability
value.description: Cloud components communicate through APIs and web services; compatible interfaces can improve interoperability.

value.name: Provider lock-in and portability
value.description: Managed services reduce operational burden but may create provider-specific dependencies that increase migration effort.

value.name: Data jurisdiction
value.description: Global cloud deployments cross legal borders; region, data handling, contracts, and applicable law influence compliance.

value.name: History described by the source
value.description: The article traces utility-computing ideas to 1960, cloud terminology to the early 1990s, AWS access in 2002, and wider research/mainstream attention in 2007–2008.

value.difference: Service delivery versus distributed computation across loosely coupled machines.
value.why_it_matters: A cloud may use grid techniques, but the terms are not synonyms.

value.difference: Service abstraction versus measured consumption and billing.
value.why_it_matters: Usage billing alone does not define cloud computing.

value.difference: Service delivery versus systems capable of self-management.
value.why_it_matters: Automation can be a characteristic but is not the entire cloud model.

value.difference: Operating cloud systems versus selling enabling products or services.
value.why_it_matters: An organization can play both roles, but responsibilities differ.

value.difference: Infrastructure service versus platform/solution-stack service.
value.why_it_matters: The model changes which layers the consumer operates.

value.difference: Application deployment platform versus hosted application.
value.why_it_matters: Building on a platform differs from consuming finished software.

value.difference: Changing capacity versus consistent operation and failure handling.
value.why_it_matters: A scalable system can still experience outages.

value.difference: Historical examples versus a current market comparison.
value.why_it_matters: The source does not establish present-day market share or provider quality.

value.difference: Operational abstraction versus coupling to provider-specific APIs and behavior.
value.why_it_matters: Managed services trade operational work against migration flexibility.

value.difference: Physical/jurisdictional location versus legal authority and rules.
value.why_it_matters: Choosing a region does not alone resolve all legal duties.

value.difference: Protection of systems/data versus rules governing use, access, retention, and disclosure.
value.why_it_matters: Security controls do not answer every privacy question.

value.difference: Directly supported by the supplied article versus general explanatory context.
value.why_it_matters: Preserves provenance and prevents newer concepts being attributed to the source.

value.name: Cloud foundations
value.goal: Understand the service model and provider-consumer relationship.

value.name: Related computing models
value.goal: Separate service delivery, metered billing, distributed work, and self-management.

value.name: IaaS, PaaS, SaaS
value.goal: Compare service abstraction levels and consumer responsibilities.

value.name: Typical cloud dependencies
value.goal: Explore an illustrative modern application dependency chain.

value.name: Cloud cost and utilization
value.goal: Connect shared resources to usage measurement and cost control.

value.name: Reliability and recovery
value.goal: Understand common resilience mechanisms and their limits.

value.name: Security, privacy, and law
value.goal: Map controls to privacy, jurisdiction, and compliance.

value.name: Providers and dependencies
value.goal: Understand provider selection, managed services, and portability tradeoffs.

value.name: History in the supplied article
value.goal: Trace the source's historical account.

value.name: Standards and interfaces
value.goal: Review the protocols and standards named by the article.

value.name: Cloud operations
value.goal: Explore an expanded operational model.

value.name: Architecture and storage
value.goal: Connect architecture, APIs, and storage design.

value.misconception: Cloud computing is just another name for the Internet.
value.correction: The cloud is a metaphor; cloud computing describes services delivered using networks and managed systems.

value.misconception: Cloud computing and grid computing mean the same thing.
value.correction: Grid computing is distributed computation; cloud computing is a service-delivery model that may use distributed infrastructure.

value.misconception: Every cloud service is billed only by usage.
value.correction: The source says many services use utility billing while others use subscriptions.

value.misconception: Cloud computing eliminates all infrastructure costs and operations work.
value.correction: It shifts some ownership to providers, but consumers still manage workloads, access, configuration, costs, and data.

value.misconception: Cloud scalability means outages cannot happen.
value.correction: Scalability and reliability are different properties; cloud services can still fail.

value.misconception: Centralizing data always improves security.
value.correction: Centralization may provide specialist controls but also concentrates sensitive data and control.

value.misconception: The provider can never access customer data.
value.correction: The supplied article explicitly raises provider access, alteration, deletion, and disclosure concerns.

value.misconception: Provider names in the source represent today's leading-provider ranking.
value.correction: The source contains historical examples and is not a current market ranking.

value.misconception: Cloud deployment guarantees compliance everywhere.
value.correction: Cross-border services raise jurisdiction, residency, privacy, and legal questions.

value.misconception: Open standards guarantee complete portability.
value.correction: Open standards help interoperability, but provider-specific services and operations may still complicate migration.

value.misconception: Multi-cloud automatically reduces cost and complexity.
value.correction: Multi-cloud adds integration and operations work even when it offers choice.

value.misconception: A backup alone proves disaster recovery works.
value.correction: Recovery depends on backup integrity, retention, restoration procedures, and testing.

value.question: Define cloud computing.
value.answer: A model where storage, processing, platforms, or applications are delivered by an external or managed provider and accessed over a network.

value.question: What does the electricity analogy explain?
value.answer: Consumers use a utility without managing how it is produced and delivered.

value.question: How does grid computing differ?
value.answer: Grid computing distributes tasks across loosely coupled computers; cloud computing is a service-delivery model.

value.question: What is utility computing?
value.answer: Measured compute or storage resources billed according to use.

value.question: What is autonomic computing?
value.answer: Systems designed to manage themselves to some degree.

value.question: What is multitenancy?
value.answer: Multiple consumers share underlying resources while being logically separated.

value.question: How can multitenancy improve utilization?
value.answer: Shared resources can serve workloads that would otherwise leave capacity idle.

value.question: Why can cloud reduce peak-load overprovisioning?
value.answer: Consumers can obtain extra capacity from a provider rather than own capacity for every peak.

value.question: What is the difference between IaaS and PaaS?
value.answer: IaaS delivers infrastructure; PaaS delivers a platform/solution stack for deploying applications.

value.question: What does SaaS deliver?
value.answer: A hosted software application.

value.question: What role does virtualization play?
value.answer: It abstracts physical resources into logical environments that can be allocated as services.

value.question: What is an SLA?
value.answer: A service-level agreement specifying service-quality expectations or commitments.

value.question: Does an SLA mean perfect availability?
value.answer: No. Outages can still occur; an SLA defines commitments or remedies.

value.question: Name cloud storage categories from the source.
value.answer: Database-like services, NAS, synchronization, and web/object storage.

value.question: What does the source say about storage metadata?
value.answer: Metadata operations may be centralized while data nodes scale independently.

value.question: Why can bandwidth affect cloud performance?
value.answer: Cloud clients depend on network connectivity; insufficient bandwidth or high network load can degrade response.

value.question: What can redundant sites support?
value.answer: Reliability, business continuity, and disaster recovery.

value.question: What is one limit of redundancy?
value.answer: It does not guarantee uninterrupted service, and customers may have limited control during provider outages.

value.question: Why does cloud raise privacy concerns?
value.answer: Providers may access, alter, delete, or disclose hosted data under policies or legal processes.

value.question: What is data residency?
value.answer: The location where data is stored or processed.

value.question: What is data sovereignty?
value.answer: Legal authority and jurisdiction that apply to data and systems.

value.question: How does a provider differ from a vendor?
value.answer: A provider operates cloud systems; a vendor sells products or services enabling cloud delivery.

value.question: Which providers does the source name?
value.answer: Google, Amazon/AWS, Yahoo!, IBM, Intel, Microsoft, HP, and SAP, among others.

value.question: What does the article associate with AWS in 2002?
value.answer: Amazon opened access to its systems through AWS on a utility-computing basis after data-center modernization.

value.question: What idea does the source attribute to John McCarthy in 1960?
value.answer: That computation might someday be organized as a public utility.

value.question: Name some standards listed by the source.
value.answer: HTTP, XMPP, OAuth, OpenID, SSL/TLS, Atom, AJAX, HTML5 offline, OVF, LAMP, XML, JSON, and REST.

value.question: What was AGPL intended to address according to the source?
value.answer: A perceived loophole involving modified free software run over a network.

value.question: Why can managed services increase lock-in?
value.answer: Applications may depend on provider-specific APIs, data models, identity systems, or operational behavior.

value.question: What does a cloud dependency graph show?
value.answer: How an application depends on compute, networks, storage, identity, databases, queues, and observability.

value.question: Why are modern additions labeled synthesis?
value.answer: They provide general architecture context not explicitly stated in the supplied historical article.

misconceptions_and_corrections.misconception: Cloud computing is just another name for the Internet.
misconceptions_and_corrections.correction: The cloud is a metaphor; cloud computing describes services delivered using networks and managed systems.

misconceptions_and_corrections.misconception: Cloud computing and grid computing mean the same thing.
misconceptions_and_corrections.correction: Grid computing is distributed computation; cloud computing is a service-delivery model that may use distributed infrastructure.

misconceptions_and_corrections.misconception: Every cloud service is billed only by usage.
misconceptions_and_corrections.correction: The source says many services use utility billing while others use subscriptions.

misconceptions_and_corrections.misconception: Cloud computing eliminates all infrastructure costs and operations work.
misconceptions_and_corrections.correction: It shifts some ownership to providers, but consumers still manage workloads, access, configuration, costs, and data.

misconceptions_and_corrections.misconception: Cloud scalability means outages cannot happen.
misconceptions_and_corrections.correction: Scalability and reliability are different properties; cloud services can still fail.

misconceptions_and_corrections.misconception: Centralizing data always improves security.
misconceptions_and_corrections.correction: Centralization may provide specialist controls but also concentrates sensitive data and control.

misconceptions_and_corrections.misconception: The provider can never access customer data.
misconceptions_and_corrections.correction: The supplied article explicitly raises provider access, alteration, deletion, and disclosure concerns.

misconceptions_and_corrections.misconception: Provider names in the source represent today's leading-provider ranking.
misconceptions_and_corrections.correction: The source contains historical examples and is not a current market ranking.

misconceptions_and_corrections.misconception: Cloud deployment guarantees compliance everywhere.
misconceptions_and_corrections.correction: Cross-border services raise jurisdiction, residency, privacy, and legal questions.

misconceptions_and_corrections.misconception: Open standards guarantee complete portability.
misconceptions_and_corrections.correction: Open standards help interoperability, but provider-specific services and operations may still complicate migration.

misconceptions_and_corrections.misconception: Multi-cloud automatically reduces cost and complexity.
misconceptions_and_corrections.correction: Multi-cloud adds integration and operations work even when it offers choice.

misconceptions_and_corrections.misconception: A backup alone proves disaster recovery works.
misconceptions_and_corrections.correction: Recovery depends on backup integrity, retention, restoration procedures, and testing.

review_questions.question: Define cloud computing.
review_questions.answer: A model where storage, processing, platforms, or applications are delivered by an external or managed provider and accessed over a network.

review_questions.question: What does the electricity analogy explain?
review_questions.answer: Consumers use a utility without managing how it is produced and delivered.

review_questions.question: How does grid computing differ?
review_questions.answer: Grid computing distributes tasks across loosely coupled computers; cloud computing is a service-delivery model.

review_questions.question: What is utility computing?
review_questions.answer: Measured compute or storage resources billed according to use.

review_questions.question: What is autonomic computing?
review_questions.answer: Systems designed to manage themselves to some degree.

review_questions.question: What is multitenancy?
review_questions.answer: Multiple consumers share underlying resources while being logically separated.

review_questions.question: How can multitenancy improve utilization?
review_questions.answer: Shared resources can serve workloads that would otherwise leave capacity idle.

review_questions.question: Why can cloud reduce peak-load overprovisioning?
review_questions.answer: Consumers can obtain extra capacity from a provider rather than own capacity for every peak.

review_questions.question: What is the difference between IaaS and PaaS?
review_questions.answer: IaaS delivers infrastructure; PaaS delivers a platform/solution stack for deploying applications.

review_questions.question: What does SaaS deliver?
review_questions.answer: A hosted software application.

review_questions.question: What role does virtualization play?
review_questions.answer: It abstracts physical resources into logical environments that can be allocated as services.

review_questions.question: What is an SLA?
review_questions.answer: A service-level agreement specifying service-quality expectations or commitments.

review_questions.question: Does an SLA mean perfect availability?
review_questions.answer: No. Outages can still occur; an SLA defines commitments or remedies.

review_questions.question: Name cloud storage categories from the source.
review_questions.answer: Database-like services, NAS, synchronization, and web/object storage.

review_questions.question: What does the source say about storage metadata?
review_questions.answer: Metadata operations may be centralized while data nodes scale independently.

review_questions.question: Why can bandwidth affect cloud performance?
review_questions.answer: Cloud clients depend on network connectivity; insufficient bandwidth or high network load can degrade response.

review_questions.question: What can redundant sites support?
review_questions.answer: Reliability, business continuity, and disaster recovery.

review_questions.question: What is one limit of redundancy?
review_questions.answer: It does not guarantee uninterrupted service, and customers may have limited control during provider outages.

review_questions.question: Why does cloud raise privacy concerns?
review_questions.answer: Providers may access, alter, delete, or disclose hosted data under policies or legal processes.

review_questions.question: What is data residency?
review_questions.answer: The location where data is stored or processed.

review_questions.question: What is data sovereignty?
review_questions.answer: Legal authority and jurisdiction that apply to data and systems.

review_questions.question: How does a provider differ from a vendor?
review_questions.answer: A provider operates cloud systems; a vendor sells products or services enabling cloud delivery.

review_questions.question: Which providers does the source name?
review_questions.answer: Google, Amazon/AWS, Yahoo!, IBM, Intel, Microsoft, HP, and SAP, among others.

review_questions.question: What does the article associate with AWS in 2002?
review_questions.answer: Amazon opened access to its systems through AWS on a utility-computing basis after data-center modernization.

review_questions.question: What idea does the source attribute to John McCarthy in 1960?
review_questions.answer: That computation might someday be organized as a public utility.

review_questions.question: Name some standards listed by the source.
review_questions.answer: HTTP, XMPP, OAuth, OpenID, SSL/TLS, Atom, AJAX, HTML5 offline, OVF, LAMP, XML, JSON, and REST.

review_questions.question: What was AGPL intended to address according to the source?
review_questions.answer: A perceived loophole involving modified free software run over a network.

review_questions.question: Why can managed services increase lock-in?
review_questions.answer: Applications may depend on provider-specific APIs, data models, identity systems, or operational behavior.

review_questions.question: What does a cloud dependency graph show?
review_questions.answer: How an application depends on compute, networks, storage, identity, databases, queues, and observability.

review_questions.question: Why are modern additions labeled synthesis?
review_questions.answer: They provide general architecture context not explicitly stated in the supplied historical article.

value.title: C vs CUDA C/C++
value.description: C/C++ is the language base; CUDA adds GPU execution, memory and API extensions.

value.title: Host vs device
value.description: Host code runs on CPU; device kernels run on GPU.

value.title: Runtime API vs Driver API
value.description: Runtime is higher-level/single-source; Driver API is lower-level/non-single-source.

value.title: Grid vs block vs thread
value.description: Grid contains blocks; blocks contain threads; warps group 32 threads.

value.title: Shared vs global memory
value.description: Shared memory is block-shared/user-managed; global memory is device-wide.

value.title: PTX vs SASS
value.description: PTX is intermediate representation; SASS is hardware machine instruction representation.

value.title: CUDA vs ROCm
value.description: CUDA is proprietary NVIDIA software; ROCm is open-source AMD software.

value.title: CUDA vs oneAPI
value.description: CUDA is NVIDIA-specific; oneAPI targets multiple architectures through open specifications.

value.title: Uniform vs divergent warp control flow
value.description: Uniform branches preserve SIMD efficiency; divergence reduces it.

value.title: Computation vs transfer cost
value.description: Host/device transfers can limit end-to-end acceleration.

value.claim: CUDA is just C
value.correction: CUDA C/C++ adds GPU kernels, execution hierarchy, memory APIs and a CUDA compilation/runtime model.

value.claim: CUDA runs all code on the GPU
value.correction: Host code remains CPU-side while kernels execute on the GPU.

value.claim: A block is a GPU core
value.correction: A block is a logical group of threads scheduled onto streaming multiprocessors.

value.claim: A thread is a CUDA core
value.correction: Threads are logical execution contexts; hardware execution is organized through warps and SMs.

value.claim: PTX is final machine code
value.correction: PTX is an intermediate representation that is lowered toward GPU machine instructions.

value.claim: More threads always means faster
value.correction: Warp divergence, memory movement, architecture and occupancy constraints can dominate.

value.claim: Shared memory is VRAM
value.correction: Shared memory is a distinct fast user-managed region shared by block threads.

value.claim: CUDA runs natively on every GPU vendor
value.correction: CUDA is proprietary/NVIDIA-specific; compatibility and alternative stacks exist for other vendors.

value.name: Basic DHT put/get lifecycle

steps.action: Choose a logical object identifier such as a filename or content identifier.
Apply the system's hash/key derivation function to obtain key k.
Send put(k, data) to any participating DHT node.
Forward the message through the overlay toward the node responsible for k.
Store the key and value at the responsible node or configured replica set.
A reader derives the same key k and sends get(k) to any DHT node.
Route get(k) through the overlay and return the stored value or a result from a replica.

value.grounding: Based on the supplied article's 160-bit-key put/get walkthrough. Replication step is a general implementation option described elsewhere in the article.

value.name: Consistent-hashing membership change

steps.action: Assign each node an identifier in the abstract keyspace.
Assign each key to the closest node according to the algorithm's keyspace distance.
When a node joins or leaves, recompute affected ownership.
Transfer only keys whose responsible ownership changed, while other key assignments remain unchanged.

value.grounding: Based on the supplied article's description of consistent and rendezvous hashing.

value.name: Kademlia-style iterative lookup and publication

steps.action: Publish or discover node-presence information in the DHT.
Start a lookup for key k and consult known routing-table neighbors.
Query closer/suitable nodes iteratively instead of flooding every participant.
Select suitable nodes for storing or retrieving the value.
Send put(k, data) to those suitable nodes; use implementation-specific repair/self-healing when placement is stale.

value.grounding: Based on the supplied article's description of advanced DHTs such as Kademlia.

value.name: DHT Sybil threat and defense concepts

steps.action: An adversary attempts to participate under many identities.
Those identities may influence routing, key ownership, or availability depending on the DHT design.
Possible defenses discussed by the article include carefully designed Byzantine fault tolerance, Whanau-style design, and social-trust approaches.
Treat defenses as design-specific; the article describes the general Sybil-defense problem as an open research question.

value.grounding: Based on the supplied article's security section; this is an explanatory threat model, not a claim that every DHT is vulnerable in the same way.

Systems named by the article among overlay networks; this grouping is a taxonomy aid and does not imply identical designs or guarantees.

value.benefit: Can identify and route to destinations independently of their currently known IP address.
value.cost_or_limit: Requires overlay-level naming, lookup, or routing mechanisms.

value.benefit: Can select overlay-node sequence and apply application/site/user-specific policies.
value.cost_or_limit: Cannot directly control the underlay's route between two overlay nodes.

value.benefit: Can detect path degradation and reroute at the overlay layer.
value.cost_or_limit: Still depends on lower-layer availability and may choose a longer path.

value.benefit: Can provide logical isolation and optionally encryption.
value.cost_or_limit: An overlay by itself does not guarantee confidentiality, authentication, or secure endpoint behavior.

value.benefit: Enables logical networks and tunnels over shared infrastructure.
value.cost_or_limit: Additional headers consume capacity and can affect MTU/fragmentation behavior (MTU note is model-expanded).

value.benefit: Can prioritize traffic by application, user, or site.
value.cost_or_limit: DiffServ prioritization does not itself guarantee end-to-end throughput.

value.benefit: Can distribute data among peers without relying on router-level IP multicast.
value.cost_or_limit: Requires maintaining an overlay topology and may create redundant transmissions.

value.core_problem: Package and execute applications consistently across differing computing environments while isolating processes, controlling resources, distributing images, coordinating multi-container applications, and supporting clustered container services.
value.central_model: Application + dependencies -> Dockerfile/build -> read-only image -> registry distribution -> container runtime -> isolated processes + shared kernel -> Compose/Swarm coordination -> persistent volumes where required.
value.central_insight: Docker is best understood as a connected packaging, runtime, distribution and orchestration ecosystem: images define reusable software artifacts, containers instantiate them, the Linux kernel supplies isolation/resource primitives, registries distribute artifacts, Compose coordinates applications, and Swarm clusters Docker Engines.

source_claims.claim: Docker packages software in lightweight containers using OS-level virtualization and automates deployment across environments.
Docker originated as a dotCloud internal project, debuted publicly in 2013, used LXC initially, then moved to libcontainer and later created Moby.
Docker adoption expanded through Red Hat, Microsoft, AWS, IBM, Oracle, Windows/WSL2, Docker Desktop licensing, AtomicJar, and major 2025 releases.
Docker uses Linux kernel interfaces, namespaces, cgroups and union-capable filesystems; macOS uses a Linux VM.
Docker software architecture includes dockerd, Docker CLI, Docker objects, registries and Dockerfiles.
Dockerfile example uses ARG, FROM, COPY, ENV, RUN, VOLUME and EXPOSE.
Docker Compose defines/runs multi-container applications and Docker Swarm provides clustering and Raft consensus.
Docker Volumes provide independent persistence and licensing differs between Docker Engine and Docker Desktop.
Related technologies include Linux, DevOps, gVisor, Kubernetes, microservices, OCI and related software architecture.

value.name: Firewall decision
value.expression: traffic + rule criteria → action
value.meaning: Traffic is evaluated against security rules to produce an action.

value.name: Packet filtering
value.expression: packet → ACL → {discard, reset/ICMP, forward}
value.meaning: Packet filter decision path.

value.name: Connection tracking
value.expression: endpoint conversation → IP/port state → inspection
value.meaning: Second-generation firewall remembers conversations.

value.name: Application filtering
value.expression: traffic → application protocol understanding → decision
value.meaning: Application firewalls understand FTP/DNS/HTTP and detect protocol misuse.

value.name: NGFW inspection
value.expression: deep packet inspection → expanded L7 inspection/features
value.meaning: Next-generation firewall expands inspection.

value.name: Endpoint process filtering
value.expression: connection → socket call → process ID → local rule
value.meaning: Endpoint firewall associates traffic with local processes.

value.name: Zone policy
value.expression: zone + trust level + ingress/egress → rules → action
value.meaning: Zones establish logical security-policy boundaries.

value.name: Service control
value.expression: service = port + protocol → access policy
value.meaning: Services are identified and controlled using network ports/protocols.

value.name: User-ID policy
value.expression: login/auth logs → user↔IP mapping → user group → rule → action
value.meaning: Identity-aware policy maps authenticated users to network traffic.

value.name: Default zone policy
value.expression: LAN→WAN = allow; WAN→LAN = drop
value.meaning: Typical defaults stated by the source.

value.name: Firewall deployment taxonomy
value.expression: network-based | host-based; software | hardware | virtual
value.meaning: Placement and implementation taxonomy.

value.name: Firewall evolution
value.expression: packet filter → stateful → application → NGFW
value.meaning: Historical progression represented by the source.

value.name: PIX/NAT
value.expression: private network + limited registered IPv4 → PIX/NAT → Internet
value.meaning: PIX connected private networks using limited registered addresses.

value.name: Configuration risk
value.expression: configuration error → security issue
value.meaning: Misconfiguration can create security issues.

value.distinction: Stateful filtering adds conversation knowledge to packet filtering.
Stateful filtering tracks conversations; application filtering understands protocols.
NGFW broadens application/deep inspection with additional features.
Network firewall sits between networks; host firewall runs on a host.
Different implementation substrates.
Virtual appliance runs on a virtual host controlled by a hypervisor.
Policy is a collection of rules; a rule is an individual decision specification.
Zone is a logical security grouping, not necessarily a physical network.
Service is port/protocol-oriented; application is software/L7-oriented.
IP identifies network addressing; User ID identifies an individual identity.
Both are listed as refusal/discard actions but remain separate labels in the source.
PIX combines both, but they are separate mechanisms.
Ingress enters; egress leaves.
Relative trust distinction across a firewall boundary.
Configuration defines controls; enforcement applies them.

value.misconception: A firewall is only a packet filter.
value.correction: The source includes stateful, application, endpoint, and next-generation firewall mechanisms.

value.misconception: A firewall must use dedicated hardware.
value.correction: The source includes software appliances on general-purpose hardware and virtual appliances.

value.misconception: Network-based and host-based firewalls have the same placement.
value.correction: Network-based firewalls sit between networks; host-based firewalls run directly on hosts.

value.misconception: Application firewalls only inspect port numbers.
value.correction: They can understand application protocols and detect non-standard ports/protocol abuse.

value.misconception: User ID is simply an IP address.
value.correction: User ID adds identity-based policy and is mapped to network activity.

value.misconception: A firewall zone is necessarily a physical network.
value.correction: The source defines zones as logical segments grouped by security requirements.

value.misconception: LAN-to-WAN and WAN-to-LAN have the same default.
value.correction: The source gives allow LAN→WAN and drop WAN→LAN as typical defaults.

value.misconception: Firewall configuration is trivial.
value.correction: The source describes configuration as complex and error-prone.

value.misconception: NGFW and NAT are the same thing.
value.correction: PIX combined firewall and NAT; NGFW is an inspection/security evolution.

value.misconception: Firewall rules use only IP addresses.
value.correction: Rules may use direction, source, destination, port, protocol, applications, and action.

value.name: Compilation pipeline
value.formula: Go source → compiler → linker → native binary → CPU/OS
value.mechanism: Compiler and linker produce statically linked native artifacts containing the Go runtime.

value.name: Package/dependency model
value.formula: module → package path → import → exported API → dependency graph
value.mechanism: Packages are identified by paths; modules and go mod manage dependencies.

value.name: Interface satisfaction
value.formula: T + required methods(I) → T satisfies I
value.mechanism: No implements declaration is needed; method sets determine satisfaction.

value.name: Generic instantiation
value.formula: generic definition + type arguments/inference → instantiated code
value.mechanism: Type parameters, constraints and compiler instantiation provide generic code.

value.name: Goroutine scheduling
value.formula: goroutines → runtime scheduler → OS threads → CPUs
value.mechanism: Runtime multiplexes lightweight goroutines over fewer OS threads.

value.name: Channel communication
value.formula: goroutine A → typed channel → goroutine B
value.mechanism: Typed send/receive and select coordinate concurrent execution.

value.name: Concurrency memory model
value.mechanism: Unsynchronized sharing may race; synchronization is required for safe concurrent access.

value.name: Error-value model
value.mechanism: Multiple returns make explicit error handling the normal package-boundary mechanism.

value.name: HTTP application model
value.mechanism: Standard library provides handlers and server startup.

value.name: Testing workflow
value.mechanism: testing package integrates automated verification.

value.name: Integrated development workflow
value.formula: source → gofmt → build → test → vet → doc/generate → deploy
value.mechanism: Go distribution integrates common software-engineering tasks.

value.name: Go infrastructure ecosystem
value.mechanism: Named major applications demonstrate Go infrastructure reach.

value.misconception: Interfaces require implements declarations.

value.misconception: Go interfaces are dynamic duck typing.

value.misconception: Slice is just a dynamic array.

value.misconception: Go has C-style pointer arithmetic.

value.misconception: Go normally uses exceptions.

value.misconception: Go always had generics.

value.source_fidelity: The uploaded source is authoritative for source-derived content. Expansion targets identify subjects not fully explained by the source rather than silently importing facts.
value.relationship_policy: Directional relationships preserve mechanism, semantic role, and source provenance where supported.

value.name: Request-response model
value.expression: client -> request -> server -> response -> client
value.meaning: Core HTTP transaction flow.

value.name: Resource addressing model
value.expression: URI/URL -> resource -> representation
value.meaning: Resources are identified through URI/URL and represented in messages.

value.name: HTTP/1.1 message model
value.expression: start-line + header-fields + CRLF delimiter + optional body
value.meaning: HTTP/1.1 message structure described in the source.

value.name: HTTP/2 multiplexing model
value.expression: one TCP/IP connection -> multiple bidirectional streams -> concurrent requests/responses
value.meaning: HTTP/2 shares a connection across streams.

value.name: HTTP/3 transport model
value.expression: HTTP/3 -> QUIC -> UDP -> IP
value.meaning: HTTP/3 replaces TCP transport with QUIC over UDP.

value.name: Caching model
value.expression: request -> cache lookup -> reuse or conditional retrieval -> response
value.meaning: Caches and conditional requests reduce repeated network transfer.

value.name: HTTP authentication model
value.expression: server challenge -> client credentials -> access decision
value.meaning: Basic/Digest authentication use challenge-response.

value.name: Status classification model
value.expression: status_code first digit -> 1xx/2xx/3xx/4xx/5xx
value.meaning: Response disposition is classified by status-code class.

value.name: Method semantics model
value.expression: method -> intended action + safety + idempotence + cacheability
value.meaning: HTTP methods have defined semantic properties.

value.name: Persistent connection model
value.expression: one TCP connection -> multiple HTTP requests/responses
value.meaning: HTTP/1.1 keep-alive reduces repeated TCP setup.

value.name: Range retrieval model
value.expression: resource -> byte range -> partial response
value.meaning: Byte serving retrieves selected portions and can resume interrupted downloads.

value.name: Application session model
value.expression: stateless HTTP + cookie/hidden variable/etc. -> application session
value.meaning: Sessions are implemented above HTTP's stateless protocol semantics.

value.difference: HTTPS is the secure variant of HTTP.
HTTP/1.1 supports reusable persistent connections; HTTP/1.0 normally closed after response.
HTTP/2 uses binary framing and multiplexed streams rather than HTTP/1.1's textual message exchange.
HTTP/2 uses TCP; HTTP/3 uses QUIC over UDP.
Hop-by-hop headers can be managed by intermediaries; end-to-end headers are managed only by endpoints.
Safe means no intended server-state effect; idempotent means repeated identical requests have the same intended effect.
Cacheability is whether responses may be stored; it is distinct from safety.
GET retrieves a representation and is safe/cacheable; POST processes a resource and is not safe/idempotent by definition.
PUT supplies state for create/update at client-specified target; PATCH applies partial state.
HTTP authentication belongs to protocol access control; application login/session is application-level.
A resource is the target concept; a representation is the data form returned for it.
Header names are case-insensitive; method names are case-sensitive.
Status codes are machine-readable; reason phrases are human-readable recommendations.
Persistent reuse keeps a connection open; pipelining sends multiple requests before responses and had interoperability problems.
Chunked transfer supports unknown-length streaming; Content-Length explicitly states known length.
Byte ranges retrieve only selected portions.
TCP is the traditional reliable transport; QUIC provides reliability over UDP for HTTP/3.
HTTP/0.9 was extremely minimal, with only GET and HTML responses.
SPDY was an alternative Google protocol whose ideas influenced HTTP/2.
The source describes HTTP as displacing Gopher for content delivery in the early 1990s.

value.misconception: HTTP itself is TCP.
value.correction: HTTP is an application protocol; TCP is a traditional underlying transport, while HTTP/3 uses QUIC over UDP.

value.misconception: HTTP/3 is just HTTP/2 with a different version number.
value.correction: HTTP/3 changes the transport model to QUIC over UDP.

value.misconception: HTTP is stateful because websites have logins.
value.correction: HTTP itself is stateless; application sessions add state above HTTP.

value.misconception: Safe means idempotent and idempotent means safe.
value.correction: They overlap for several methods but describe different semantic properties.

value.misconception: GET can never cause side effects.
value.correction: The source says implementations can misuse GET; safe describes intended semantics, not technical enforcement.

value.misconception: POST is idempotent.
value.correction: The source explicitly says POST is not necessarily idempotent.

value.misconception: All HTTP methods are cacheable.
value.correction: The source defines only GET, HEAD and POST as cacheable.

value.misconception: HTTP/1.1 always opens a new TCP connection for every resource.
value.correction: HTTP/1.1 can reuse persistent connections.

value.misconception: HTTP/2 sends multiple independent TCP connections for every request.
value.correction: The source describes multiplexed streams over a shared TCP/IP connection.

value.misconception: HTTP/3 uses TCP underneath QUIC.
value.correction: QUIC runs over UDP.

value.misconception: Header field names and method names use the same case rules.
value.correction: Methods are case-sensitive; header field names are case-insensitive.

value.misconception: A response body is always present.
value.correction: The body is optional.

value.misconception: A resource is always a static file.
value.correction: The source says resources may be files or dynamically generated/executable output.

value.misconception: Authentication and application login are the same HTTP mechanism.
value.correction: The source distinguishes HTTP authentication from application-session login.

value.misconception: HTTP/0.9 supported POST and arbitrary content formats.
value.correction: The source says HTTP/0.9 supported only GET and returned HTML pages.

value.misconception: HTTP/2 made HTTP/1.1 obsolete.
value.correction: The source describes HTTP/2 as an evolution while HTTP/1.1 remains a standard version.

value.misconception: HTTPS is a different application protocol unrelated to HTTP.
value.correction: HTTPS is described as the secure variant of HTTP.

value.misconception: Byte-range serving always downloads the whole resource.
value.correction: It retrieves selected portions and can resume interrupted downloads.

value.misconception: Chunked transfer requires Content-Length.
value.correction: Chunked transfer is specifically useful when length is not known in advance.

value.misconception: Status reason phrases are the machine-readable part of responses.
value.correction: Status codes are machine-readable; reason phrases are human-readable.

source_claims.statement: HTTP is an application-layer protocol in the Internet protocol suite for distributed, collaborative hypermedia information systems.
HTTP is foundational to World Wide Web data communication.
HTTP uses request-response in the client-server model.
Browsers, crawlers, voice browsers, mobile apps and other software can act as user agents.
HTTP supports intermediate caches and proxies; some headers are hop-by-hop and others end-to-end.
Web resources are located through URL/URI schemes http and https.
HTTP/0.9, 1.0, 1.1, 2 and 3 are the versions listed with their introduction years/statuses.
HTTP/1.0 used a separate TCP connection per resource; HTTP/1.1 introduced reusable persistent connections.
HTTP/2 adds binary header representation, multiplexed streams, and server push.
HTTP/3 uses QUIC over UDP rather than TCP.
HTTP data exchange uses reliable transport; TCP is the pre-HTTP/3 standard choice.
HTTP/1.1 messages have start line, header fields, blank line, and optional body.
HTTP methods classify requested actions and have safety, idempotence, and cacheability properties.
GET is intended to retrieve without modifying server state, while other methods can modify state.
Safe methods are GET, HEAD, OPTIONS, TRACE and QUERY in the supplied source.
Idempotent methods include PUT, DELETE and safe methods; POST, CONNECT and PATCH are not necessarily idempotent.
GET, HEAD and POST are defined as cacheable in the source table.
HTTP response status codes are three-digit classes 1xx through 5xx.
HTTP is stateless; application sessions can be implemented with cookies, hidden variables or other mechanisms.
HTTP provides Basic and Digest authentication through challenge-response.
HTTPS is the popular encrypted form of HTTP.
HTTP/1.1 message headers use ASCII lines terminated by CRLF.
HTTP/1.1 supports conditional retrieval, chunked transfer and byte-range serving.
Tim Berners-Lee and CERN are credited with HTTP's invention/development.
HTTP/0.9 supported only GET and returned HTML pages.
SPDY influenced HTTP/2 and was developed by Google.
HTTP/2 was published in 2015 and HTTP/3 was standardized in 2022.
RFC 9110/9111/9112/9113/9114 are the current semantic/caching/version documents listed by the source.

semantic_distinctions.difference: HTTPS is the secure variant of HTTP.
HTTP/1.1 supports reusable persistent connections; HTTP/1.0 normally closed after response.
HTTP/2 uses binary framing and multiplexed streams rather than HTTP/1.1's textual message exchange.
HTTP/2 uses TCP; HTTP/3 uses QUIC over UDP.
Hop-by-hop headers can be managed by intermediaries; end-to-end headers are managed only by endpoints.
Safe means no intended server-state effect; idempotent means repeated identical requests have the same intended effect.
Cacheability is whether responses may be stored; it is distinct from safety.
GET retrieves a representation and is safe/cacheable; POST processes a resource and is not safe/idempotent by definition.
PUT supplies state for create/update at client-specified target; PATCH applies partial state.
HTTP authentication belongs to protocol access control; application login/session is application-level.
A resource is the target concept; a representation is the data form returned for it.
Header names are case-insensitive; method names are case-sensitive.
Status codes are machine-readable; reason phrases are human-readable recommendations.
Persistent reuse keeps a connection open; pipelining sends multiple requests before responses and had interoperability problems.
Chunked transfer supports unknown-length streaming; Content-Length explicitly states known length.
Byte ranges retrieve only selected portions.
TCP is the traditional reliable transport; QUIC provides reliability over UDP for HTTP/3.
HTTP/0.9 was extremely minimal, with only GET and HTML responses.
SPDY was an alternative Google protocol whose ideas influenced HTTP/2.
The source describes HTTP as displacing Gopher for content delivery in the early 1990s.

misconceptions.misconception: HTTP itself is TCP.
misconceptions.correction: HTTP is an application protocol; TCP is a traditional underlying transport, while HTTP/3 uses QUIC over UDP.

misconceptions.misconception: HTTP/3 is just HTTP/2 with a different version number.
misconceptions.correction: HTTP/3 changes the transport model to QUIC over UDP.

misconceptions.misconception: HTTP is stateful because websites have logins.
misconceptions.correction: HTTP itself is stateless; application sessions add state above HTTP.

misconceptions.misconception: Safe means idempotent and idempotent means safe.
misconceptions.correction: They overlap for several methods but describe different semantic properties.

misconceptions.misconception: GET can never cause side effects.
misconceptions.correction: The source says implementations can misuse GET; safe describes intended semantics, not technical enforcement.

misconceptions.misconception: POST is idempotent.
misconceptions.correction: The source explicitly says POST is not necessarily idempotent.

misconceptions.misconception: All HTTP methods are cacheable.
misconceptions.correction: The source defines only GET, HEAD and POST as cacheable.

misconceptions.misconception: HTTP/1.1 always opens a new TCP connection for every resource.
misconceptions.correction: HTTP/1.1 can reuse persistent connections.

misconceptions.misconception: HTTP/2 sends multiple independent TCP connections for every request.
misconceptions.correction: The source describes multiplexed streams over a shared TCP/IP connection.

misconceptions.misconception: HTTP/3 uses TCP underneath QUIC.
misconceptions.correction: QUIC runs over UDP.

misconceptions.misconception: Header field names and method names use the same case rules.
misconceptions.correction: Methods are case-sensitive; header field names are case-insensitive.

misconceptions.misconception: A response body is always present.
misconceptions.correction: The body is optional.

misconceptions.misconception: A resource is always a static file.
misconceptions.correction: The source says resources may be files or dynamically generated/executable output.

misconceptions.misconception: Authentication and application login are the same HTTP mechanism.
misconceptions.correction: The source distinguishes HTTP authentication from application-session login.

misconceptions.misconception: HTTP/0.9 supported POST and arbitrary content formats.
misconceptions.correction: The source says HTTP/0.9 supported only GET and returned HTML pages.

misconceptions.misconception: HTTP/2 made HTTP/1.1 obsolete.
misconceptions.correction: The source describes HTTP/2 as an evolution while HTTP/1.1 remains a standard version.

misconceptions.misconception: HTTPS is a different application protocol unrelated to HTTP.
misconceptions.correction: HTTPS is described as the secure variant of HTTP.

misconceptions.misconception: Byte-range serving always downloads the whole resource.
misconceptions.correction: It retrieves selected portions and can resume interrupted downloads.

misconceptions.misconception: Chunked transfer requires Content-Length.
misconceptions.correction: Chunked transfer is specifically useful when length is not known in advance.

misconceptions.misconception: Status reason phrases are the machine-readable part of responses.
misconceptions.correction: Status codes are machine-readable; reason phrases are human-readable.

value.label: No IPv6 broadcast
value.description: IPv6 has no broadcast address; all-nodes multicast is used for the analogous attached-link function.

value.label: IPv6 vs IPv4
value.description: IPv6 uses 128-bit addresses and a different packet/header model; IPv4 uses 32-bit addresses and its own packet format.

value.label: Unicast vs anycast vs multicast
value.description: IPv6 defines all three transmission/addressing modes with different destination semantics.

value.label: Multicast vs broadcast
value.description: IPv6 has no broadcast; all-nodes multicast supplies the analogous attached-link all-host function.

value.label: SLAAC vs DHCPv6
value.description: SLAAC is stateless host/router-based prefix configuration; DHCPv6 can supply additional stateful addresses or information.

value.label: Link-local vs global unicast
value.description: Link-local addresses are local-link and required on IPv6 interfaces; global unicast addresses are globally routable.

value.label: Base header vs extension headers
value.description: The base header is fixed at 40 octets; optional functions are moved to extension headers.

value.label: Router fragmentation vs endpoint fragmentation
value.description: IPv6 routers do not fragment; endpoints can fragment and hosts can use PMTU discovery.

value.label: IPv6 no header checksum vs IPv4 checksum
value.description: IPv6 omits the base-header checksum, unlike IPv4, reducing router recalculation work.

value.label: Dual-stack vs tunneling
value.description: Dual-stack runs both stacks natively; tunneling encapsulates one protocol within another network.

value.label: IPv4-mapped vs IPv4-compatible
value.description: IPv4-mapped addresses remain a hybrid representation; IPv4-compatible addresses are deprecated.

value.label: Stable vs temporary addresses
value.description: Stable/global identifiers support reachability but can facilitate tracking; temporary addresses reduce persistence.

value.label: AAAA vs A DNS records
value.description: AAAA resolves IPv6; A resolves IPv4.

value.label: PMTU discovery vs fragmentation
value.description: PMTU discovery sizes packets for the path; fragmentation is endpoint-only when needed.

value.label: IPsec vs higher-layer security
value.description: The source discusses IPsec at the IP layer but does not equate it with TLS; both occupy different architectural positions.

value.label: Native vs tunneled IPv6
value.description: Native IPv6 traverses IPv6-capable infrastructure; tunneling carries IPv6 over IPv4 infrastructure.

value.title: IPv6 is just IPv4 with bigger addresses
value.correction: IPv6 changes packet format, address architecture, fragmentation behavior, neighbor discovery, multicast/broadcast semantics and other protocol functions.

value.title: IPv6 supports broadcast
value.correction: IPv6 does not define traditional broadcast addresses; multicast is used instead.

value.title: Routers fragment IPv6 packets
value.correction: IPv6 routers do not fragment; hosts use PMTU discovery or endpoint fragmentation.

value.title: IPv6 addresses always need DHCP
value.correction: IPv6 supports SLAAC and hosts generate link-local addresses automatically; DHCPv6 is optional for additional state.

value.title: Every IPv6 address is globally routable
value.correction: IPv6 interfaces require link-local addressing and may have multiple address types; global unicast is only one category.

value.title: IPv6 cannot be scanned
value.correction: The source explicitly notes that configuration patterns can make scanning feasible in real-world scenarios.

value.title: IPv6 has a header checksum like IPv4
value.correction: IPv6 omits the base-header checksum.

value.title: IPv6 and IPv4 interoperate directly
value.correction: The source states the protocols are not directly interoperable and require transition mechanisms.

value.title: IPv6 extension headers are always harmless to routers
value.correction: Some implementations process extension headers in software/CPU paths, causing performance or security issues.

value.title: Global IPv6 addressing eliminates privacy concerns
value.correction: Stable globally addressable identifiers can facilitate tracking; temporary addresses mitigate this concern.

value.title: Tunneling is equivalent to native IPv6
value.correction: Tunneling adds encapsulation and can reduce MTU/increase latency.

value.title: NDP is just ARP with a new address format
value.correction: NDP uses ICMPv6 and multicast and also handles router discovery and address configuration.

value.title: AAAA records are IPv4 DNS records
value.correction: AAAA records map names to IPv6 addresses; A records map names to IPv4.

value.title: IPv6 deployment means IPv4 disappears immediately
value.correction: The source describes coexistence and transition mechanisms because both protocols operate simultaneously.

value.title: IPv6 security is automatically stronger because of the larger address space
value.correction: The source identifies implementation and operational security risks, including shadow networks and fragmentation evasion.
