source_claims.title: IPv6 purpose and origin
source_claims.claim: IPv6 was developed to address anticipated IPv4 address exhaustion and provide a successor IP protocol.

source_claims.title: 128-bit addressing
source_claims.claim: IPv6 uses 128-bit addresses and an address space of 2^128.

source_claims.title: Address architecture
source_claims.claim: IPv6 uses hierarchical addressing, generally with a 64-bit routing prefix and 64-bit interface identifier.

source_claims.title: Transmission modes
source_claims.claim: IPv6 supports unicast, anycast and multicast and omits broadcast.

source_claims.title: Autoconfiguration
source_claims.claim: IPv6 hosts create link-local addresses and can configure global addresses using router advertisements and SLAAC.

source_claims.title: Neighbor discovery
source_claims.claim: NDP replaces the IPv4 ARP role using ICMPv6 and multicast.

source_claims.title: Packet structure
source_claims.claim: IPv6 packets have a 40-octet base header plus optional extension headers and payload.

source_claims.title: Router fragmentation
source_claims.claim: IPv6 routers do not fragment; hosts use PMTU discovery or endpoint fragmentation.

source_claims.title: DNS integration
source_claims.claim: AAAA records provide IPv6 DNS resolution and ip6.arpa supports reverse resolution.

source_claims.title: Transition
source_claims.claim: Dual-stack and tunneling allow IPv4/IPv6 coexistence; NAT64 provides translation mechanisms.

source_claims.title: Security
source_claims.claim: IPv6 security includes IPsec support but also shadow-network and fragmentation-evasion risks.

source_claims.title: Standardization
source_claims.claim: IPv6 evolved from IPng through RFC 1883, RFC 2460 and RFC 8200.

source_claims.title: Deployment
source_claims.claim: IPv6 deployment has expanded through ISPs, operating systems, mobile networks and Internet services, with the source citing 2026 adoption measurements.

semantic_distinctions.label: No IPv6 broadcast
semantic_distinctions.description: IPv6 has no broadcast address; all-nodes multicast is used for the analogous attached-link function.

semantic_distinctions.label: IPv6 vs IPv4
semantic_distinctions.description: IPv6 uses 128-bit addresses and a different packet/header model; IPv4 uses 32-bit addresses and its own packet format.

semantic_distinctions.label: Unicast vs anycast vs multicast
semantic_distinctions.description: IPv6 defines all three transmission/addressing modes with different destination semantics.

semantic_distinctions.label: Multicast vs broadcast
semantic_distinctions.description: IPv6 has no broadcast; all-nodes multicast supplies the analogous attached-link all-host function.

semantic_distinctions.label: SLAAC vs DHCPv6
semantic_distinctions.description: SLAAC is stateless host/router-based prefix configuration; DHCPv6 can supply additional stateful addresses or information.

semantic_distinctions.label: Link-local vs global unicast
semantic_distinctions.description: Link-local addresses are local-link and required on IPv6 interfaces; global unicast addresses are globally routable.

semantic_distinctions.label: Base header vs extension headers
semantic_distinctions.description: The base header is fixed at 40 octets; optional functions are moved to extension headers.

semantic_distinctions.label: Router fragmentation vs endpoint fragmentation
semantic_distinctions.description: IPv6 routers do not fragment; endpoints can fragment and hosts can use PMTU discovery.

semantic_distinctions.label: IPv6 no header checksum vs IPv4 checksum
semantic_distinctions.description: IPv6 omits the base-header checksum, unlike IPv4, reducing router recalculation work.

semantic_distinctions.label: Dual-stack vs tunneling
semantic_distinctions.description: Dual-stack runs both stacks natively; tunneling encapsulates one protocol within another network.

semantic_distinctions.label: IPv4-mapped vs IPv4-compatible
semantic_distinctions.description: IPv4-mapped addresses remain a hybrid representation; IPv4-compatible addresses are deprecated.

semantic_distinctions.label: Stable vs temporary addresses
semantic_distinctions.description: Stable/global identifiers support reachability but can facilitate tracking; temporary addresses reduce persistence.

semantic_distinctions.label: AAAA vs A DNS records
semantic_distinctions.description: AAAA resolves IPv6; A resolves IPv4.

semantic_distinctions.label: PMTU discovery vs fragmentation
semantic_distinctions.description: PMTU discovery sizes packets for the path; fragmentation is endpoint-only when needed.

semantic_distinctions.label: IPsec vs higher-layer security
semantic_distinctions.description: The source discusses IPsec at the IP layer but does not equate it with TLS; both occupy different architectural positions.

semantic_distinctions.label: Native vs tunneled IPv6
semantic_distinctions.description: Native IPv6 traverses IPv6-capable infrastructure; tunneling carries IPv6 over IPv4 infrastructure.

misconceptions.title: IPv6 is just IPv4 with bigger addresses
misconceptions.correction: IPv6 changes packet format, address architecture, fragmentation behavior, neighbor discovery, multicast/broadcast semantics and other protocol functions.

misconceptions.title: IPv6 supports broadcast
misconceptions.correction: IPv6 does not define traditional broadcast addresses; multicast is used instead.

misconceptions.title: Routers fragment IPv6 packets
misconceptions.correction: IPv6 routers do not fragment; hosts use PMTU discovery or endpoint fragmentation.

misconceptions.title: IPv6 addresses always need DHCP
misconceptions.correction: IPv6 supports SLAAC and hosts generate link-local addresses automatically; DHCPv6 is optional for additional state.

misconceptions.title: Every IPv6 address is globally routable
misconceptions.correction: IPv6 interfaces require link-local addressing and may have multiple address types; global unicast is only one category.

misconceptions.title: IPv6 cannot be scanned
misconceptions.correction: The source explicitly notes that configuration patterns can make scanning feasible in real-world scenarios.

misconceptions.title: IPv6 has a header checksum like IPv4
misconceptions.correction: IPv6 omits the base-header checksum.

misconceptions.title: IPv6 and IPv4 interoperate directly
misconceptions.correction: The source states the protocols are not directly interoperable and require transition mechanisms.

misconceptions.title: IPv6 extension headers are always harmless to routers
misconceptions.correction: Some implementations process extension headers in software/CPU paths, causing performance or security issues.

misconceptions.title: Global IPv6 addressing eliminates privacy concerns
misconceptions.correction: Stable globally addressable identifiers can facilitate tracking; temporary addresses mitigate this concern.

misconceptions.title: Tunneling is equivalent to native IPv6
misconceptions.correction: Tunneling adds encapsulation and can reduce MTU/increase latency.

misconceptions.title: NDP is just ARP with a new address format
misconceptions.correction: NDP uses ICMPv6 and multicast and also handles router discovery and address configuration.

misconceptions.title: AAAA records are IPv4 DNS records
misconceptions.correction: AAAA records map names to IPv6 addresses; A records map names to IPv4.

misconceptions.title: IPv6 deployment means IPv4 disappears immediately
misconceptions.correction: The source describes coexistence and transition mechanisms because both protocols operate simultaneously.

misconceptions.title: IPv6 security is automatically stronger because of the larger address space
misconceptions.correction: The source identifies implementation and operational security risks, including shadow networks and fragmentation evasion.

value.misconception: IP guarantees packets arrive exactly once and in order.
value.correction: IP is best-effort and connectionless; loss, duplication, corruption and reordering are possible.

value.misconception: IP and TCP are the same protocol.
value.correction: IP is network layer; TCP is transport layer and connection-oriented.

value.misconception: An IP datagram and Ethernet frame are the same unit.
value.correction: The IP datagram is encapsulated inside a link-layer frame.

value.misconception: Routers always notify endpoints when they discard packets.
value.correction: ICMP may report errors, but router notification is not required for every error.

value.misconception: IPv6 routers fragment packets like IPv4 routers.
value.correction: IPv6 network elements do not fragment; endpoints must respect Path MTU.

value.misconception: IPv6 has the same IP header checksum as IPv4.
value.correction: IPv4 has a header checksum; IPv6 omits it under the source-stated assumption.

value.misconception: If a packet fits the local MTU, it fits the whole path.
value.correction: Path MTU can be smaller because another link may impose a tighter limit.

value.misconception: Multicast and broadcast both reach every node.
value.correction: Broadcast reaches all nodes in scope; multicast reaches a selected group.

value.misconception: Anycast always chooses the geographically closest machine.
value.correction: The source describes a distance or cost measure, not necessarily geography.

value.misconception: IPv5 was the deployed successor to IPv4.
value.correction: Version 5 was used by experimental Internet Stream Protocol.

value.misconception: Every IP version number is a deployed standard.
value.correction: The version list includes experimental, obsolete, reserved, unassigned and joke/proposal entries.

value.misconception: IP alone guarantees confidentiality and security.
value.correction: The source notes vulnerabilities and names IPsec; it does not claim IP itself guarantees confidentiality.

value.misconception: TCP and UDP adapt to MTU identically.
value.correction: TCP adjusts segment size; oversized UDP/ICMP may trigger IP fragmentation.

value.misconception: The source details NIC ASIC, CPU and RAM-buffer architecture.
value.correction: The article explicitly names routers and Layer 3 switches; other hardware details are synthesis.

value.misconception: Every packet to a destination takes the same path.
value.correction: Datagrams are routed independently and may take different paths.

value.misconception: The IP header is the application data.
value.correction: Header carries addressing/metadata; payload carries transported data.

value.misconception: OSI Layer 3 and the TCP/IP Internet layer are unrelated.
value.correction: The article maps IP to OSI network layer and TCP/IP Internet layer.

value.misconception: Broadcast reaches every Internet host.
value.correction: Broadcast scope is generally a network subnet.

value.misconception: IPv6 immediately replaced IPv4.
value.correction: The article describes a gradual increase in IPv6 deployment since around 2006.

value.misconception: Link-layer error detection eliminates end-to-end reliability needs.
value.correction: Endpoint and upper-layer compensation remains part of the described design.

value.misconception: Link capacity and MTU mean the same thing.
value.correction: Capacity is transmission rate; MTU is maximum packet size.

value.misconception: Anycast sends to every member of a group.
value.correction: Anycast selects one receiver; multicast can send to a group.

value.misconception: Routing protocols carry user payload instead of IP.
value.correction: Routing protocols exchange route information; IP forwarding carries datagrams.

value.misconception: IPv4 header checksum verifies all payload end-to-end.
value.correction: The source says it safeguards the IPv4 header, not end-to-end payload integrity.

value.misconception: All routers use the same CPU/ASIC architecture.
value.correction: Implementation varies; CPU/ASIC mapping is explanatory, not universal.

value.misconception: IP fragmentation is always preferred for TCP.
value.correction: TCP adjusts segment size to fit MTU in the source description.

value.misconception: Dynamic routing guarantees ordered delivery.
value.correction: Different paths can cause out-of-order delivery; hosts/upper layers may buffer.

value.misconception: All graph hardware extensions are externally verified.
value.correction: No external research was used; extensions are labeled synthesis/expansion.

Routers forward datagrams across network boundaries
MTU and link capacity constrain each hop
Transport/host compensates for reliability issues as needed
formal_models.scope: Synthesis joining function, encapsulation, routing, MTU and reliability sections.

formal_models.name: Source versus engineering synthesis
source_explicit: Routers and Layer 3 switches are named hardware
IP packets are encapsulated into link frames
IPv4 and IPv6 differ in fragmentation and checksum behavior
synthesis: NIC, CPU, ASIC and RAM buffer mapping
formal_models.scope: No external research used; synthesis nodes are labeled.

misconceptions.misconception: IP guarantees packets arrive exactly once and in order.
misconceptions.correction: IP is best-effort and connectionless; loss, duplication, corruption and reordering are possible.

misconceptions.misconception: IP and TCP are the same protocol.
misconceptions.correction: IP is network layer; TCP is transport layer and connection-oriented.

misconceptions.misconception: An IP datagram and Ethernet frame are the same unit.
misconceptions.correction: The IP datagram is encapsulated inside a link-layer frame.

misconceptions.misconception: Routers always notify endpoints when they discard packets.
misconceptions.correction: ICMP may report errors, but router notification is not required for every error.

misconceptions.misconception: IPv6 routers fragment packets like IPv4 routers.
misconceptions.correction: IPv6 network elements do not fragment; endpoints must respect Path MTU.

misconceptions.misconception: IPv6 has the same IP header checksum as IPv4.
misconceptions.correction: IPv4 has a header checksum; IPv6 omits it under the source-stated assumption.

misconceptions.misconception: If a packet fits the local MTU, it fits the whole path.
misconceptions.correction: Path MTU can be smaller because another link may impose a tighter limit.

misconceptions.misconception: Multicast and broadcast both reach every node.
misconceptions.correction: Broadcast reaches all nodes in scope; multicast reaches a selected group.

misconceptions.misconception: Anycast always chooses the geographically closest machine.
misconceptions.correction: The source describes a distance or cost measure, not necessarily geography.

misconceptions.misconception: IPv5 was the deployed successor to IPv4.
misconceptions.correction: Version 5 was used by experimental Internet Stream Protocol.

misconceptions.misconception: Every IP version number is a deployed standard.
misconceptions.correction: The version list includes experimental, obsolete, reserved, unassigned and joke/proposal entries.

misconceptions.misconception: IP alone guarantees confidentiality and security.
misconceptions.correction: The source notes vulnerabilities and names IPsec; it does not claim IP itself guarantees confidentiality.

misconceptions.misconception: TCP and UDP adapt to MTU identically.
misconceptions.correction: TCP adjusts segment size; oversized UDP/ICMP may trigger IP fragmentation.

misconceptions.misconception: The source details NIC ASIC, CPU and RAM-buffer architecture.
misconceptions.correction: The article explicitly names routers and Layer 3 switches; other hardware details are synthesis.

misconceptions.misconception: Every packet to a destination takes the same path.
misconceptions.correction: Datagrams are routed independently and may take different paths.

misconceptions.misconception: The IP header is the application data.
misconceptions.correction: Header carries addressing/metadata; payload carries transported data.

misconceptions.misconception: OSI Layer 3 and the TCP/IP Internet layer are unrelated.
misconceptions.correction: The article maps IP to OSI network layer and TCP/IP Internet layer.

misconceptions.misconception: Broadcast reaches every Internet host.
misconceptions.correction: Broadcast scope is generally a network subnet.

misconceptions.misconception: IPv6 immediately replaced IPv4.
misconceptions.correction: The article describes a gradual increase in IPv6 deployment since around 2006.

misconceptions.misconception: Link-layer error detection eliminates end-to-end reliability needs.
misconceptions.correction: Endpoint and upper-layer compensation remains part of the described design.

misconceptions.misconception: Link capacity and MTU mean the same thing.
misconceptions.correction: Capacity is transmission rate; MTU is maximum packet size.

misconceptions.misconception: Anycast sends to every member of a group.
misconceptions.correction: Anycast selects one receiver; multicast can send to a group.

misconceptions.misconception: Routing protocols carry user payload instead of IP.
misconceptions.correction: Routing protocols exchange route information; IP forwarding carries datagrams.

misconceptions.misconception: IPv4 header checksum verifies all payload end-to-end.
misconceptions.correction: The source says it safeguards the IPv4 header, not end-to-end payload integrity.

misconceptions.misconception: All routers use the same CPU/ASIC architecture.
misconceptions.correction: Implementation varies; CPU/ASIC mapping is explanatory, not universal.

misconceptions.misconception: IP fragmentation is always preferred for TCP.
misconceptions.correction: TCP adjusts segment size to fit MTU in the source description.

misconceptions.misconception: Dynamic routing guarantees ordered delivery.
misconceptions.correction: Different paths can cause out-of-order delivery; hosts/upper layers may buffer.

misconceptions.misconception: All graph hardware extensions are externally verified.
misconceptions.correction: No external research was used; extensions are labeled synthesis/expansion.

value.name: Runtime execution pipeline
value.expression: source → JavaScript engine → execution frames/call stack → event loop/message processing → host APIs/I/O
value.mechanism: The engine executes JavaScript inside a host runtime; the runtime supplies APIs and schedules messages.

value.name: Event-loop processing
value.expression: message_queue → event_loop → call_stack_frame → run_to_completion → next_message
value.mechanism: Messages are processed one at a time; each message runs to completion before the next is considered.

value.name: Dynamic value typing
value.expression: variable → value(type A) → reassignment → value(type B)
value.mechanism: Type is associated with the value rather than the variable/expression.

value.name: Operator-dependent coercion
value.expression: operands + operator → coercion rules → result
value.mechanism: Binary + may concatenate after string coercion, while - converts operands to numbers.

value.name: Prototype delegation
value.expression: object.property → own property? → prototype chain lookup → inherited method/property
value.mechanism: Property lookup walks prototype relationships when a property is not directly owned.

value.name: Lexical closure
value.expression: outer lexical environment + nested function → retained internal state
value.mechanism: A nested function retains access to outer bindings after the outer function finishes.

value.name: Promise/async model
value.expression: async operation → Promise → handlers / await → eventual result
value.mechanism: Promises represent eventual results; async/await structures non-blocking asynchronous code.

value.name: Browser security boundary
value.expression: Web script → sandbox + same-origin policy + CSP → constrained execution
value.mechanism: Browser restrictions limit system capabilities and cross-origin data access, while CSP constrains trusted executable content.

value.name: XSS attack chain
value.expression: attacker-controlled input → malicious script in target page → victim privileges → data/action compromise
value.mechanism: The malicious script executes in the target application's security context.

value.name: CSRF attack chain
value.expression: attacker page → victim browser → authenticated target request → unintended state change
value.mechanism: Cookie-based authentication can cause cross-site requests to carry valid credentials.

value.name: ECMAScript standardization evolution
value.expression: Netscape JavaScript → Ecma submission → ECMAScript editions → annual proposal process
value.mechanism: Standardization moved from browser-specific implementations toward a shared evolving language specification.

value.name: JavaScript/WebAssembly execution complement
value.expression: JavaScript → performance-critical region → WebAssembly → same engine sandbox
value.mechanism: WebAssembly complements JavaScript for performance-critical portions while remaining inside the engine's sandbox.

value.distinction: JavaScript is the language/ecosystem as used in practice; ECMAScript is the standardized language specification.
Despite name/syntax similarities, JavaScript is dynamically typed and prototype-based while Java is statically typed and class-based.
ECMAScript defines language semantics but not I/O; a runtime supplies networking, storage, graphics, and host APIs.
Dynamic typing concerns when/how types are associated with values; weak typing concerns implicit coercion across operations.
JavaScript's underlying inheritance remains prototype-based even when class/extends/super syntax is used.
The source states there is no distinct definition form; invocation context determines whether a function acts as a method via this.
The source describes JavaScript execution as single-threaded with queued messages and non-blocking I/O.
Promise is an asynchronous result abstraction; async/await is syntax for structuring asynchronous operations.
Sandbox limits system capabilities; same-origin policy limits cross-origin information access.
XSS executes attacker-controlled script in a target page; CSRF induces a victim browser to send an unintended authenticated request.
Client-side validation improves user experience but cannot be the sole security enforcement point.
Obfuscation can hinder inspection but does not make client-side code or embedded secrets confidential.
The source lists both but does not define a strict semantic boundary between them.
TypeScript is presented as a statically typed/strict language that transpiles to JavaScript.
WebAssembly complements JavaScript for performance-critical portions and runs in the same sandbox.
Vanilla JS means standard JavaScript without third-party libraries/frameworks.
Both use JavaScript engines, but their host runtimes expose different environment APIs.
The source contrasts Java's compiled-bytecode loading with JavaScript being loaded as human-readable source code.
var is function-scoped; let and const are block-scoped.
const prevents reassignment of the binding; the source does not state that referenced objects become deeply immutable.

value.misconception: JavaScript is Java.
value.correction: They are distinct languages with substantially different typing, object models, loading models, and histories.

value.misconception: ECMAScript and JavaScript are completely separate languages.
value.correction: JavaScript conforms to the ECMAScript standard; ECMAScript specifies the core language while hosts provide APIs.

value.misconception: Dynamic typing means JavaScript has no types.
value.correction: Types exist on values; variables can be rebound to values of different types.

value.misconception: Weak typing means JavaScript is dynamically typed.
value.correction: Dynamic typing and weak typing describe different properties: value-associated typing versus implicit coercion.

value.misconception: JavaScript inheritance is class-based underneath.
value.correction: The source states class syntax abstracts an underlying prototype inheritance mechanism.

value.misconception: const makes an object immutable.
value.correction: The source states const prevents reassignment of the binding; it does not define deep object immutability.

value.misconception: Client-side JavaScript can securely enforce validation.
value.correction: Client validation is convenience; security enforcement must also occur on the server.

value.misconception: Obfuscating JavaScript hides secrets.
value.correction: Client source can be extracted and obfuscation can be reverse-engineered.

value.misconception: CSP alone fixes all JavaScript security problems.
value.correction: CSP is one control; XSS, CSRF, dependency, browser, and sandbox issues remain distinct.

value.misconception: XSS and CSRF are the same attack.
value.correction: XSS executes malicious script in a target context; CSRF abuses a victim browser to make an unintended authenticated request.

value.misconception: JavaScript is single-threaded, therefore it cannot perform concurrent I/O.
value.correction: The event-loop model permits non-blocking I/O while messages are processed sequentially.

value.misconception: Web APIs are part of ECMAScript itself.
value.correction: The source explicitly separates ECMAScript language facilities from host-provided I/O and Web APIs.

value.misconception: WebAssembly replaces JavaScript.
value.correction: The source presents WebAssembly as complementary, especially for performance-critical portions.

value.misconception: Vanilla JS is a separate programming language.
value.correction: It is a term for using standard JavaScript without libraries/frameworks.

value.misconception: JavaScript only runs in browsers.
value.correction: It runs in Node.js, Deno, Bun, application frameworks, JVM contexts, and some embedded systems.

value.misconception: A function and a method are different language constructs in JavaScript.
value.correction: The source says the distinction occurs during invocation; method calls bind this to the receiver.

value.misconception: All JavaScript engines interpret source without compilation.
value.correction: Modern engines commonly use JIT compilation to improve performance.

value.misconception: Prototype pollution is ordinary prototype inheritance.
value.correction: Prototype pollution is a runtime vulnerability involving attacker modification of prototype properties.

value.misconception: Third-party package dependencies are automatically trustworthy.
value.correction: The source highlights stale, vulnerable, malicious, or removed dependencies as a supply-chain risk.

value.misconception: Browser sandbox bugs are only theoretical.
value.correction: The source cites historical cases where incorrect privilege handling enabled vulnerabilities.

source_claims.claim: JavaScript is a core Web technology, alongside HTML and CSS, and conforms to ECMAScript.
Browsers contain dedicated JavaScript engines; engines are also used in servers and applications, with Node.js a major non-browser runtime.
Modern engines use JIT compilation and a runtime/event-loop model for non-blocking I/O.
JavaScript originated at Netscape in 1995 and was standardized as ECMAScript beginning in 1997.
ECMAScript 4 was mothballed; ECMAScript 5 emerged from a 2008 convergence and ECMAScript 6 arrived in 2015.
Node.js combined V8, an event loop, and I/O APIs, driving major non-browser JavaScript adoption.
JavaScript dominates client-side Web scripting and is widely used through libraries/frameworks.
JavaScript is dynamically and weakly typed, prototype-based, multi-paradigm, and supports first-class functions and closures.
Browser sandboxing and same-origin policy constrain JavaScript, while XSS, CSRF, prototype pollution, dependency risks, and browser flaws are security concerns.
JavaScript extends beyond browsers through Node.js, Electron, Cordova, React Native, Acrobat, GNOME Shell, and embedded systems.
Browser developer tools, linters, profilers, and benchmark tools support JavaScript development.
JavaScript influenced and was influenced by other languages/technologies and is complemented by JSON, transpilers, and WebAssembly.

value.preservation_rule: Preserve meaningful concepts, architecture, mechanisms, relationships, historical context, examples, distinctions, security model, APIs, workloads, storage, networking, criticisms, references and source-specific claims. Do not flatten relationships into generic related_to edges.

value.principle: Relationships are first-class objects. Each relationship records what connects two concepts, how the connection works, conditions, direction, effects, inverse/converse where meaningful, context, scope, source provenance and mathematical/formal representation where applicable.
central_system_model: human/client intent → Kubernetes API server → API objects → etcd persistent state → scheduler/controllers/watchers → nodes → kubelet/CRI/runtime → Pods/containers → observed state → status/API → reconciliation
Service → selector → Pod set → stable IP/DNS → load balancing
CRD → Custom Resource → Custom Controller → Operator behavior
Node heartbeat → failure detection → controller reconciliation → replacement workload

value.name: Reconciliation invariant
value.expression: actual_state → desired_state through repeated observe/compare/correct cycles
value.meaning: Conceptual control-loop model underlying Kubernetes controllers.

value.name: Replica count invariant
value.expression: running_replicas ≈ desired_replicas
value.meaning: ReplicaSet controller attempts to maintain the declared number of replicas.

value.name: Service selection relation
value.expression: Service endpoints = Pods matching label selector
value.meaning: Service membership is determined by label selection.

value.name: Scheduler matching model
value.expression: placement = match(workload demand, resource supply, constraints)
value.meaning: Scheduler matches workload requirements against node resources and policies.

value.name: API object state model
value.expression: object = metadata + spec(desired) + status(actual)
value.meaning: Kubernetes objects represent intent and observed state.

value.name: Deployment control hierarchy
value.expression: Deployment → ReplicaSet → Pods → Containers
value.meaning: Deployment manages ReplicaSets; ReplicaSets maintain Pods; Pods contain containers.

value.name: Node failure recovery chain
value.expression: node failure → heartbeat/status change → controller observes → replacement Pod on healthy node
value.meaning: Source-described recovery sequence for controller-managed workloads.

value.name: Kubernetes API flow
value.expression: client → API server → persisted API object/etcd → watchers/controllers → cluster changes
value.meaning: Conceptual flow connecting external intent to persistent state and reconciliation.

fields.label: Semantic distinctions
value: Kubernetes primarily represents desired state as objects; controllers determine corrective actions rather than requiring users to script every individual machine operation.
Control plane coordinates state; nodes execute workloads.
spec expresses desired state; status records current state.
Container is the runtime unit; Pod is the Kubernetes deployable unit that groups one or more containers.
Service provides stable identity/load balancing over a changing set of Pods.
ReplicaSet maintains replica count; Deployment manages ReplicaSets and rollout/rollback.
Stateful workloads require stable identity/order/persistence; stateless workloads generally scale by adding equivalent replicas.
Container filesystems can disappear on restart; volumes provide persistent/shared storage.
CRD defines an API type; Operator combines custom resources with controllers to automate domain-specific behavior.
Authentication establishes identity; authorization decides what that identity may do.
kubelet manages Pod state; runtime executes container lifecycle through CRI.
Pod IPs are tied to individual Pods; Service identity remains stable while matching Pods change.
Namespaces organize/partition resources; authorization determines permitted API actions.
CSI separates storage integration implementation from Kubernetes core.
Scheduler decides where an unscheduled Pod runs; controllers continuously reconcile resource state.

source_claims.title: Definition
source_claims.claim: Kubernetes is an open-source container orchestration system for automating deployment, scaling, and management of containerized workloads.

source_claims.title: Cluster model
source_claims.claim: Kubernetes assembles virtual or bare-metal computers into a cluster capable of running container workloads.

source_claims.title: Control-plane/node architecture
source_claims.claim: Kubernetes separates management/control-plane components from worker nodes and exposes resources through an object/API model.

source_claims.title: etcd state store
source_claims.claim: etcd persistently represents cluster configuration/state and favors consistency during network partitions.

source_claims.title: API server
source_claims.claim: The API server exposes the Kubernetes API, validates REST requests, persists API-object state, and participates in watch-driven coordination.

source_claims.title: Scheduler
source_claims.claim: The scheduler matches unscheduled Pods to nodes using resource availability and constraints.

source_claims.title: Controllers
source_claims.claim: Controllers reconcile actual cluster state toward desired state and can replace failed workloads.

source_claims.title: kubelet
source_claims.claim: kubelet maintains Pod/container state on each node and reports node status.

source_claims.title: Runtime_CRi
source_claims.claim: The container runtime manages container lifecycle while CRI decouples kubelet from implementation.

source_claims.title: Networking
source_claims.claim: kube-proxy implements network proxy/load-balancing behavior for Services.

source_claims.title: Namespaces
source_claims.claim: Namespaces segregate Kubernetes resources across teams/projects/environments.

source_claims.title: Pods
source_claims.claim: Pods are the basic deployable unit and group one or more co-located containers with a Pod network identity.

source_claims.title: Workloads
source_claims.claim: Higher-level workload objects declaratively manage Pods, including ReplicaSets, Deployments, StatefulSets and DaemonSets.

source_claims.title: Services
source_claims.claim: Services provide stable IP/DNS identity and load-balance traffic to Pods selected by labels.

source_claims.title: Storage
source_claims.claim: Volumes, persistent storage, Container Attached Storage, and CSI address storage persistence and external storage integration.

source_claims.title: Configuration
source_claims.claim: ConfigMaps and Secrets externalize configuration; Secrets are intended for confidential data and require additional protection for at-rest encryption.

source_claims.title: API objects
source_claims.claim: Kubernetes objects record intent with metadata, spec, status, ownership, and lifecycle semantics.

source_claims.title: Extensions
source_claims.claim: CRDs, custom controllers, and Operators extend Kubernetes declaratively.

source_claims.title: API security
source_claims.claim: TLS, authentication, and authorization mechanisms protect the Kubernetes API.

source_claims.title: Cluster API
source_claims.claim: Cluster API applies Kubernetes object/API principles to infrastructure and machines.

source_claims.title: Uses
source_claims.claim: Kubernetes is used across deployment, scaling, cloud/data-center management, observability, and related infrastructure workflows.

source_claims.title: Complexity/criticism
source_claims.claim: The source discusses complexity, ecosystem fragmentation, operational difficulty, and reasons managed services/PaaS approaches emerged.

source_claims.title: History
source_claims.claim: Kubernetes originated at Google, drew on Borg and Promise Theory, was announced in 2014, and was contributed to CNCF.

source_claims.title: Release timeline
source_claims.claim: The source contains a release/support timeline through Kubernetes 1.36 and related support windows.

equations.name: Reconciliation invariant

equations.name: Replica count invariant
equations.expression: running_replicas ≈ desired_replicas
equations.meaning: ReplicaSet controller attempts to maintain the declared number of replicas.

equations.name: Service selection relation
equations.expression: Service endpoints = Pods matching label selector
equations.meaning: Service membership is determined by label selection.

equations.name: Scheduler matching model
equations.expression: placement = match(workload demand, resource supply, constraints)
equations.meaning: Scheduler matches workload requirements against node resources and policies.

equations.name: API object state model
equations.expression: object = metadata + spec(desired) + status(actual)
equations.meaning: Kubernetes objects represent intent and observed state.

equations.name: Deployment control hierarchy
equations.expression: Deployment → ReplicaSet → Pods → Containers
equations.meaning: Deployment manages ReplicaSets; ReplicaSets maintain Pods; Pods contain containers.

equations.name: Node failure recovery chain
equations.expression: node failure → heartbeat/status change → controller observes → replacement Pod on healthy node
equations.meaning: Source-described recovery sequence for controller-managed workloads.

equations.name: Kubernetes API flow
equations.expression: client → API server → persisted API object/etcd → watchers/controllers → cluster changes
equations.meaning: Conceptual flow connecting external intent to persistent state and reconciliation.

fields.label: Topic summary
fields.value: Lua is a compact, portable, dynamically typed multi-paradigm language designed for embedding and extending host applications. Its small core, tables, first-class functions, closures, metatables, bytecode VM, and C API enable a wide range of programming patterns and integrations.

value.name: Source-to-VM execution pipeline
value.mechanism: Source text is compiled to bytecode; the VM executes bytecode. Compilation may happen at runtime or offline, and JIT implementations may compile code to native instructions.
conditions: Standard Lua bytecode execution model described by the article
JIT behavior varies by implementation

value.name: Embedded-language integration model
value.mechanism: The host creates a Lua state and uses the C API to load scripts and exchange values, enabling extension without moving the entire application into Lua.
conditions: Host application integrates the C API
Host explicitly exposes capabilities to scripts

value.name: C API call stack model
value.mechanism: The C API stack is the transfer mechanism for arguments and results; the example calls foo(5,3) and reads 8.
conditions: C program invokes a Lua function through the stack API

value.name: Table-based object model
value.mechanism: An object's table stores its fields; metatable lookup delegates missing methods to a prototype table.
conditions: The programmer implements this pattern; it is not a built-in class system

value.name: Table reference and aliasing model
value.mechanism: Both variables refer to the same table object, so a field mutation is visible through both references.
conditions: No copy/clone operation is performed

value.name: Closure capture model
value.mechanism: Each invocation of addto creates a function retaining access to that invocation's x value.
conditions: The returned function references a local from its defining lexical scope

value.name: Metatable-driven memoization
value.mechanism: A metatable's __index function handles missing keys and writes computed values into the table.
conditions: The metatable is attached to fibs
Required lower Fibonacci values are available or recursively computed

value.name: Lua control-flow selection
value.mechanism: Explicit then/end delimit conditional blocks, while optional else/elseif supply alternatives.
conditions: A conditional expression is evaluated

value.name: Lua loop families
value.mechanism: Lua provides four loop forms in the article's taxonomy, each suited to different termination or iteration logic.
conditions: Loop body and termination condition are correctly specified

value.name: Table as universal composite data model
value.mechanism: The same table primitive represents heterogeneous associative arrays, sequences, records, nested structures, namespaces, and object fields.
conditions: Programmer defines conventions for keys and shape

value.name: Lua module loading model
steps: Search/load Lua module or native extension
value.mechanism: Lua's module system can load Lua modules or native shared objects; native modules conventionally expose luaopen_foo.
conditions: Module is discoverable and compatible with the active runtime

value.name: Managed object lifetime
value.mechanism: Lua garbage collection manages objects such as closures and avoids requiring the host C program to manually reference-count every Lua object.
conditions: Object is managed by the Lua runtime

value.name: Lua dialect and target-language relationships
value.mechanism: Luau, Ravi, Teal, Pluto, GLua, PICO-8 Lua, LuaJIT and other variants differ in compatibility, typing, syntax, performance or host-specific APIs.
conditions: Features are dialect/version-specific; do not assume every implementation supports all extensions

value.name: Historical influence graph
steps: Syntax and semantics influenced by other languages
value.mechanism: Lua's design emerged from practical embedding requirements and selective borrowing from earlier languages rather than adopting a single paradigm wholesale.
conditions: Historical details are limited to the supplied article

value.name: Game scripting integration
value.mechanism: Lua's embedding design allows game developers to expose scriptable behavior while retaining core engine functionality in native code.
conditions: A game uses Lua or a dialect and exposes a scripting API

value.name: Lua typing profile
steps: Variables may refer to different types over time
value.mechanism: The article characterizes base Lua as dynamic, strong, and duck typed while also describing coercion; dialects such as Luau and Ravi add other typing features.
conditions: Typing behavior and extensions vary by Lua version/dialect

value.name: Bytecode precompilation and loading
value.mechanism: The article describes string.dump and load-family functions, as well as offline compilation to reduce load time or omit the compiler.
conditions: Bytecode compatibility depends on implementation/version; source excerpt does not detail compatibility rules

value.name: Namespace via table
value.mechanism: A table containing related functions can act as a namespace without requiring a dedicated namespace construct.
conditions: Programmer follows a table naming convention

value.name: Prototype inheritance via metatables
value.mechanism: Metatable delegation makes inherited methods visible without copying them into each object.
conditions: Programmer sets metatable relationships correctly

value.distinction: Embedding describes how the runtime is integrated into a host; extension describes the purpose of allowing users to add behavior to that host.
Lua source is human-readable text; bytecode is the compiled VM instruction representation.
The Lua VM executes bytecode as a software runtime; the CPU executes native instructions implementing that runtime.
Lua's VM is described as register-based, while the C API used to exchange values is stack-based; these are different layers and do not conflict.
Base Lua is described as dynamically typed; Luau adds gradual typing as a dialect feature.
An array is a usage pattern of a general key-value table, not a separate built-in composite type.
Assigning a table variable copies a reference; creating a new table constructor creates a distinct table.
nil denotes an absent table value; a nil gap in a sequence can make the # length result ambiguous.
Dot syntax is shorthand for a string-key lookup and does not introduce a separate field-storage mechanism.
A closure is a function that retains access to lexical variables from its defining environment.
Lua's examples use prototype delegation; class-like APIs are programmer-built conventions rather than a built-in class construct.
A metatable is the table of customization rules; a metamethod is a named hook such as __index or __add.
Coroutines provide cooperative task switching; the source does not describe them as operating-system threads.
The baseline execution model compiles to VM bytecode; a JIT is an implementation technique that can compile code during execution.
The core API provides base functionality; the auxiliary library supplies helper operations and macros.
Luau derives from Lua 5.1 and adds dialect-specific typing, performance, and sandbox features; it is not identical to every Lua version.
require is the loading interface; a native extension is a compiled shared object that exposes an entry point such as luaopen_foo.
A namespace table is a programming convention built using a general table, not a dedicated namespace primitive.
Source claims capture what the article states; formal models may organize those statements into explanatory pipelines.
A named stable Lua version and an implementation targeting an older language version are different kinds of release identity.

value.misconception: Lua has separate built-in array, record, and object composite types.
value.correction: The source describes tables as the only built-in composite type; arrays, records, namespaces, and objects are patterns built with tables.

value.misconception: Lua has native class declarations like class-based languages.
value.correction: The article says Lua has no built-in class concept in the described model; class-like behavior is emulated with tables, functions, and metatables.

value.misconception: Lua source text is executed directly without compilation.
value.correction: The article states that Lua source is compiled into bytecode that runs on the Lua VM.

value.misconception: Lua's VM and C API both use the same stack architecture.
value.correction: The VM is described as register-based, whereas the C API uses a stack to exchange values.

value.misconception: Lua's automatic sequence indexing starts at zero.
value.correction: The source says automatic array-style indexing starts at 1, although explicit key 0 is legal.

value.misconception: The # operator always returns an unambiguous count for any table.
value.correction: The article notes that tables with holes can have more than one valid boundary for the length operator.

value.misconception: Assigning one table variable to another clones the table.
value.correction: The source example shows both variables referring to the same table; mutation through one is visible through the other.

value.misconception: Metatables are only for object-oriented programming.
value.correction: The source shows metatables also supporting missing-key lookup, memoization, operator overloading, and semantic customization.

value.misconception: A returned function loses access to its outer local when the outer call returns.
value.correction: The closure example retains access to its own captured x value, managed by the garbage collector.

value.misconception: Lua is used only for games.
value.correction: The article lists editors, web servers, databases, packet analyzers, typesetting, and MediaWiki among non-game uses.

value.misconception: Luau, LuaJIT, Teal, and standard Lua are identical implementations.
value.correction: The article describes dialects/implementations with different compatibility, typing, performance, syntax, or sandbox behavior.

value.misconception: Embedding Lua requires manual reference counting for every Lua object.
value.correction: The article explicitly contrasts Lua's C API with APIs that require manual reference counting.

value.misconception: Dynamic typing necessarily means weak typing.
value.correction: The source metadata describes Lua as dynamic, strong, and duck typed, and separately lists supported runtime coercion; these labels are not synonyms.

value.misconception: Lua includes every advanced feature as a fixed built-in construct.
value.correction: The design emphasizes small extensible meta-features, with classes and inheritance implemented by conventions rather than dedicated constructs.

value.misconception: Coroutines automatically provide preemptive parallel threads.
value.correction: The source characterizes coroutines as cooperative multitasking; it does not claim OS-thread parallelism.

metadata.topic_summary: Lua is a compact, portable, dynamically typed multi-paradigm language designed for embedding and extending host applications. Its small core, tables, first-class functions, closures, metatables, bytecode VM, and C API enable a wide range of programming patterns and integrations.

formal_models.name: Source-to-VM execution pipeline
formal_models.mechanism: Source text is compiled to bytecode; the VM executes bytecode. Compilation may happen at runtime or offline, and JIT implementations may compile code to native instructions.
conditions: Standard Lua bytecode execution model described by the article
JIT behavior varies by implementation

formal_models.name: Embedded-language integration model
formal_models.mechanism: The host creates a Lua state and uses the C API to load scripts and exchange values, enabling extension without moving the entire application into Lua.
conditions: Host application integrates the C API
Host explicitly exposes capabilities to scripts

formal_models.name: C API call stack model
formal_models.mechanism: The C API stack is the transfer mechanism for arguments and results; the example calls foo(5,3) and reads 8.
conditions: C program invokes a Lua function through the stack API

formal_models.name: Table-based object model
formal_models.mechanism: An object's table stores its fields; metatable lookup delegates missing methods to a prototype table.
conditions: The programmer implements this pattern; it is not a built-in class system

formal_models.name: Table reference and aliasing model
formal_models.mechanism: Both variables refer to the same table object, so a field mutation is visible through both references.
conditions: No copy/clone operation is performed

formal_models.name: Closure capture model
formal_models.mechanism: Each invocation of addto creates a function retaining access to that invocation's x value.
conditions: The returned function references a local from its defining lexical scope

formal_models.name: Metatable-driven memoization
formal_models.mechanism: A metatable's __index function handles missing keys and writes computed values into the table.
conditions: The metatable is attached to fibs
Required lower Fibonacci values are available or recursively computed

formal_models.name: Lua control-flow selection
formal_models.mechanism: Explicit then/end delimit conditional blocks, while optional else/elseif supply alternatives.
conditions: A conditional expression is evaluated

formal_models.name: Lua loop families
formal_models.mechanism: Lua provides four loop forms in the article's taxonomy, each suited to different termination or iteration logic.
conditions: Loop body and termination condition are correctly specified

formal_models.name: Table as universal composite data model
formal_models.mechanism: The same table primitive represents heterogeneous associative arrays, sequences, records, nested structures, namespaces, and object fields.
conditions: Programmer defines conventions for keys and shape

formal_models.name: Lua module loading model
steps: Search/load Lua module or native extension
formal_models.mechanism: Lua's module system can load Lua modules or native shared objects; native modules conventionally expose luaopen_foo.
conditions: Module is discoverable and compatible with the active runtime

formal_models.name: Managed object lifetime
formal_models.mechanism: Lua garbage collection manages objects such as closures and avoids requiring the host C program to manually reference-count every Lua object.
conditions: Object is managed by the Lua runtime

formal_models.name: Lua dialect and target-language relationships
formal_models.mechanism: Luau, Ravi, Teal, Pluto, GLua, PICO-8 Lua, LuaJIT and other variants differ in compatibility, typing, syntax, performance or host-specific APIs.
conditions: Features are dialect/version-specific; do not assume every implementation supports all extensions

formal_models.name: Historical influence graph
steps: Syntax and semantics influenced by other languages
formal_models.mechanism: Lua's design emerged from practical embedding requirements and selective borrowing from earlier languages rather than adopting a single paradigm wholesale.
conditions: Historical details are limited to the supplied article

formal_models.name: Game scripting integration
formal_models.mechanism: Lua's embedding design allows game developers to expose scriptable behavior while retaining core engine functionality in native code.
conditions: A game uses Lua or a dialect and exposes a scripting API

formal_models.name: Lua typing profile
steps: Variables may refer to different types over time
formal_models.mechanism: The article characterizes base Lua as dynamic, strong, and duck typed while also describing coercion; dialects such as Luau and Ravi add other typing features.
conditions: Typing behavior and extensions vary by Lua version/dialect

formal_models.name: Bytecode precompilation and loading
formal_models.mechanism: The article describes string.dump and load-family functions, as well as offline compilation to reduce load time or omit the compiler.
conditions: Bytecode compatibility depends on implementation/version; source excerpt does not detail compatibility rules

formal_models.name: Namespace via table
formal_models.mechanism: A table containing related functions can act as a namespace without requiring a dedicated namespace construct.
conditions: Programmer follows a table naming convention

formal_models.name: Prototype inheritance via metatables
formal_models.mechanism: Metatable delegation makes inherited methods visible without copying them into each object.
conditions: Programmer sets metatable relationships correctly

source_claims.claim: Lua is a lightweight, high-level, multi-paradigm language designed mainly for embedding in applications.
Lua was created in 1993 at Tecgraf by Roberto Ierusalimschy, Luiz Henrique de Figueiredo, and Waldemar Celes.
SOL and DEL were predecessor configuration/data-description languages whose limitations motivated a more expressive language.
Lua favors a small base language and extensible meta-features over a large set of paradigm-specific built-ins.
Tables are Lua's only built-in composite type and support associative arrays, records, arrays, namespaces, and objects.
First-class functions, lexical scoping, and closures support higher-order programming and information hiding.
Metatables customize table behavior and enable lookup delegation, memoization, operator overloading, and object-oriented patterns.
Lua source is compiled to bytecode for a register-based virtual machine; compilation may occur at runtime or offline.
The C API is stack-based and provides core and auxiliary libraries for embedding and calling Lua from C.
Lua can load Lua modules and native shared-object extensions, with LuaRocks providing package management.
Lua is widely used in game development due to its embeddability, execution speed, and short learning curve.
The article lists non-game applications such as Lightroom, LuaTeX, Redis, Neovim, Nginx, Wireshark, and MediaWiki Scribunto.
Lua has derivatives and dialects that differ in typing, performance, syntax, compatibility, and host integration.
Lua versions before 5.0 used a BSD-like license; versions from 5.0 onward use the MIT License.
The article says the register-based VM can reduce value copying and the number of instructions per function compared with stack-based VM architectures.
Luau is described as a Lua 5.1 derivative with gradual typing, performance focus, and improved sandboxing for untrusted scripts.

semantic_distinctions.distinction: Embedding describes how the runtime is integrated into a host; extension describes the purpose of allowing users to add behavior to that host.
Lua source is human-readable text; bytecode is the compiled VM instruction representation.
The Lua VM executes bytecode as a software runtime; the CPU executes native instructions implementing that runtime.
Lua's VM is described as register-based, while the C API used to exchange values is stack-based; these are different layers and do not conflict.
Base Lua is described as dynamically typed; Luau adds gradual typing as a dialect feature.
An array is a usage pattern of a general key-value table, not a separate built-in composite type.
Assigning a table variable copies a reference; creating a new table constructor creates a distinct table.
nil denotes an absent table value; a nil gap in a sequence can make the # length result ambiguous.
Dot syntax is shorthand for a string-key lookup and does not introduce a separate field-storage mechanism.
A closure is a function that retains access to lexical variables from its defining environment.
Lua's examples use prototype delegation; class-like APIs are programmer-built conventions rather than a built-in class construct.
A metatable is the table of customization rules; a metamethod is a named hook such as __index or __add.
Coroutines provide cooperative task switching; the source does not describe them as operating-system threads.
The baseline execution model compiles to VM bytecode; a JIT is an implementation technique that can compile code during execution.
The core API provides base functionality; the auxiliary library supplies helper operations and macros.
Luau derives from Lua 5.1 and adds dialect-specific typing, performance, and sandbox features; it is not identical to every Lua version.
require is the loading interface; a native extension is a compiled shared object that exposes an entry point such as luaopen_foo.
A namespace table is a programming convention built using a general table, not a dedicated namespace primitive.
Source claims capture what the article states; formal models may organize those statements into explanatory pipelines.
A named stable Lua version and an implementation targeting an older language version are different kinds of release identity.

misconceptions.misconception: Lua has separate built-in array, record, and object composite types.
misconceptions.correction: The source describes tables as the only built-in composite type; arrays, records, namespaces, and objects are patterns built with tables.

misconceptions.misconception: Lua has native class declarations like class-based languages.
misconceptions.correction: The article says Lua has no built-in class concept in the described model; class-like behavior is emulated with tables, functions, and metatables.

misconceptions.misconception: Lua source text is executed directly without compilation.
misconceptions.correction: The article states that Lua source is compiled into bytecode that runs on the Lua VM.

misconceptions.misconception: Lua's VM and C API both use the same stack architecture.
misconceptions.correction: The VM is described as register-based, whereas the C API uses a stack to exchange values.

misconceptions.misconception: Lua's automatic sequence indexing starts at zero.
misconceptions.correction: The source says automatic array-style indexing starts at 1, although explicit key 0 is legal.

misconceptions.misconception: The # operator always returns an unambiguous count for any table.
misconceptions.correction: The article notes that tables with holes can have more than one valid boundary for the length operator.

misconceptions.misconception: Assigning one table variable to another clones the table.
misconceptions.correction: The source example shows both variables referring to the same table; mutation through one is visible through the other.

misconceptions.misconception: Metatables are only for object-oriented programming.
misconceptions.correction: The source shows metatables also supporting missing-key lookup, memoization, operator overloading, and semantic customization.

misconceptions.misconception: A returned function loses access to its outer local when the outer call returns.
misconceptions.correction: The closure example retains access to its own captured x value, managed by the garbage collector.

misconceptions.misconception: Lua is used only for games.
misconceptions.correction: The article lists editors, web servers, databases, packet analyzers, typesetting, and MediaWiki among non-game uses.

misconceptions.misconception: Luau, LuaJIT, Teal, and standard Lua are identical implementations.
misconceptions.correction: The article describes dialects/implementations with different compatibility, typing, performance, syntax, or sandbox behavior.

misconceptions.misconception: Embedding Lua requires manual reference counting for every Lua object.
misconceptions.correction: The article explicitly contrasts Lua's C API with APIs that require manual reference counting.

misconceptions.misconception: Dynamic typing necessarily means weak typing.
misconceptions.correction: The source metadata describes Lua as dynamic, strong, and duck typed, and separately lists supported runtime coercion; these labels are not synonyms.

misconceptions.misconception: Lua includes every advanced feature as a fixed built-in construct.
misconceptions.correction: The design emphasizes small extensible meta-features, with classes and inheritance implemented by conventions rather than dedicated constructs.

misconceptions.misconception: Coroutines automatically provide preemptive parallel threads.
misconceptions.correction: The source characterizes coroutines as cooperative multitasking; it does not claim OS-thread parallelism.

value.misconception: A switch simply repeats every frame to all ports.
value.correction: A switch learns MAC-to-port mappings and selectively forwards frames where forwarding state permits; hubs repeat traffic broadly.

value.misconception: Switches eliminate all broadcast traffic.
value.correction: Switch ports separate collision domains, but broadcasts are still forwarded within the broadcast domain.

value.misconception: Every network switch routes IP packets.
value.correction: Ordinary Ethernet switches commonly operate at Layer 2; Layer 3/multilayer switches add routing functionality.

value.misconception: MAC and IP addresses are interchangeable.
value.correction: MAC addresses guide link-layer forwarding; IP addresses support network-layer routing.

value.misconception: STP forwards on every redundant link.
value.correction: STP disables forwarding on selected links to create a loop-free active topology; SPB/TRILL are alternatives described as allowing multiple active paths.

value.misconception: A VLAN is a separate physical switch.
value.correction: A VLAN is logical Layer 2 segmentation that can be configured and tagged on managed switches.

value.misconception: Smart and enterprise switches have the same feature set.
value.correction: Smart switches offer limited features; enterprise switches provide broader configuration and monitoring capabilities.

value.misconception: Any device on a switch can sniff all switched traffic.
value.correction: Ordinary visibility is limited to relevant ports; port mirroring, taps, hubs or monitoring systems are used to observe additional traffic.

value.misconception: Cut-through waits for the entire frame before forwarding.
value.correction: Cut-through can begin forwarding after enough header data has arrived to make the decision.

value.misconception: PoE and UPS mean the same thing.
value.correction: PoE powers compatible endpoints over Ethernet; UPS backs up power to keep the switch and attached devices running during power loss.

value.misconception: The MAC table and CAM are exactly the same kind of thing.
value.correction: The MAC table is the logical mapping; CAM is a common high-speed hardware implementation.

value.misconception: Every switch port must use fiber modules.
value.correction: Switch interfaces can use different media; the source describes pluggable optics and DAC copper alternatives.

value.misconception: Full-duplex point-to-point links behave like shared half-duplex segments.
value.correction: The article says full-duplex has simultaneous transmit/receive and makes collisions impossible in the described model.

value.misconception: A managed switch by itself guarantees network security.
value.correction: ACLs, MAC filtering, 802.1X, VLANs, firewall and IDS integrations are features or controls, not a universal security guarantee.

value.misconception: Every internal switch hardware detail is explicitly specified by the article.
value.correction: CAM and transceivers/CPO are mentioned explicitly; detailed switch-fabric, ASIC pipeline and plane-separation descriptions are labeled engineering synthesis.

source_claims.claim: A network switch is a multiport bridge that forwards traffic toward destination devices, typically using MAC addresses at Layer 2.
Unlike a repeater hub, a switch learns device addresses and forwards data toward the destination port rather than repeating everything to all ports.
Each switch port forms a separate collision domain in the described Ethernet model, while broadcasts remain within the broadcast domain.
Switches may use SFP and other pluggable transceiver modules, DAC cables and co-packaged optics.
Some switches add Layer 3 routing and are called Layer 3 or multilayer switches.
The MAC address table maps MAC addresses to ports and is often implemented with high-speed CAM.
Cut-through switches may begin forwarding before the entire frame payload has arrived, reducing latency.
STP disables forwarding on selected links to avoid switching loops; SPB and TRILL are described as alternatives supporting active paths.
PoE can power endpoints such as VoIP phones and wireless access points; UPS-backed switch power can support continuity.
Managed switch features include VLANs, link aggregation, QoS, ACLs, SNMP, port mirroring, NTP, 802.1X, LLDP and IGMP snooping.
Port mirroring sends a copy of selected traffic to a monitoring port; alternatives include SMON, RMON, sFlow, a network tap or a Layer 1 hub.
The article credits Mark Kempf/DEC with the 1983 MAC bridge and dates Kalpana's seven-port EtherSwitch to 1989–1990.
The article warns that its lead may be too technical for most readers.

misconceptions.misconception: A switch simply repeats every frame to all ports.
misconceptions.correction: A switch learns MAC-to-port mappings and selectively forwards frames where forwarding state permits; hubs repeat traffic broadly.

misconceptions.misconception: Switches eliminate all broadcast traffic.
misconceptions.correction: Switch ports separate collision domains, but broadcasts are still forwarded within the broadcast domain.

misconceptions.misconception: Every network switch routes IP packets.
misconceptions.correction: Ordinary Ethernet switches commonly operate at Layer 2; Layer 3/multilayer switches add routing functionality.

misconceptions.misconception: MAC and IP addresses are interchangeable.
misconceptions.correction: MAC addresses guide link-layer forwarding; IP addresses support network-layer routing.

misconceptions.misconception: STP forwards on every redundant link.
misconceptions.correction: STP disables forwarding on selected links to create a loop-free active topology; SPB/TRILL are alternatives described as allowing multiple active paths.

misconceptions.misconception: A VLAN is a separate physical switch.
misconceptions.correction: A VLAN is logical Layer 2 segmentation that can be configured and tagged on managed switches.

misconceptions.misconception: Smart and enterprise switches have the same feature set.
misconceptions.correction: Smart switches offer limited features; enterprise switches provide broader configuration and monitoring capabilities.

misconceptions.misconception: Any device on a switch can sniff all switched traffic.
misconceptions.correction: Ordinary visibility is limited to relevant ports; port mirroring, taps, hubs or monitoring systems are used to observe additional traffic.

misconceptions.misconception: Cut-through waits for the entire frame before forwarding.
misconceptions.correction: Cut-through can begin forwarding after enough header data has arrived to make the decision.

misconceptions.misconception: PoE and UPS mean the same thing.
misconceptions.correction: PoE powers compatible endpoints over Ethernet; UPS backs up power to keep the switch and attached devices running during power loss.

misconceptions.misconception: The MAC table and CAM are exactly the same kind of thing.
misconceptions.correction: The MAC table is the logical mapping; CAM is a common high-speed hardware implementation.

misconceptions.misconception: Every switch port must use fiber modules.
misconceptions.correction: Switch interfaces can use different media; the source describes pluggable optics and DAC copper alternatives.

misconceptions.misconception: Full-duplex point-to-point links behave like shared half-duplex segments.
misconceptions.correction: The article says full-duplex has simultaneous transmit/receive and makes collisions impossible in the described model.

misconceptions.misconception: A managed switch by itself guarantees network security.
misconceptions.correction: ACLs, MAC filtering, 802.1X, VLANs, firewall and IDS integrations are features or controls, not a universal security guarantee.

misconceptions.misconception: Every internal switch hardware detail is explicitly specified by the article.
misconceptions.correction: CAM and transceivers/CPO are mentioned explicitly; detailed switch-fabric, ASIC pipeline and plane-separation descriptions are labeled engineering synthesis.

historical_context.event: Mark Kempf at DEC is credited with inventing the first MAC bridge.
DEC introduced the two-port LANBridge 100 product.
MAC bridging helped Ethernet shift from shared access toward point-to-point switched connections.
Pluggable interface families evolved from MAU/AUI and GBIC through XENPAK, SFP, XFP, QSFP, QSFP-DD and OSFP; the article also discusses CPO.

value.label: Rendering choice
value.description: rendering_mode ∈ {client, server, static}
value.expression: rendering_mode ∈ {client, server, static}
value.meaning: Next.js expands React's client-rendering model with server/static rendering.

value.label: Static delivery flow
value.description: source → build → .next → static HTML → cache → browser
value.expression: source → build → .next → static HTML → cache → browser
value.meaning: Build-time static generation produces artifacts that can be cached and served.

value.label: Automatic code splitting
value.description: page_request → required_code_only
value.expression: page_request → required_code_only
value.meaning: Only code necessary to load a page is included.

value.label: Serverless execution
value.description: application_code → lambda_functions → on_demand_execution
value.expression: application_code → lambda_functions → on_demand_execution
value.meaning: Next.js 8 split code into on-demand lambda functions.

value.label: App Router architecture
value.description: route → layout + server_component + stream + data_fetching
value.expression: route → layout + server_component + stream + data_fetching
value.meaning: App Router combines layouts, React Server Components, streaming and new data fetching.

value.label: Compilation toolchain
value.description: source → SWC/compiler → bundler → browser/deployment
value.expression: source → SWC/compiler → bundler → browser/deployment
value.meaning: Next.js uses compiler/transpiler and bundling stages.

value.label: Development update loop
value.description: code_change → detect → rerender/replace_module → browser
value.expression: code_change → detect → rerender/replace_module → browser
value.meaning: Hot reload/HMR provides immediate development feedback.

value.label: Incremental regeneration
value.description: static_output + later_regeneration
value.expression: static_output + later_regeneration
value.meaning: ISR extends static generation with incremental regeneration.

value.label: Routing
value.description: URL/path → routing_system → page/component
value.expression: URL/path → routing_system → page/component
value.meaning: Next.js provides page-based and dynamic routing plus App Router.

value.label: Security update chain
value.description: vulnerability → CVE → affected_versions → fix_package → updated_version
value.expression: vulnerability → CVE → affected_versions → fix_package → updated_version
value.meaning: Source describes a React vulnerability propagating downstream to Next.js and being fixed through an npm package.

value.label: Server-side vs client-side rendering
value.description: Server rendering occurs before content is sent to the browser; traditional React client rendering occurs in the browser.

value.label: Static vs dynamic rendering
value.description: Static output is built/cached ahead of requests; interactive/changing sites may not fit pure static generation.

value.label: SSR vs ISR
value.description: SSR renders on the server; ISR retains static output while supporting incremental regeneration.

value.label: App Router vs page-based routing
value.description: App Router is the newer routing architecture with layouts/RSC/streaming; page-based routing is the older routing model described by the source.

value.label: Webpack vs Turbopack
value.description: Webpack was the established bundler; Turbopack is described as its successor/replacement.

value.label: Compiler/transpiler vs bundler
value.description: SWC transforms/compiles code while Webpack/Turbopack bundle modules.

value.label: Code splitting vs prefetching
value.description: Code splitting reduces shipped code; prefetching anticipates resources to reduce load time.

value.label: Hot reload vs HMR
value.description: Both provide rapid development updates; HMR specifically replaces modules live.

value.label: Node/server vs browser runtime
value.description: Next.js spans server/runtime execution and browser delivery rather than being purely client-side.

value.label: Serverless vs self-deployment
value.description: Serverless uses on-demand functions; self-deployment is separately supported.

value.label: Next.js vs React
value.description: React is the underlying UI library; Next.js is a framework adding application architecture and rendering/deployment capabilities.

value.label: Edge runtime vs traditional server rendering
value.description: Edge capabilities are a deployment/runtime feature; server rendering is an application rendering model.

value.label: Framework vs toolchain
value.description: Next.js is the framework; Turbo/Turbopack/Turborepo are supporting development/build tools.

value.label: Vulnerability vs remediation
value.description: CVE records identify vulnerabilities; fix-react2shell-next is the remediation package described by the source.

value.label: Next.js is just React
value.description: Next.js is described as a full-stack framework built around React, adding server/static rendering, routing, data fetching, bundling and deployment capabilities.

value.label: Next.js only renders on the server
value.description: Next.js supports server rendering, static rendering, and client-side React behavior.

value.label: Static generation works for every site
value.description: The source explicitly notes static output is not suitable for every site, particularly highly interactive sites with frequent changes/user input.

value.label: SSR and static generation are identical
value.description: The source distinguishes server-side rendering from build-time static generation and caching.

value.label: App Router was always the Next.js routing system
value.description: App Router was introduced in Next.js 13 and stabilized in 13.4.

value.label: Turbopack and SWC do the same thing
value.description: SWC is described as a transpiler/compiler; Turbopack is a bundler.

value.label: Hot reload means the server must restart
value.description: Hot reloading is specifically described as avoiding server restart while reflecting code changes.

value.label: Next.js cannot deploy without Vercel
value.description: The source says Next.js has supported self-deployment since 2016 and Next.js 16 adds Build Adapters for hosting integration.

value.label: Next.js 13.4 only added another experimental router
value.description: The source says 13.4 made App Router stable for production.

value.label: Server rendering automatically makes every application secure
value.description: The source attributes an enhanced-security benefit to server rendering but separately documents a severe Next.js/React vulnerability.

value.label: Next.js versions have no architectural evolution
value.description: The source documents a progression from page routing/server rendering through App Router, RSC, streaming, Rust tooling and Build Adapters.

value.label: Webpack is the only bundler Next.js uses
value.description: The source describes Webpack and its replacement/evolution toward Turbopack.
