formal_models.label: Rendering choice
formal_models.description: rendering_mode ∈ {client, server, static}
formal_models.meaning: Next.js expands React's client-rendering model with server/static rendering.

formal_models.label: Static delivery flow
formal_models.description: source → build → .next → static HTML → cache → browser
formal_models.expression: source → build → .next → static HTML → cache → browser
formal_models.meaning: Build-time static generation produces artifacts that can be cached and served.

formal_models.label: Automatic code splitting
formal_models.description: page_request → required_code_only
formal_models.meaning: Only code necessary to load a page is included.

formal_models.label: Serverless execution
formal_models.description: application_code → lambda_functions → on_demand_execution
formal_models.meaning: Next.js 8 split code into on-demand lambda functions.

formal_models.label: App Router architecture
formal_models.description: route → layout + server_component + stream + data_fetching
formal_models.meaning: App Router combines layouts, React Server Components, streaming and new data fetching.

formal_models.label: Compilation toolchain
formal_models.description: source → SWC/compiler → bundler → browser/deployment
formal_models.meaning: Next.js uses compiler/transpiler and bundling stages.

formal_models.label: Development update loop
formal_models.description: code_change → detect → rerender/replace_module → browser
formal_models.meaning: Hot reload/HMR provides immediate development feedback.

formal_models.label: Incremental regeneration
formal_models.description: static_output + later_regeneration
formal_models.meaning: ISR extends static generation with incremental regeneration.

formal_models.label: Routing
formal_models.description: URL/path → routing_system → page/component
formal_models.meaning: Next.js provides page-based and dynamic routing plus App Router.

formal_models.label: Security update chain
formal_models.description: vulnerability → CVE → affected_versions → fix_package → updated_version
formal_models.meaning: Source describes a React vulnerability propagating downstream to Next.js and being fixed through an npm package.

source_claims.label: Next.js identity
source_claims.description: Next.js is an open-source full-stack React-based web framework maintained by Vercel and the open-source community.

source_claims.label: Rendering
source_claims.description: Next.js extends traditional React client rendering with server-side and static rendering.

source_claims.label: Development history
source_claims.description: The source documents releases from 2016 through 2026 and a progression of routing, rendering, tooling and deployment capabilities.

source_claims.label: Toolchain
source_claims.description: Next.js uses compiler/transpiler and bundler tooling including SWC, Webpack and increasingly Turbopack.

source_claims.label: Features
source_claims.description: Routing, code splitting, prefetching, hot reload/HMR, ISR, styling and data fetching are core framework capabilities.

source_claims.label: Security
source_claims.description: The source describes a severe React Server Component vulnerability and downstream Next.js impact in 2025.

semantic_distinctions.label: Server-side vs client-side rendering
semantic_distinctions.description: Server rendering occurs before content is sent to the browser; traditional React client rendering occurs in the browser.

semantic_distinctions.label: Static vs dynamic rendering
semantic_distinctions.description: Static output is built/cached ahead of requests; interactive/changing sites may not fit pure static generation.

semantic_distinctions.label: SSR vs ISR
semantic_distinctions.description: SSR renders on the server; ISR retains static output while supporting incremental regeneration.

semantic_distinctions.label: App Router vs page-based routing
semantic_distinctions.description: App Router is the newer routing architecture with layouts/RSC/streaming; page-based routing is the older routing model described by the source.

semantic_distinctions.label: Webpack vs Turbopack
semantic_distinctions.description: Webpack was the established bundler; Turbopack is described as its successor/replacement.

semantic_distinctions.label: Compiler/transpiler vs bundler
semantic_distinctions.description: SWC transforms/compiles code while Webpack/Turbopack bundle modules.

semantic_distinctions.label: Code splitting vs prefetching
semantic_distinctions.description: Code splitting reduces shipped code; prefetching anticipates resources to reduce load time.

semantic_distinctions.label: Hot reload vs HMR
semantic_distinctions.description: Both provide rapid development updates; HMR specifically replaces modules live.

semantic_distinctions.label: Node/server vs browser runtime
semantic_distinctions.description: Next.js spans server/runtime execution and browser delivery rather than being purely client-side.

semantic_distinctions.label: Serverless vs self-deployment
semantic_distinctions.description: Serverless uses on-demand functions; self-deployment is separately supported.

semantic_distinctions.label: Next.js vs React
semantic_distinctions.description: React is the underlying UI library; Next.js is a framework adding application architecture and rendering/deployment capabilities.

semantic_distinctions.label: Edge runtime vs traditional server rendering
semantic_distinctions.description: Edge capabilities are a deployment/runtime feature; server rendering is an application rendering model.

semantic_distinctions.label: Framework vs toolchain
semantic_distinctions.description: Next.js is the framework; Turbo/Turbopack/Turborepo are supporting development/build tools.

semantic_distinctions.label: Vulnerability vs remediation
semantic_distinctions.description: CVE records identify vulnerabilities; fix-react2shell-next is the remediation package described by the source.

misconceptions.label: Next.js is just React
misconceptions.description: Next.js is described as a full-stack framework built around React, adding server/static rendering, routing, data fetching, bundling and deployment capabilities.

misconceptions.label: Next.js only renders on the server
misconceptions.description: Next.js supports server rendering, static rendering, and client-side React behavior.

misconceptions.label: Static generation works for every site
misconceptions.description: The source explicitly notes static output is not suitable for every site, particularly highly interactive sites with frequent changes/user input.

misconceptions.label: SSR and static generation are identical
misconceptions.description: The source distinguishes server-side rendering from build-time static generation and caching.

misconceptions.label: App Router was always the Next.js routing system
misconceptions.description: App Router was introduced in Next.js 13 and stabilized in 13.4.

misconceptions.label: Turbopack and SWC do the same thing
misconceptions.description: SWC is described as a transpiler/compiler; Turbopack is a bundler.

misconceptions.label: Hot reload means the server must restart
misconceptions.description: Hot reloading is specifically described as avoiding server restart while reflecting code changes.

misconceptions.label: Next.js cannot deploy without Vercel
misconceptions.description: The source says Next.js has supported self-deployment since 2016 and Next.js 16 adds Build Adapters for hosting integration.

misconceptions.label: Next.js 13.4 only added another experimental router
misconceptions.description: The source says 13.4 made App Router stable for production.

misconceptions.label: Server rendering automatically makes every application secure
misconceptions.description: The source attributes an enhanced-security benefit to server rendering but separately documents a severe Next.js/React vulnerability.

misconceptions.label: Next.js versions have no architectural evolution
misconceptions.description: The source documents a progression from page routing/server rendering through App Router, RSC, streaming, Rust tooling and Build Adapters.

misconceptions.label: Webpack is the only bundler Next.js uses
misconceptions.description: The source describes Webpack and its replacement/evolution toward Turbopack.

value.core_thesis: An operating system is system software that manages computer hardware/software resources and provides common services, while mediating hardware access, isolating applications, abstracting hardware, scheduling execution, managing memory/I/O, and providing security and portability mechanisms.
value.relationship_policy: Relationships are directional and mechanism-bearing where possible. Rich edges preserve mechanism, effect, conditions, inverse/converse, scope and architectural context.

value.mechanism: The OS decides when applications receive CPU time and how much memory/resources they receive.
value.effect: Prevents a single application from monopolizing limited hardware and enables concurrent application execution.
value.conditions: Multiple applications contend for finite CPU and memory resources.
value.inverse_or_converse: Without allocation, one program could monopolize resources.

value.mechanism: The OS separates applications so errors and security vulnerabilities in one application are contained while communication remains possible.
value.effect: Improves reliability and security without eliminating application communication.
value.conditions: Isolation must coexist with controlled inter-application communication.
value.inverse_or_converse: Unrestricted sharing increases interference risk.

value.mechanism: OS interfaces hide hardware-access details such as physical memory behind standardized services/interfaces.
value.effect: Programmers can develop against OS abstractions rather than hardware-specific details.
value.conditions: Hardware differences remain beneath the abstraction.
value.inverse_or_converse: Bypassing abstractions increases hardware dependence.

value.mechanism: OS exposes reusable interfaces for networking, disks and other common facilities.
value.effect: Applications can run across different hardware without being rewritten for each hardware implementation.
value.conditions: Service set varies greatly between OS designs.
value.inverse_or_converse: Missing services can force applications to depend on hardware-specific implementations.

value.mechanism: Paging/segmentation let the kernel choose mappings and use disk/RAM as a larger logical memory space.
value.effect: A program can perceive a large continuous address space even when physical memory is scattered or limited.
value.conditions: Requires hardware support and OS memory-management mechanisms.
value.inverse_or_converse: Invalid/restricted addresses can trigger faults.

value.mechanism: Kernel-enforced protection separates applications/users and limits their resource authority.
value.effect: Errors remain isolated and malicious software has less power to compromise private data or monopolize resources.
value.conditions: Depends on hardware privilege/memory-protection mechanisms.
value.inverse_or_converse: Broken protection increases cross-process interference.

value.mechanism: Hardware checks user-mode software for legal instructions while kernel mode has unrestricted powers.
value.effect: Separates ordinary application execution from privileged OS control.
value.conditions: Requires processor support for privilege modes.
value.inverse_or_converse: Executing privileged operations from user mode is prevented or traps to the kernel.

value.mechanism: The kernel creates a process, assigns memory/resources/priority, loads its binary and starts execution.
value.effect: Turns an application program into a managed unit of execution.
value.conditions: Exact process model varies by OS.
value.inverse_or_converse: An application may also execute another application within the same process or via a separate thread in systems described.

value.mechanism: An interrupt changes CPU control flow to an interrupt service routine; state is saved and later restored.
value.effect: Allows the OS to react efficiently to hardware/software events.
value.conditions: Architecture-specific interrupt handling differs.
value.inverse_or_converse: No interrupt handling would prevent timely OS reaction to device/events.

value.mechanism: When a device completes I/O it can interrupt the running process/CPU and provide status information.
value.effect: The OS can resume or schedule the process associated with the completed I/O.
value.conditions: Uses interrupt handlers, process state and context switching.
value.inverse_or_converse: If completion is not handled, the waiting process cannot be resumed normally.

value.mechanism: The scheduler changes the running process by saving one process's CPU state and restoring another's.
value.effect: CPU time is shared among runnable processes.
value.conditions: Depends on saved CPU state such as registers and program counter.
value.inverse_or_converse: A context switch is unnecessary when no process change occurs.

value.mechanism: Hardware-supported segmentation or paging restricts which addresses a process may access.
value.effect: One process cannot normally overwrite another process's memory; invalid access triggers an interrupt/fault.
value.conditions: Requires hardware support such as an MMU.
value.inverse_or_converse: A faulty/malicious access can cause a segmentation violation and process termination.

value.mechanism: Protected registers define permitted address regions; invalid access causes an interrupt and re-entry into supervisor mode.
value.effect: The kernel regains control and can terminate the offending program.
value.conditions: The source describes segmentation violation as a common response.
value.inverse_or_converse: Valid access avoids the fault.

value.mechanism: When one job waits for I/O, another job can use the CPU; multiple jobs are held in memory with partitioning and safeguards.
value.effect: Improves CPU utilization while preventing one job from accessing another's memory.
value.conditions: Requires memory partitioning/protection.
value.inverse_or_converse: Without multiprogramming, I/O wait would leave CPU less utilized.

value.mechanism: IEEE POSIX standardizes OS application-programming interfaces supported by most UNIX systems.
value.effect: Applications gain a common API target across compatible UNIX systems.
value.conditions: POSIX is an API compatibility standard, not an operating system.
value.inverse_or_converse: Nonstandard APIs reduce portability.

value.mechanism: OS services are provided as libraries and composed with one application/configuration code into a specialized single-address-space image.
value.effect: Avoids usual context-switch overhead and can deploy a minimal machine image.
value.conditions: Single application means traditional inter-application protection domains are unnecessary in the described model.
value.inverse_or_converse: More conventional OS boundaries reintroduce mode/context-switch overhead.

value.mechanism: Mode switching can pollute important processor structures including caches and the instruction pipeline.
value.effect: System-call/mode-switch overhead can reduce user- and kernel-mode performance beyond direct switching cost.
value.conditions: The cited FlexSC discussion emphasizes both direct and indirect costs.
value.inverse_or_converse: Avoiding or reducing mode switches can reduce this source of overhead.

value.mechanism: Remote direct memory access permits one CPU to access memory belonging to another CPU.
value.effect: Reduces reliance on packet copying for cross-CPU data movement.
value.conditions: Architecture/network support is required.
value.inverse_or_converse: Without RDMA, explicit communication/copying mechanisms are used.

value.mechanism: Middleware sits between OS and applications and is used to improve consistency across distinct networked computers.
value.effect: Provides a higher-level coordination layer without becoming the OS.
value.conditions: Each participating computer can retain its own OS and filesystem.
value.inverse_or_converse: Middleware is not itself a true OS.

value.mechanism: Hard real-time systems require exact processing by or at specified moments.
value.effect: Missed deadlines are unacceptable in the intended timing model.
value.conditions: Common in manufacturing, avionics and military uses per source.
value.inverse_or_converse: Soft real-time permits occasional missed events.

value.mechanism: Soft real-time accepts occasional missed events.
value.effect: Supports workloads such as audio/multimedia and smartphones where occasional deadline misses are acceptable.
value.conditions: Timing guarantee is weaker than hard real-time.
value.inverse_or_converse: Hard real-time does not permit the same relaxation.

value.mechanism: Windows uses ACLs, integrity levels, process authentication tokens and object security descriptors.
value.effect: Controls access to objects and processes and strengthens OS security.
value.conditions: Later releases add further security features.
value.inverse_or_converse: Removing access controls broadens authority.

value.mechanism: Android is closely based on Linux and uses a Linux kernel with Bionic.
value.effect: Provides a Linux-derived OS foundation for mobile and embedded systems.
value.conditions: Much Android code is written in Java and uses object-oriented design.
value.inverse_or_converse: The Android user-space stack differs from a conventional Linux distribution.

value.mechanism: Linux is written in C according to the source.
value.effect: Provides a low-level systems implementation foundation.
value.conditions: The source also describes UNIX-compatible syntax/networking and multiple-user preemptive multitasking.
value.inverse_or_converse: Different language choices would change implementation properties but not the OS abstraction itself.

value.mechanism: VMs can be paused, saved and resumed and can emulate hardware for an OS.
value.effect: Useful for OS research, development and debugging, while improving portability.
value.conditions: The VM acts as an application emulating hardware.
value.inverse_or_converse: Without virtualization, incompatible applications may require compatible base OS/hardware.

value.mechanism: Embedded systems described do not load user-installed software, so they may not need protection between applications.
value.effect: Permits very small/simple OS designs.
value.conditions: Applies to the embedded systems described in the source.
value.inverse_or_converse: General-purpose user-installed software would create stronger isolation requirements.

value.expression: finite_resource -> scheduler/allocation -> application_share
value.meaning: OS divides scarce CPU time and memory/resource space among applications.

value.name: Program execution
value.expression: program -> kernel -> process -> memory/resources/priority -> binary_loaded -> execution
value.meaning: Typical application launch path described by the source.

value.name: Interrupt flow
value.expression: event -> interrupt -> ISR -> save_state -> service -> restore_state
value.meaning: Common hardware/software interrupt control-flow sequence.

value.name: Context switch
value.expression: old_process_state -> save -> new_process_state -> restore -> resume
value.meaning: CPU changes from one process to another.

value.name: Memory protection
value.expression: virtual_address -> paging/segmentation -> allowed_region | fault -> kernel
value.meaning: Hardware-supported protection restricts process memory access.

value.name: Virtual memory
value.expression: RAM + backing_store -> virtual_address_space -> process
value.meaning: Kernel presents memory as a logical address space larger/different from physical layout.

value.name: Linux system structure
value.expression: kernel + system_libraries + system_utilities -> Linux_distribution
value.meaning: Structure explicitly described for Linux distributions.

value.name: Library OS / unikernel
value.expression: libraries + application + configuration -> single_address_space_machine_image
value.meaning: Specialized machine image with only necessary library code.

value.name: Multicomputer communication
value.expression: CPU_A <-> messages/RDMA/RPC/DSM <-> CPU_B
value.meaning: Communication techniques listed for multicomputers.

value.name: POSIX portability
value.expression: UNIX_application -> POSIX_API -> compatible_UNIX_systems
value.meaning: POSIX improves compatibility among UNIX systems.

value.name: Windows security object model
value.expression: process -> authentication_token; object -> security_descriptor/ACL/integrity_level
value.meaning: Security mechanisms described for Windows.

value.name: Real-time timing
value.expression: event/data -> deadline -> hard_exact | soft_occasional_miss
value.meaning: Distinguishes hard and soft real-time behavior.

OS vs kernel
value.description: Kernel is the always-running core; an OS can include system programs and other software beyond the kernel.

value.label: OS vs application
value.description: OS provides resource management/services; applications are other software running on the computer.

value.label: OS abstraction vs direct hardware execution
value.description: Application code generally executes directly on hardware but requests OS services and follows OS rules for privileged/hardware operations.

value.label: Multiprocessor vs multicomputer
value.description: Multiprocessors share memory; multicomputers have multiple CPUs with separate memory.

value.label: Multicomputer vs distributed system
value.description: Multicomputers are tightly coupled CPU/memory systems; distributed systems are distinct networked computers potentially dispersed worldwide.

value.label: Middleware vs OS
value.description: Middleware can function similarly to an OS but is an additional layer and not a true OS.

value.label: Embedded vs general purpose
value.description: Embedded systems may omit user-application protection because they do not load user-installed software.

value.label: Hard vs soft real-time
value.description: Hard real-time requires exact timing; soft real-time tolerates occasional missed events.

value.label: Hypervisor vs VM
value.description: The source describes the hypervisor as running a VM, while the VM is the application that emulates hardware.

value.label: Library OS vs conventional OS
value.description: libOS provides OS services as libraries composed with an application, reducing protection/context-switch overhead in the described single-application model.

value.label: User mode vs kernel mode
value.description: User mode is hardware-restricted; kernel mode has unrestricted OS privilege.

value.label: Hardware vs software interrupt
value.description: Hardware interrupt reports an event to the CPU; software interrupt communicates an event to a process/change of execution.

value.label: Interrupt vs signal
value.description: Signals are Unix-like process notifications analogous to software/hardware interrupt behavior but are an OS process communication mechanism.

value.label: Segmentation vs paging
value.description: Both provide memory protection, but they are distinct address-management mechanisms requiring hardware support.

value.label: Virtual memory vs physical memory
value.description: Virtual memory presents a logical address space whose backing can span RAM and disk rather than exposing physical layout directly.

value.label: Context switch vs interrupt
value.description: An interrupt can cause a context switch, but an interrupt is the event/control-transfer mechanism whereas a context switch changes the running process.

value.label: Resource allocation vs isolation
value.description: Allocation shares finite resources; isolation prevents one application's errors/authority from interfering with others.

value.label: Portability vs abstraction
value.description: Hardware abstraction and common OS services let applications run across different hardware without rewriting hardware-specific access.

value.label: UNIX vs POSIX
value.description: UNIX is an OS family/history; POSIX is an API standard for compatibility.

value.label: Linux vs Android
value.description: Android is closely based on Linux but uses a distinct user-space stack including Bionic and substantial Java code.

value.label: GUI vs CLI
value.description: GUI provides graphical interaction; CLI is text-based command interaction.

value.label: Preemptive vs cooperative behavior
value.description: Preemptive multitasking lets the OS scheduler interrupt/reassign CPU execution rather than relying entirely on voluntary cooperation.

value.label: System call vs library call
value.description: System calls request kernel services; libOS services can be accessed through simple library calls without usual context switches.

value.label: Protection vs no protection
value.description: Some specialized OS designs deliberately omit conventional application protection when their workload model makes it unnecessary.

value.statement: An operating system is just the kernel.
value.correction: The source explicitly distinguishes the kernel from system programs and applications; an OS can include software beyond the kernel.

value.statement: Applications never execute directly on hardware.
value.correction: The source says application code is usually executed directly by hardware while interacting with OS services through calls/interrupts.

value.statement: OS abstraction means hardware is irrelevant.
value.correction: The OS abstracts hardware details, but the kernel, drivers and hardware privilege mechanisms still mediate execution.

value.statement: Multicomputer and multiprocessor mean the same thing.
value.correction: Multiprocessors share memory; multicomputers have separate memory per CPU.

value.statement: A distributed system is one giant computer.
value.correction: The source describes distinct networked computers, potentially dispersed worldwide, each with its own OS/filesystem.

value.statement: All operating systems require full application isolation.
value.correction: Embedded and some hard-real-time/library OS designs may omit protection between applications under their workload assumptions.

value.statement: Real-time means merely fast.
value.correction: Real-time is defined by timing guarantees/deadlines; hard real-time requires exact timing, not simply high throughput.

value.statement: A VM is the same thing as a hypervisor.
value.correction: The source distinguishes the hypervisor from the VM it runs.

value.statement: Virtual memory is the same as physical RAM.
value.correction: Virtual memory abstracts physical memory and can use scattered RAM and disk/backing storage.

value.statement: Every interrupt is a context switch.
value.correction: An interrupt can cause a context switch; the interrupt itself is the event/control-transfer mechanism.

value.statement: A software interrupt is a hardware interrupt.
value.correction: The source distinguishes software interrupts/messages to processes from hardware interrupts/messages to the CPU.

value.statement: POSIX is a UNIX operating system.
value.correction: POSIX is an API standard intended to increase compatibility among UNIX systems.

source_claims.statement: An operating system manages computer hardware/software resources and provides common services for computer programs.
Time-sharing OSes schedule tasks for efficient system use and may account for resource consumption.
OS acts as an intermediary for input/output and memory allocation while application code usually executes directly on hardware.
OS resource allocation shares CPU time/memory and prevents one program monopolizing limited hardware.
OS isolates applications to protect against errors/security vulnerabilities while enabling communication.
OS abstracts hardware access and virtualization can mask limited hardware resources.
OS common services for network/disk access enable applications to run across different hardware.
Multicomputers have multiple CPUs with separate memory and need efficient communication.
Distributed systems consist of distinct networked computers that may have their own OS/filesystem; middleware can improve consistency.
Embedded OSes target embedded systems and may omit application protection when no user-installed software is loaded.
Hard real-time systems require exact timing; soft real-time permits occasional missed events.
Hypervisors run VMs that emulate hardware and support OS research/development/debugging and portability.
Library OS services can be composed into a specialized single-address-space unikernel.
Early computers were directly programmed without OSes; operators manually performed scheduling/resource-management tasks.
OS/360 popularized multiprogramming and required memory partitioning and safeguards.
MULTICS targeted hundreds of simultaneous users; UNIX originated as a single-user development of MULTICS.
UNIX source availability led to System V and BSD; POSIX improved compatibility.
MINIX inspired Linux; MINIX later appeared in Intel microchip controllers.
CP/M was popular on early microcomputers; MS-DOS/IBM PC DOS became widespread on IBM PC compatibles.
Macintosh popularized GUI; Windows evolved from a GUI overlay to standalone Windows NT.
Android became a major mobile OS, using a Linux kernel and Bionic C library.
Kernel protects applications/users, manages memory, controls I/O, and separates user/kernel privilege.
Program execution typically creates a process, assigns resources/priority, loads binary code and starts execution.
Interrupts transfer control to an ISR and require saving/restoring execution state.
Software interrupts can represent normal timing, errors, user messages, and process communication.
Unix signals communicate asynchronous events; pipes coordinate producer/consumer processes.
Memory protection uses hardware-supported segmentation/paging; invalid access can trigger a segmentation violation.
Virtual memory can map scattered RAM/disk storage into a logical continuous address space.
Windows uses NTFS, Windows Driver Model, demand paging, preemptive scheduling, ACLs, integrity levels, authentication tokens and security descriptors.
Linux is distributed under GPL, uses a kernel/libraries/utilities structure, supports UNIX networking and preemptive multitasking, and can operate from small systems to large multiprocessors.

semantic_distinctions.label: OS vs kernel
semantic_distinctions.description: Kernel is the always-running core; an OS can include system programs and other software beyond the kernel.

semantic_distinctions.label: OS vs application
semantic_distinctions.description: OS provides resource management/services; applications are other software running on the computer.

semantic_distinctions.label: OS abstraction vs direct hardware execution
semantic_distinctions.description: Application code generally executes directly on hardware but requests OS services and follows OS rules for privileged/hardware operations.

semantic_distinctions.label: Multiprocessor vs multicomputer
semantic_distinctions.description: Multiprocessors share memory; multicomputers have multiple CPUs with separate memory.

semantic_distinctions.label: Multicomputer vs distributed system
semantic_distinctions.description: Multicomputers are tightly coupled CPU/memory systems; distributed systems are distinct networked computers potentially dispersed worldwide.

semantic_distinctions.label: Middleware vs OS
semantic_distinctions.description: Middleware can function similarly to an OS but is an additional layer and not a true OS.

semantic_distinctions.label: Embedded vs general purpose
semantic_distinctions.description: Embedded systems may omit user-application protection because they do not load user-installed software.

semantic_distinctions.label: Hard vs soft real-time
semantic_distinctions.description: Hard real-time requires exact timing; soft real-time tolerates occasional missed events.

semantic_distinctions.label: Hypervisor vs VM
semantic_distinctions.description: The source describes the hypervisor as running a VM, while the VM is the application that emulates hardware.

semantic_distinctions.label: Library OS vs conventional OS
semantic_distinctions.description: libOS provides OS services as libraries composed with an application, reducing protection/context-switch overhead in the described single-application model.

semantic_distinctions.label: User mode vs kernel mode
semantic_distinctions.description: User mode is hardware-restricted; kernel mode has unrestricted OS privilege.

semantic_distinctions.label: Hardware vs software interrupt
semantic_distinctions.description: Hardware interrupt reports an event to the CPU; software interrupt communicates an event to a process/change of execution.

semantic_distinctions.label: Interrupt vs signal
semantic_distinctions.description: Signals are Unix-like process notifications analogous to software/hardware interrupt behavior but are an OS process communication mechanism.

semantic_distinctions.label: Segmentation vs paging
semantic_distinctions.description: Both provide memory protection, but they are distinct address-management mechanisms requiring hardware support.

semantic_distinctions.label: Virtual memory vs physical memory
semantic_distinctions.description: Virtual memory presents a logical address space whose backing can span RAM and disk rather than exposing physical layout directly.

semantic_distinctions.label: Context switch vs interrupt
semantic_distinctions.description: An interrupt can cause a context switch, but an interrupt is the event/control-transfer mechanism whereas a context switch changes the running process.

semantic_distinctions.label: Resource allocation vs isolation
semantic_distinctions.description: Allocation shares finite resources; isolation prevents one application's errors/authority from interfering with others.

semantic_distinctions.label: Portability vs abstraction
semantic_distinctions.description: Hardware abstraction and common OS services let applications run across different hardware without rewriting hardware-specific access.

semantic_distinctions.label: UNIX vs POSIX
semantic_distinctions.description: UNIX is an OS family/history; POSIX is an API standard for compatibility.

semantic_distinctions.label: Linux vs Android
semantic_distinctions.description: Android is closely based on Linux but uses a distinct user-space stack including Bionic and substantial Java code.

semantic_distinctions.label: GUI vs CLI
semantic_distinctions.description: GUI provides graphical interaction; CLI is text-based command interaction.

semantic_distinctions.label: Preemptive vs cooperative behavior
semantic_distinctions.description: Preemptive multitasking lets the OS scheduler interrupt/reassign CPU execution rather than relying entirely on voluntary cooperation.

semantic_distinctions.label: System call vs library call
semantic_distinctions.description: System calls request kernel services; libOS services can be accessed through simple library calls without usual context switches.

semantic_distinctions.label: Protection vs no protection
semantic_distinctions.description: Some specialized OS designs deliberately omit conventional application protection when their workload model makes it unnecessary.

misconceptions.statement: An operating system is just the kernel.
misconceptions.correction: The source explicitly distinguishes the kernel from system programs and applications; an OS can include software beyond the kernel.

misconceptions.statement: Applications never execute directly on hardware.
misconceptions.correction: The source says application code is usually executed directly by hardware while interacting with OS services through calls/interrupts.

misconceptions.statement: OS abstraction means hardware is irrelevant.
misconceptions.correction: The OS abstracts hardware details, but the kernel, drivers and hardware privilege mechanisms still mediate execution.

misconceptions.statement: Multicomputer and multiprocessor mean the same thing.
misconceptions.correction: Multiprocessors share memory; multicomputers have separate memory per CPU.

misconceptions.statement: A distributed system is one giant computer.
misconceptions.correction: The source describes distinct networked computers, potentially dispersed worldwide, each with its own OS/filesystem.

misconceptions.statement: All operating systems require full application isolation.
misconceptions.correction: Embedded and some hard-real-time/library OS designs may omit protection between applications under their workload assumptions.

misconceptions.statement: Real-time means merely fast.
misconceptions.correction: Real-time is defined by timing guarantees/deadlines; hard real-time requires exact timing, not simply high throughput.

misconceptions.statement: A VM is the same thing as a hypervisor.
misconceptions.correction: The source distinguishes the hypervisor from the VM it runs.

misconceptions.statement: Virtual memory is the same as physical RAM.
misconceptions.correction: Virtual memory abstracts physical memory and can use scattered RAM and disk/backing storage.

misconceptions.statement: Every interrupt is a context switch.
misconceptions.correction: An interrupt can cause a context switch; the interrupt itself is the event/control-transfer mechanism.

misconceptions.statement: A software interrupt is a hardware interrupt.
misconceptions.correction: The source distinguishes software interrupts/messages to processes from hardware interrupts/messages to the CPU.

misconceptions.statement: POSIX is a UNIX operating system.
misconceptions.correction: POSIX is an API standard intended to increase compatibility among UNIX systems.

value.distinction: Layer is an architectural scope; protocol implements peer communication.
A PDU becomes an SDU when passed to the lower layer.
Sender adds metadata downward; receiver strips it upward.
Service describes functionality; protocol defines peer behavior.
Physical sends signals; link frames and controls directly connected nodes.
Link is node-to-node; network crosses different networks.
Network routes packets; transport manages application data sequences.
Session manages dialogs; transport manages end-to-end transfer.
Presentation translates data; application provides high-level services.
OSI explicitly has seven layers; TCP/IP uses broader functional scopes.

value.misconception: Every protocol fits cleanly in one layer.
value.correction: The source explicitly describes cross-layer functions and approximate mappings.

value.misconception: Every PDU is called a packet.
value.correction: OSI uses data, segment, packet/datagram, frame, and bit/symbol terminology.

value.misconception: Each layer is a separate physical device.
value.correction: Layers are abstractions that may be implemented across software and hardware.

value.misconception: Physical layer only means cables.
value.correction: It includes electrical/radio/optical signals, timing, modulation, connectors, and wireless parameters.

value.misconception: Network layer guarantees delivery.
value.correction: Network delivery need not be reliable.

value.misconception: Transport means TCP.
value.correction: The source includes multiple transport protocols and connection modes.

value.misconception: TCP/IP has a mandatory session layer.
value.correction: TCP/IP does not distinguish a separate session layer.

value.misconception: Presentation only means encryption.
value.correction: It also covers translation, encoding, and compression.

value.misconception: OSI and TCP/IP layers are identical.
value.correction: The source gives approximate mappings and important differences.

value.misconception: OSI protocols became the dominant Internet stack.
value.correction: TCP/IP became widespread while OSI protocols did not gain broad popularity.

fields.label: Design principles
value: Packet analyzer is a first-class operational tool node.
Capture, decode, analyze, store, display, generate, and test are modeled as distinct capabilities/processes.
Capture visibility is modeled as a function of network topology, capture location, interfaces, and modes.
Full-packet and header-only capture are separate modes with explicit storage/privacy tradeoffs.
Wired and wireless capture architectures are distinct branches.
Security, operations, debugging, compliance, and testing uses are represented as downstream applications.
Notable analyzers are retained as individual nodes rather than collapsed into a generic list.
Source-derived legal and privacy framing is preserved without adding external legal claims.

design_principles: Packet analyzer is a first-class operational tool node.
Capture, decode, analyze, store, display, generate, and test are modeled as distinct capabilities/processes.
Capture visibility is modeled as a function of network topology, capture location, interfaces, and modes.
Full-packet and header-only capture are separate modes with explicit storage/privacy tradeoffs.
Wired and wireless capture architectures are distinct branches.
Security, operations, debugging, compliance, and testing uses are represented as downstream applications.
Notable analyzers are retained as individual nodes rather than collapsed into a generic list.
Source-derived legal and privacy framing is preserved without adding external legal claims.

value.note: Graph preserves source-derived claims and labels deeper expansion targets separately rather than presenting them as source facts.

value.name: Automatic differentiation model
value.expression: forward pass → computation DAG → loss → backward/backpropagation → gradients
value.meaning: PyTorch records operations during forward execution and uses the resulting graph to compute gradients.

value.name: Tensor execution model
value.expression: tensor + operation + device → device-resident result
value.meaning: Tensor operations execute according to the selected CPU/GPU backend.

value.name: Neural network composition
value.expression: nn.Module → Sequential/layers/activations → forward() → logits
value.meaning: The source example constructs a network from reusable modules and returns logits.

value.name: Gradient training loop
value.expression: input → forward → loss → backward → gradient → optimizer update
value.meaning: A conceptual training cycle derived directly from the source's autograd and training description.

value.name: PyTorch compiler path
value.expression: Python/model execution → TorchDynamo graph capture → optimized execution
value.meaning: PyTorch 2.0 introduced a Python-level compiler path centered on TorchDynamo.

value.name: Serialization structure
value.expression: model weights + metadata → ZIP64 archive → .pt/.pth
value.meaning: The source describes PyTorch serialization as ZIP64 containing weights and metadata.

value.name: Framework interoperability
value.expression: PyTorch model → ONNX → provider/runtime such as TensorRT
value.meaning: ONNX provides a framework-neutral path for conversion/optimization.

value.name: Backend abstraction
value.expression: PyTorch API → runtime → backend → CPU/GPU execution
value.meaning: High-level PyTorch operations map through runtime/backend layers to hardware.

value.name: Framework lineage
value.expression: Torch → Torch7/LuaTorch → autograd/refactoring influences → PyTorch
value.meaning: The source establishes a historical lineage from Torch into PyTorch.

value.name: Governance transition
value.expression: Meta AI → independent PyTorch Foundation → Linux Foundation
value.meaning: The source describes the 2022 governance transition.

value.name: Device placement
value.expression: torch.device(cuda:0) → CUDA GPU tensor operations
value.meaning: The source example demonstrates explicit device selection.

value.name: Model artifact lifecycle
value.expression: trained weights → serialization → file artifact → load/deploy
value.meaning: Connects model training to persistence and later deployment; deployment is an expansion target.

value.distinction: Similar multidimensional numeric-array abstraction, but PyTorch tensors are integrated with device backends and automatic differentiation.
Autograd is the automatic differentiation system/graph mechanism; backpropagation is the backward gradient computation enabled by the recorded graph.
PyTorch is the successor to Torch rather than merely a renamed release.
Python is the primary high-level API language while C++ participates in the implementation/runtime stack.
CUDA is NVIDIA's GPU platform; ROCm and Metal represent other supported accelerator backends.
Training optimizes model parameters; inference executes a trained model for outputs.
nn.Module is the compositional base abstraction; layers such as Linear/ReLU are concrete modules.
Serialization persists PyTorch model artifacts; ONNX is intended for framework/hardware interoperability.
Bindings are software integration; the GPU is the hardware execution target.
TorchDynamo is a compiler/graph-capture mechanism; Autograd computes derivatives.
Meta originally developed/operated PyTorch; governance later moved toward an independent foundation.
Tensor operations are primitive numerical computations; neural networks compose many operations/modules into a trainable model.

value.misconception: PyTorch is just Python code.
value.correction: The source identifies Python, C++ and CUDA together; the high-level Python API sits over lower-level implementation and acceleration layers.

value.misconception: A PyTorch tensor is exactly the same as a NumPy array.
value.correction: The source says tensors are similar to NumPy arrays but additionally support CUDA-capable GPUs and other device backends.

value.misconception: Autograd and backpropagation are identical concepts.
value.correction: Autograd records the computation graph and automatic differentiation machinery; backpropagation is the backward gradient computation through that graph.

value.misconception: PyTorch only works with NVIDIA GPUs.
value.correction: The source explicitly names AMD ROCm and Apple Metal support in addition to CUDA-capable NVIDIA GPUs.

value.misconception: PyTorch has no relationship to Torch.
value.correction: The source explicitly calls PyTorch the successor to Torch and describes the Torch7/LuaTorch lineage.

value.misconception: ONNX is PyTorch's native model-file format.
value.correction: PyTorch serialization is described separately using ZIP64/.pt/.pth, while ONNX is an interoperability format.

value.misconception: Caffe2 remained a permanently separate Meta framework.
value.correction: The source states that Caffe2 merged into PyTorch at the end of March 2018.

value.misconception: PyTorch only provides neural-network layers.
value.correction: The source describes tensors, automatic differentiation, optimized algorithms, architectures, GPU bindings, serialization and broader ecosystem capabilities.

value.misconception: TorchDynamo is the automatic differentiation engine.
value.correction: TorchDynamo is described as a Python-level compiler; Autograd is the automatic differentiation system.

value.misconception: PyTorch model files are just raw Python objects.
value.correction: The source describes a ZIP64 archive containing weights and metadata, with Python pickle used for the model weights.

source_claims.claim: PyTorch metadata identifies original authors, developer, release, stable version, languages, operating systems, architectures, license and official resources.
PyTorch is an open-source deep-learning library, successor to Torch, with high-level APIs over optimized low-level algorithms and CUDA bindings.
Tensor is fundamental; Autograd constructs a DAG during forward execution and backpropagates from loss.
PyTorch is popular alongside TensorFlow/Keras, installable with Anaconda, and named as the basis of several commercial systems.
Torch originated around 2001, evolved through Torch7/LuaTorch, and its refactoring was influenced by torch-autograd, HIPS/autograd and Chainer.
ONNX was created by Meta and Microsoft; Caffe2 later merged into PyTorch; independent foundation governance was announced in 2022.
PyTorch 2.0 introduced TorchDynamo as a Python-level compiler and reported performance improvements.
PyTorch tensors resemble NumPy arrays while supporting CUDA-capable NVIDIA GPUs and other GPU platforms such as AMD ROCm and Apple Metal.
torch.nn provides neural-network/training abstractions; networks inherit from nn.Module and define forward().
Serialization uses ZIP64 with model weights in Python pickle plus metadata such as byte order; .pt and .pth are used.
Source examples demonstrate CPU/cuda:0 devices and tensor creation, multiplication, sum, indexing and max.
Source neural-network example uses Flatten, Sequential, Linear, ReLU and returns logits.

source_claims.title: Identity and design
source_claims.statement: Python is high-level, general-purpose, multi-paradigm, readability-oriented, indentation-based, standard-library-rich and garbage-collected.

source_claims.title: Origin
source_claims.statement: Python was conceived by Guido van Rossum at CWI as a successor to ABC; implementation began in 1989 and first release was 0.9.0 in 1991.

source_claims.title: Governance
source_claims.statement: Guido left the BDFL role in 2018 and a five-member Steering Council was elected in 2019.

source_claims.title: Version history
source_claims.statement: Python 2.0 added major features; Python 3.0 was a major non-fully-compatible revision; typing capabilities began in Python 3.5.

source_claims.title: Philosophy
source_claims.statement: The Zen of Python emphasizes explicitness, simplicity, readability and practical consistency, while remaining a guideline.

source_claims.title: PEPs
source_claims.statement: PEPs document information, processes, naming and language proposals and are overseen by the Steering Council.

source_claims.title: Syntax
source_claims.statement: Python uses significant indentation and provides statements for assignment, control flow, exceptions, classes, functions, context management, imports, matching and generators.

source_claims.title: Expressions and semantics
source_claims.statement: Python distinguishes expressions and statements and supports comprehensions, lambdas, slicing, unpacking, string forms and dynamic references.

source_claims.title: Typing
source_claims.statement: Python uses duck typing with typed objects and untyped names while remaining strongly typed; annotations may be checked externally.

source_claims.title: Built-in types
source_claims.statement: Python provides bool, bytearray, bytes, complex, dict, float, frozenset, int, list, NoneType, range, set, str and tuple.

source_claims.title: Numeric semantics
source_claims.statement: Python supports true/floor division, modulo, exponentiation, matrix multiplication, arbitrary precision integers, Decimal and Fraction.

source_claims.title: Libraries
source_claims.statement: The standard library covers Internet protocols/formats, GUI, relational databases, pseudorandom numbers, decimals, regex and unit testing.

source_claims.title: Environments
source_claims.statement: Python implementations commonly provide REPLs; CPython includes IDLE and the ecosystem includes IPython, Jupyter and desktop/web IDEs.

source_claims.title: CPython
source_claims.statement: CPython is the reference implementation, written in C, compiling Python to bytecode executed by a VM.

source_claims.title: Alternative implementations
source_claims.statement: The source describes PyPy, Codon, MicroPython, CircuitPython, Pyston, Cinder, RustPython and Stackless Python.

source_claims.title: Compilers and transpilers
source_claims.statement: The ecosystem includes Brython, Transcrypt, Cython, PyJL, Nuitka, Numba, Pythran, RPython and MyHDL.

source_claims.title: Performance
source_claims.statement: JIT, static compilation, multiprocessing, efficient data structures and native numerical libraries can improve performance.

source_claims.title: Development lifecycle
source_claims.statement: Python development uses PEPs, community review, GitHub and a release process with incompatible, feature and bug-fix releases.

source_claims.title: Culture and influence
source_claims.statement: PyCon, Monty Python naming/culture, Pythonic terminology and the influence graph are described.

value.name: Component render and reconciliation cycle
steps: component receives props and reads state
component produces JSX or React nodes
React computes a virtual UI representation
reconciliation compares new and previous representations
React DOM applies required changes to the live DOM
value.mechanism: Declarative components specify the UI for a state; reconciliation computes the live DOM changes required to reflect the new output.

value.name: Props and state relationship
steps: child renders from props and local state
value.mechanism: Props carry values across component boundaries; state is internal component data that can influence the view.

value.name: Rules of Hooks
steps: call Hooks only at top level
call Hooks only from React function components or custom Hooks
keep call order consistent across renders
use linting to detect many violations
value.mechanism: Stable call order lets React associate Hook state and behavior with the correct call positions.

value.name: React Server Component flow
steps: server output passes data or JSX to client components
client component supplies browser interactivity when needed
value.mechanism: Server Components access server data sources and avoid shipping corresponding component JavaScript for client hydration; Client Components handle browser behavior.

value.name: Server-side rendering and hydration distinction
steps: server renders component tree into initial HTML
client React may take over and attach event handlers
value.mechanism: SSR supplies pre-rendered HTML for early display; hydration establishes client-side React behavior. The source distinguishes this from Server Components, which do not undergo hydration for their own output.

value.name: Flux unidirectional data-flow loop
steps: user interaction or event creates action
updated state propagates to view through props
value.mechanism: Actions describe events; stores change in response and views receive updated state, maintaining downward data flow and upward actions.

value.name: Class component lifecycle resource management
value.mechanism: Lifecycle methods expose points where data loading and resource cleanup can be performed.

value.name: JSX compilation pipeline
steps: React executes component code and renders output
value.mechanism: JSX is a syntax extension that resembles HTML but is converted to JavaScript during compilation.

value.name: Fiber incremental rendering model
steps: rendering work is represented in units/segments
segments can be maintained and updated separately
work can be spread across multiple frames
UI updates and animation can proceed more smoothly
value.mechanism: Fiber replaced the older Stack rendering algorithm and enabled work to be segmented rather than handled in one large chunk.

fixes are backported to supported release lines
value.mechanism: The supplied source lists CVE identifiers, impact categories, severity ratings and specific React release versions said to address them.

value.name: React license evolution
steps: 2026 foundation transfer with MIT license retained
value.mechanism: Licensing changes followed community controversy around patent termination terms; the source says the MIT license remains after transfer.

value.name: Project governance evolution
steps: community and companies participate in maintenance
Meta announces transfer to independent foundation
React Foundation launches under Linux Foundation
value.mechanism: The source describes a transition from corporate origin to foundation governance while preserving the MIT license.

value.distinction: React focuses on UI and rendering; routing, networking, storage and other application-level capabilities may come from additional libraries or frameworks.
Props are values passed between components; state is internal component data.
Function components can use Hooks; class components use React.Component lifecycle methods. Classes remain supported, while functions are recommended for new components in the source.
Hooks expose state/effect and other capabilities to function components; lifecycle methods are used by class components.

SSR sends rendered HTML to the browser and may be followed by hydration; the source says Server Components execute only on the server and do not send corresponding JavaScript for client hydration of their output.
Server Components execute on the server and can access server-side data; Client Components provide browser-side interactivity and event handlers.
The Virtual DOM is an in-memory representation used for comparison; the browser DOM is the live document updated with computed differences.
Rendering produces a UI representation; reconciliation compares representations to determine necessary live DOM changes.
JSX resembles HTML but is a JavaScript syntax extension transformed during compilation; it is not itself HTML markup sent unchanged to the browser.
React supplies the UI library; React Router and Next.js provide routing and broader application-level features.
Flux is an architecture with actions, dispatcher, stores and views; Redux is a later state-management library often organized around a single store.
The source characterizes React's pattern as props flowing down and actions flowing up, contrasted with AngularJS's bidirectional flow.
Fiber segments work across frames; Stack is the older renderer described as less suited to complex dynamic changes in one chunk.
Server Components are server-executed UI components; Server Functions are asynchronous server-executed functions callable from Client Components.
The source describes an earlier BSD-plus-patent arrangement that caused controversy, followed by a 2017 MIT relicensing; the MIT license remains after foundation transfer.
CVE identifiers describe disclosed issues; remediation is tied to specific fixed or backported React versions in the source.
The source describes error boundaries as a React component type that catches JavaScript errors in a child tree and renders fallback UI.
SSR can let the browser display UI before client JavaScript has fully downloaded and executed; client hydration may then attach handlers for interactive UI.

value.misconception: React includes a full routing and application stack by itself.
value.correction: The source says React focuses on UI/rendering and relies on external libraries or frameworks for routing and other application capabilities.

value.misconception: Props and state mean the same thing.
value.correction: Props are passed between components; state is internal to a component.

value.misconception: Hooks can be called inside class components.
value.correction: The source explicitly says Hooks do not work inside classes.

value.misconception: Hooks may be called inside conditions or loops.
value.correction: Hooks should be called at the top level so call order remains stable across renders.

value.misconception: React Server Components are simply another name for server-side rendering.
value.correction: The source distinguishes them: Server Components execute on the server and do not ship corresponding component JavaScript for client hydration of their own output.

value.misconception: React only supports browser execution.
value.correction: The source describes SSR, Server Components and Server Functions in addition to client rendering.

value.misconception: The Virtual DOM is the browser's live DOM.
value.correction: The Virtual DOM is an in-memory representation compared during reconciliation; React applies computed changes to the live DOM.

value.misconception: Every UI update replaces the entire live DOM.
value.correction: The source says React computes differences and updates only the parts of the live DOM that need changing.

value.misconception: JSX is just HTML embedded in JavaScript.
value.correction: JSX is a JavaScript syntax extension that resembles HTML and is transformed into JavaScript during compilation.

value.misconception: Class components are no longer supported.
value.correction: Class components remain supported, although the source recommends function components for new components.

value.misconception: React Fiber changed the syntax developers write.
value.correction: The source says Fiber changed internal execution/rendering algorithms, not the React programming syntax.

value.misconception: Every form of server-rendered React output necessarily hydrates the same way.
value.correction: The source distinguishes Server Components, whose output does not undergo client hydration, from SSR interactive UI that may be hydrated.

value.misconception: Using useReducer requires a centralized Redux store.
value.correction: The source says useReducer can create reducer-based state local to a component without a centralized store.

value.misconception: React has always been distributed under MIT.
value.correction: The source documents Apache 2.0 at initial release, BSD plus patent text in 2014, and MIT from the 2017 release onward.

value.misconception: A vulnerability disclosure by itself means every deployed application is already fixed.
value.correction: The source lists specific fixed/backported versions; operators need to identify their installed versions and apply the relevant remediation.

value.misconception: A React component under Flux should directly mutate props passed to it.
value.correction: The source says components should not directly modify props; callbacks create actions sent through the dispatcher to update stores.

value.question: What problem is React primarily designed to solve?
value.answer: Build component-based user interfaces and manage their rendering.

value.question: How does declarative UI differ from imperative programming in the source?
value.answer: The developer describes the view for a state; React updates it when data changes.

value.question: What are components?
value.answer: Reusable modular UI entities arranged in layers.

value.question: How do props differ from state?
value.answer: Props are passed between components; state is internal component data.

value.question: What does React DOM do?
value.answer: Renders components into a root element in the browser DOM.

value.question: What is the Virtual DOM?
value.answer: An in-memory UI representation used in comparison between renders.

value.question: What is reconciliation?
value.answer: Comparing new and prior UI representations to compute necessary live DOM updates.

value.question: What is JSX?
value.answer: A JavaScript syntax extension resembling HTML that is transformed into JavaScript.

value.question: What is a function component?
value.answer: A JavaScript function returning JSX or other React nodes.

value.question: What is a class component?
value.answer: An ES6 class extending React.Component and using lifecycle methods.

value.question: Why were Hooks introduced?
value.answer: To let function components access state and lifecycle-related features without classes.

value.question: What are the two Rules of Hooks?
value.answer: Call Hooks only at the top level and only from React functions/custom Hooks.

value.question: Why must Hook call order remain stable?
value.answer: The React Hook model relies on consistent call order across renders.

value.question: What does useState do?
value.answer: Manages component-local state.

value.question: What does useEffect do?
value.answer: Manages side effects.

value.question: What does useReducer do?
value.answer: Manages state transitions through a reducer, including local Redux-like patterns.

value.question: What is a custom Hook?
value.answer: Reusable stateful logic shared between components without changing component hierarchy.

value.question: What are React Server Components?
value.answer: Function components that execute exclusively on the server.

value.question: How do Server Components differ from SSR?
value.answer: Server Components do not send corresponding component JavaScript for hydration of their own output; SSR sends rendered HTML and may be hydrated.

value.question: What is hydration?
value.answer: Browser React takes over server-rendered UI and attaches event handlers.

value.question: What are Server Functions?
value.answer: Asynchronous functions executed on the server and callable from Client Components.

value.question: Does React include built-in routing?
value.answer: The source says it does not include a full-fledged routing solution out of the box.

value.question: What does React Router provide?
value.answer: Routes, navigation and URL-change handling.

value.question: What is SSR's initial-display benefit?
value.answer: The browser can display server-rendered HTML before client JavaScript has fully downloaded and executed.

value.question: What is Flux?
value.answer: A unidirectional data-flow architecture using actions, dispatcher, stores and views.

value.question: What does a Flux action describe?
value.answer: What happened, for example one user following another.

value.question: What does the dispatcher do?
value.answer: Routes actions to stores.

value.question: How does Redux relate to Flux?
value.answer: Redux is a later state-management library commonly using a single store as a source of truth.

value.question: What is React Fiber?
value.answer: An internal rendering architecture that segments work across frames.

value.question: What did React 16 introduce according to the source?
value.answer: Error boundaries, among other release changes.

value.question: What changed in React 18?
value.answer: Concurrent renderer, automatic batching and SSR support with Suspense.

value.question: What did React 19 introduce according to the source?
value.answer: Actions, Server Components support and improvements to static site generation.

value.question: Who created React?
value.answer: Jordan Walke.

value.question: When was React open-sourced?
value.answer: May 2013, at JSConf US according to the source.

value.question: What influenced React's early design?
value.answer: XHP, an HTML component library for PHP.

value.question: How did React licensing evolve?
value.answer: Initial Apache 2.0; BSD plus patent text in 2014; revised patent grant in 2015; MIT in 2017.

value.question: What organization hosts the React Foundation?
value.answer: The Linux Foundation.

value.question: What is CVE-2025-55182 called in the source?
value.answer: React2Shell.

value.question: What CVSS score does the source assign React2Shell?
Which releases does the source list as fixes for React2Shell?
Which additional RSC vulnerability categories are described?
value.answer: Denial of service and source-code exposure.

value.question: Why are lifecycle cleanup methods important?
value.answer: They can clear intervals and remove event listeners before component teardown.

value.question: What is the distinction between Server Component and Server Function?
value.answer: A Server Component is a server-executed UI component; a Server Function is an async server-executed function callable by a Client Component.

value.question: What does shouldComponentUpdate allow?
value.answer: Returning false can prevent unnecessary re-rendering.

value.question: What is error-boundary behavior described in the source?
value.answer: Catch JavaScript errors in a child tree and render fallback UI.

value.question: What does unidirectional data flow mean in the article's shorthand?
value.answer: Properties flow down; actions flow up.

value.question: What are the cited non-HTML targets or architectures?
value.answer: Canvas-based charts, universal server/client HTML rendering, and native mobile apps via React Native.

value.question: What is the source's stated license after the foundation transfer?
value.answer: MIT License.

value.question: What does the source say about linting Rules of Hooks?
value.answer: Linting can detect many mistakes, but the rules are not enforced at runtime.

value.question: Why might SSR help slower devices?
value.answer: The browser can display initial rendered HTML without waiting for all client JavaScript.

value.question: Why might an app use external libraries with React?
value.answer: React intentionally focuses on UI, leaving networking, storage, routing and other capabilities to other tools.

value.question: What is the source's description of React's governance change?
value.answer: Transfer from Meta to an independent React Foundation hosted by the Linux Foundation.

value.question: What should a security consumer do with the listed fixed versions?

value.question: How does Fiber differ from Stack?

value.question: What is the key distinction between virtual and live DOM?
value.answer: Virtual DOM is an in-memory representation; live DOM is the browser's actual document structure.

value.question: Why is React not identical to React Native?

value.question: What is the relation between a store and a view in Flux?

formal_models.name: Component render and reconciliation cycle
steps: component receives props and reads state
component produces JSX or React nodes
React computes a virtual UI representation
reconciliation compares new and previous representations
React DOM applies required changes to the live DOM
formal_models.mechanism: Declarative components specify the UI for a state; reconciliation computes the live DOM changes required to reflect the new output.

formal_models.name: Props and state relationship
steps: child renders from props and local state
formal_models.mechanism: Props carry values across component boundaries; state is internal component data that can influence the view.

formal_models.name: Rules of Hooks
steps: call Hooks only at top level
call Hooks only from React function components or custom Hooks
keep call order consistent across renders
use linting to detect many violations
formal_models.mechanism: Stable call order lets React associate Hook state and behavior with the correct call positions.

formal_models.name: React Server Component flow
steps: server output passes data or JSX to client components
client component supplies browser interactivity when needed
formal_models.mechanism: Server Components access server data sources and avoid shipping corresponding component JavaScript for client hydration; Client Components handle browser behavior.

formal_models.name: Server-side rendering and hydration distinction
steps: server renders component tree into initial HTML
client React may take over and attach event handlers
formal_models.mechanism: SSR supplies pre-rendered HTML for early display; hydration establishes client-side React behavior. The source distinguishes this from Server Components, which do not undergo hydration for their own output.

formal_models.name: Flux unidirectional data-flow loop
steps: user interaction or event creates action
updated state propagates to view through props
formal_models.mechanism: Actions describe events; stores change in response and views receive updated state, maintaining downward data flow and upward actions.

formal_models.name: Class component lifecycle resource management
formal_models.mechanism: Lifecycle methods expose points where data loading and resource cleanup can be performed.

formal_models.name: JSX compilation pipeline
steps: React executes component code and renders output
formal_models.mechanism: JSX is a syntax extension that resembles HTML but is converted to JavaScript during compilation.

formal_models.name: Fiber incremental rendering model
steps: rendering work is represented in units/segments
segments can be maintained and updated separately
work can be spread across multiple frames
UI updates and animation can proceed more smoothly
formal_models.mechanism: Fiber replaced the older Stack rendering algorithm and enabled work to be segmented rather than handled in one large chunk.

formal_models.name: React Server Components security disclosure and remediation
steps: vulnerability is disclosed with CVE identifier
fixes are backported to supported release lines
formal_models.mechanism: The supplied source lists CVE identifiers, impact categories, severity ratings and specific React release versions said to address them.

formal_models.name: React license evolution
steps: 2026 foundation transfer with MIT license retained
formal_models.mechanism: Licensing changes followed community controversy around patent termination terms; the source says the MIT license remains after transfer.

formal_models.name: Project governance evolution
steps: community and companies participate in maintenance
Meta announces transfer to independent foundation
React Foundation launches under Linux Foundation
formal_models.mechanism: The source describes a transition from corporate origin to foundation governance while preserving the MIT license.

source_claims.claim: React is a front-end JavaScript library focused on component-based user interfaces and rendering rather than a complete application library.
Developers describe the view for each application state and React updates the UI when data changes.
Components are modular and reusable; props carry values between components and state is internal component data.
Hooks allow function components to access state and lifecycle-related React features and must follow call-order rules.
Server Components execute exclusively on the server, can access server data sources and do not undergo client hydration for their own output.
React does not include a full routing solution out of the box; external libraries and frameworks provide routing and other application features.
React compares virtual UI representations and updates computed differences in the live DOM.
Server-side rendering sends initially rendered UI as HTML so the browser can display it before client JavaScript has fully downloaded and executed.
Flux expresses unidirectional flow through actions, a dispatcher, stores and views; props carry updated state back to views.
React was created by Jordan Walke, first deployed internally in 2011, used at Instagram in 2012 and open-sourced in May 2013.
React Fiber replaced the older Stack rendering algorithm with segmented work that can be spread across multiple frames.
The source records React Server Components vulnerabilities disclosed in late 2025 and lists fixed versions.
React was relicensed under MIT in 2017 after controversy about an earlier patent clause and remained MIT-licensed after the 2026 foundation transfer.

semantic_distinctions.distinction: React focuses on UI and rendering; routing, networking, storage and other application-level capabilities may come from additional libraries or frameworks.
Props are values passed between components; state is internal component data.
Function components can use Hooks; class components use React.Component lifecycle methods. Classes remain supported, while functions are recommended for new components in the source.
Hooks expose state/effect and other capabilities to function components; lifecycle methods are used by class components.

SSR sends rendered HTML to the browser and may be followed by hydration; the source says Server Components execute only on the server and do not send corresponding JavaScript for client hydration of their output.
Server Components execute on the server and can access server-side data; Client Components provide browser-side interactivity and event handlers.
The Virtual DOM is an in-memory representation used for comparison; the browser DOM is the live document updated with computed differences.
Rendering produces a UI representation; reconciliation compares representations to determine necessary live DOM changes.
JSX resembles HTML but is a JavaScript syntax extension transformed during compilation; it is not itself HTML markup sent unchanged to the browser.
React supplies the UI library; React Router and Next.js provide routing and broader application-level features.
Flux is an architecture with actions, dispatcher, stores and views; Redux is a later state-management library often organized around a single store.
The source characterizes React's pattern as props flowing down and actions flowing up, contrasted with AngularJS's bidirectional flow.
Fiber segments work across frames; Stack is the older renderer described as less suited to complex dynamic changes in one chunk.
Server Components are server-executed UI components; Server Functions are asynchronous server-executed functions callable from Client Components.
The source describes an earlier BSD-plus-patent arrangement that caused controversy, followed by a 2017 MIT relicensing; the MIT license remains after foundation transfer.
CVE identifiers describe disclosed issues; remediation is tied to specific fixed or backported React versions in the source.
The source describes error boundaries as a React component type that catches JavaScript errors in a child tree and renders fallback UI.
SSR can let the browser display UI before client JavaScript has fully downloaded and executed; client hydration may then attach handlers for interactive UI.
