misconceptions.misconception: React includes a full routing and application stack by itself.
misconceptions.correction: The source says React focuses on UI/rendering and relies on external libraries or frameworks for routing and other application capabilities.

misconceptions.misconception: Props and state mean the same thing.
misconceptions.correction: Props are passed between components; state is internal to a component.

misconceptions.misconception: Hooks can be called inside class components.
misconceptions.correction: The source explicitly says Hooks do not work inside classes.

misconceptions.misconception: Hooks may be called inside conditions or loops.
misconceptions.correction: Hooks should be called at the top level so call order remains stable across renders.

misconceptions.misconception: React Server Components are simply another name for server-side rendering.
misconceptions.correction: The source distinguishes them: Server Components execute on the server and do not ship corresponding component JavaScript for client hydration of their own output.

misconceptions.misconception: React only supports browser execution.
misconceptions.correction: The source describes SSR, Server Components and Server Functions in addition to client rendering.

misconceptions.misconception: The Virtual DOM is the browser's live DOM.
misconceptions.correction: The Virtual DOM is an in-memory representation compared during reconciliation; React applies computed changes to the live DOM.

misconceptions.misconception: Every UI update replaces the entire live DOM.
misconceptions.correction: The source says React computes differences and updates only the parts of the live DOM that need changing.

misconceptions.misconception: JSX is just HTML embedded in JavaScript.
misconceptions.correction: JSX is a JavaScript syntax extension that resembles HTML and is transformed into JavaScript during compilation.

misconceptions.misconception: Class components are no longer supported.
misconceptions.correction: Class components remain supported, although the source recommends function components for new components.

misconceptions.misconception: React Fiber changed the syntax developers write.
misconceptions.correction: The source says Fiber changed internal execution/rendering algorithms, not the React programming syntax.

misconceptions.misconception: Every form of server-rendered React output necessarily hydrates the same way.
misconceptions.correction: The source distinguishes Server Components, whose output does not undergo client hydration, from SSR interactive UI that may be hydrated.

misconceptions.misconception: Using useReducer requires a centralized Redux store.
misconceptions.correction: The source says useReducer can create reducer-based state local to a component without a centralized store.

misconceptions.misconception: React has always been distributed under MIT.
misconceptions.correction: The source documents Apache 2.0 at initial release, BSD plus patent text in 2014, and MIT from the 2017 release onward.

misconceptions.misconception: A vulnerability disclosure by itself means every deployed application is already fixed.
misconceptions.correction: The source lists specific fixed/backported versions; operators need to identify their installed versions and apply the relevant remediation.

misconceptions.misconception: A React component under Flux should directly mutate props passed to it.
misconceptions.correction: The source says components should not directly modify props; callbacks create actions sent through the dispatcher to update stores.

questions.question: What problem is React primarily designed to solve?
questions.answer: Build component-based user interfaces and manage their rendering.

questions.question: How does declarative UI differ from imperative programming in the source?
questions.answer: The developer describes the view for a state; React updates it when data changes.

questions.question: What are components?
questions.answer: Reusable modular UI entities arranged in layers.

questions.question: How do props differ from state?
questions.answer: Props are passed between components; state is internal component data.

questions.question: What does React DOM do?
questions.answer: Renders components into a root element in the browser DOM.

questions.question: What is the Virtual DOM?
questions.answer: An in-memory UI representation used in comparison between renders.

questions.question: What is reconciliation?
questions.answer: Comparing new and prior UI representations to compute necessary live DOM updates.

questions.question: What is JSX?
questions.answer: A JavaScript syntax extension resembling HTML that is transformed into JavaScript.

questions.question: What is a function component?
questions.answer: A JavaScript function returning JSX or other React nodes.

questions.question: What is a class component?
questions.answer: An ES6 class extending React.Component and using lifecycle methods.

questions.question: Why were Hooks introduced?
questions.answer: To let function components access state and lifecycle-related features without classes.

questions.question: What are the two Rules of Hooks?
questions.answer: Call Hooks only at the top level and only from React functions/custom Hooks.

questions.question: Why must Hook call order remain stable?
questions.answer: The React Hook model relies on consistent call order across renders.

questions.question: What does useState do?
questions.answer: Manages component-local state.

questions.question: What does useEffect do?
questions.answer: Manages side effects.

questions.question: What does useReducer do?
questions.answer: Manages state transitions through a reducer, including local Redux-like patterns.

questions.question: What is a custom Hook?
questions.answer: Reusable stateful logic shared between components without changing component hierarchy.

questions.question: What are React Server Components?
questions.answer: Function components that execute exclusively on the server.

questions.question: How do Server Components differ from SSR?
questions.answer: Server Components do not send corresponding component JavaScript for hydration of their own output; SSR sends rendered HTML and may be hydrated.

questions.question: What is hydration?
questions.answer: Browser React takes over server-rendered UI and attaches event handlers.

questions.question: What are Server Functions?
questions.answer: Asynchronous functions executed on the server and callable from Client Components.

questions.question: Does React include built-in routing?
questions.answer: The source says it does not include a full-fledged routing solution out of the box.

questions.question: What does React Router provide?
questions.answer: Routes, navigation and URL-change handling.

questions.question: What is SSR's initial-display benefit?
questions.answer: The browser can display server-rendered HTML before client JavaScript has fully downloaded and executed.

questions.question: What is Flux?
questions.answer: A unidirectional data-flow architecture using actions, dispatcher, stores and views.

questions.question: What does a Flux action describe?
questions.answer: What happened, for example one user following another.

questions.question: What does the dispatcher do?
questions.answer: Routes actions to stores.

questions.question: How does Redux relate to Flux?
questions.answer: Redux is a later state-management library commonly using a single store as a source of truth.

questions.question: What is React Fiber?
questions.answer: An internal rendering architecture that segments work across frames.

questions.question: What did React 16 introduce according to the source?
questions.answer: Error boundaries, among other release changes.

questions.question: What changed in React 18?
questions.answer: Concurrent renderer, automatic batching and SSR support with Suspense.

questions.question: What did React 19 introduce according to the source?
questions.answer: Actions, Server Components support and improvements to static site generation.

questions.question: Who created React?
questions.answer: Jordan Walke.

questions.question: When was React open-sourced?
questions.answer: May 2013, at JSConf US according to the source.

questions.question: What influenced React's early design?
questions.answer: XHP, an HTML component library for PHP.

questions.question: How did React licensing evolve?
questions.answer: Initial Apache 2.0; BSD plus patent text in 2014; revised patent grant in 2015; MIT in 2017.

questions.question: What organization hosts the React Foundation?
questions.answer: The Linux Foundation.

questions.question: What is CVE-2025-55182 called in the source?
questions.answer: React2Shell.

questions.question: What CVSS score does the source assign React2Shell?
Which releases does the source list as fixes for React2Shell?
Which additional RSC vulnerability categories are described?

questions.question: Why are lifecycle cleanup methods important?
questions.answer: They can clear intervals and remove event listeners before component teardown.

questions.question: What is the distinction between Server Component and Server Function?
questions.answer: A Server Component is a server-executed UI component; a Server Function is an async server-executed function callable by a Client Component.

questions.question: What does shouldComponentUpdate allow?
questions.answer: Returning false can prevent unnecessary re-rendering.

questions.question: What is error-boundary behavior described in the source?
questions.answer: Catch JavaScript errors in a child tree and render fallback UI.

questions.question: What does unidirectional data flow mean in the article's shorthand?
questions.answer: Properties flow down; actions flow up.

questions.question: What are the cited non-HTML targets or architectures?

questions.question: What is the source's stated license after the foundation transfer?

questions.question: What does the source say about linting Rules of Hooks?
questions.answer: Linting can detect many mistakes, but the rules are not enforced at runtime.

questions.question: Why might SSR help slower devices?

questions.question: Why might an app use external libraries with React?
questions.answer: React intentionally focuses on UI, leaving networking, storage, routing and other capabilities to other tools.

questions.question: What is the key distinction between virtual and live DOM?
questions.answer: Virtual DOM is an in-memory representation; live DOM is the browser's actual document structure.

questions.question: Why is React not identical to React Native?
questions.answer: React is the UI library; React Native extends React concepts to native mobile platforms.

questions.question: Which version introduced Hooks?
questions.answer: React 16.8, released in February 2019.

questions.question: What was notable about React 17?
questions.answer: The source says it was the first major release without major developer-facing API changes.

questions.question: What did the source say about React usage popularity?
questions.answer: It cites the 2025 Stack Overflow survey and an estimated 6.1% of websites.

questions.question: What is the relation between JSX and compilation?
questions.answer: JSX is transformed into JavaScript during compilation.

questions.question: What is the relation between a store and a view in Flux?
questions.answer: Store changes propagate back to the view through component props.

questions.question: Why can a class componentDidMount load data?
questions.answer: It runs once after the component mounts and is commonly used to initiate remote API requests.

questions.question: What is the article's distinction between Server Components and Client Components?
questions.answer: Server Components access server-side data and execute on the server; Client Components run in the browser for interaction.

questions.question: What does the article say about server components in Next.js?
questions.answer: They are most readily usable with Next.js.

questions.question: Which React release line is cited for useEffectEvent?
questions.answer: React 19.2.

questions.question: What is the role of an error boundary fallback?
questions.answer: Provide fallback UI instead of allowing a child-tree JavaScript error to crash the whole app.

questions.question: What was the licensing controversy about?
questions.answer: An earlier patent termination clause was considered potentially broad and raised downstream adoption concerns.

questions.question: What does the source say about React's current maintenance?
questions.answer: A community of individual developers and companies maintains it, with governance attributed to the React Foundation.

questions.question: Which source is identified for vulnerability details?
questions.answer: National Vulnerability Database CVE records.

questions.question: What is the relation between props and actions in Flux?
questions.answer: Props carry state down to views; callbacks create actions that travel through the dispatcher to stores.

historical_context.label: React prototype created
historical_context.description: Jordan Walke developed F-Bolt/FaxJS; React was deployed on Facebook News Feed in 2011, used at Instagram in 2012, and open-sourced in May 2013.

historical_context.label: React Native announced and open-sourced
historical_context.description: React Native was announced at React Conf in February and open-sourced in March.

historical_context.label: React Fiber announced
historical_context.description: Fiber introduced an internal rendering architecture designed to split work into segments across frames.

historical_context.label: React 16.0 released
historical_context.description: Introduced error boundaries and the MIT license release.

historical_context.label: React 17.0 released
historical_context.description: First major release described as having no major developer-facing API changes.

historical_context.label: React 18 released
historical_context.description: Introduced a concurrent renderer, automatic batching and SSR with Suspense; dropped Internet Explorer 11 support.

historical_context.label: React Hooks introduced
historical_context.description: React 16.8 introduced Hooks for function components.

historical_context.label: React 19 released
historical_context.description: Introduced Actions, support for Server Components and improvements to static site generation.

historical_context.label: React Foundation transfer announced
historical_context.description: Meta announced plans to transfer React, React Native and JSX software to a new React Foundation.

historical_context.label: React Foundation launched
historical_context.description: React Foundation officially launched under the Linux Foundation; Meta contributed React.

historical_context.label: React2Shell remote code execution vulnerability
historical_context.description: CVE-2025-55182 was reported; source states CVSS 10.0 and fixes in versions 19.0.1, 19.1.2 and 19.2.1.

historical_context.label: Additional React Server Components vulnerabilities disclosed
historical_context.description: Source identifies denial-of-service CVEs CVE-2025-55184 and CVE-2025-67779 and source-code exposure CVE-2025-55183, with fixes backported to specified release lines.

historical_context.label: React relicensed under MIT
historical_context.description: Following controversy about an earlier patent clause, React 16.0 was released under MIT; the change was backported to 15.6.2.

historical_context.label: License changed to BSD plus patent grant
historical_context.description: React 0.12 replaced Apache 2.0 with 3-clause BSD plus a patent text, leading to community and ASF concerns.

historical_context.label: Patent grant updated
historical_context.description: Facebook revised the patent grant following community feedback.

value.misconception: React Native renders the application by manipulating browser DOM nodes through React's Virtual DOM.
value.correction: The supplied article explicitly contrasts React Native with DOM manipulation and describes messages updating native views.

value.misconception: React Native directly uses standard browser CSS.
value.correction: The article says the styling syntax resembles CSS but React Native does not use CSS itself; styles affect native views.

value.misconception: A React Native screen is an HTML document.
value.correction: The source says React Native does not use HTML and presents View, Text and Button as framework components.

value.misconception: Cross-platform means no native platform code or APIs are involved.
value.correction: The article says React components wrap native code and interact with native APIs.

value.misconception: Every platform listed has identical support and maintenance.
value.correction: The source lists many targets and separately identifies Microsoft as maintainer of Windows/macOS implementations; it does not claim equal support across all targets.

value.misconception: TypeScript replaces JavaScript as the runtime described by the article.
value.correction: The source describes JavaScript interpretation on device and TypeScript as a commonly used typed authoring option.

value.misconception: Props and state are interchangeable.
value.correction: Props are component inputs; state is updated by a setter such as setCount.

value.misconception: baseNumber is required in the TypeScript example.
value.correction: The question mark marks baseNumber as optional; title has no question mark and is required.

value.misconception: The article describes the JavaScript/native bridge as synchronous and unbatched.
value.correction: The source explicitly describes serialized data over an asynchronous and batched bridge.

value.misconception: The described bridge details necessarily apply identically to every React Native version and platform.
value.correction: This graph preserves the article's architecture description with a version/scope qualification; it does not assert universal implementation identity.

value.misconception: React Native is only for Android and iOS.
value.correction: The supplied article lists additional targets including desktop, TV, web, UWP, Vega OS, OpenHarmony and visionOS.

value.misconception: React and React Native are identical products.
value.correction: React provides the component/declarative model, while React Native integrates it with native platform views and APIs.

value.misconception: Open-source status and MIT license are the same type of fact.
value.correction: The article states the project is open-source and separately lists MIT as the license.

value.misconception: Version 0.87.1 was the initial React Native release.
value.correction: The article gives 2015 as the initial release date and 0.87.1 as a later stable release listed in the infobox.

value.misconception: Any performance consequence inferred from bridge serialization is a direct measured claim in the article.
value.correction: The source states serialization, asynchrony and batching; specific performance effects are explanatory hypotheses requiring workload-specific measurement.

value.misconception: Every organization listed as a user still uses React Native in the same way today.
value.correction: The article specifically notes Shopify is retiring its use, so adoption statements must preserve their time context.

value.misconception: The article's 2025 foundation announcement by itself proves every governance or transfer detail is complete.
value.correction: The supplied text reports an announcement; this graph does not independently verify its implementation status.

value.misconception: The article's citation warning proves all of its listed references are unreliable.
value.correction: The notice says some sources may be unreliable, not that every citation is invalid.

Do not treat the warning as proof that every citation is unreliable
Verify individual claims against primary sources before using for high-stakes decisions
formal_models.scope: Process recommendation prompted by the article's own disclaimer; no external verification was performed.

source_claims.claim: React Native is an open-source UI software framework developed by Meta and the community.
The article lists Android, Android TV, iOS, macOS, tvOS, OpenHarmony, Web, Windows, UWP, VR, Vega OS and visionOS among platform targets or application domains.
The infobox identifies the MIT License.
The infobox gives 26 April 2015 as the release date and 0.87.1 dated 26 August 2026 as the stable release.
The implementation section describes JavaScript running in a background process on the end device and communicating with native platforms through serialized data over an asynchronous batched bridge.
The article says React Native does not manipulate the DOM via the Virtual DOM.
React components wrap existing native code and interact with native APIs through React's declarative UI paradigm and JavaScript.
React Native styling syntax resembles CSS, but the article says React Native does not use HTML or CSS.
The article says TypeScript is often used over JavaScript due to increased type safety.
The history connects Facebook's dissatisfaction with its HTML5 mobile experience to an internal UI prototype and React Native's public release.
The article says React Native was already used in production for Facebook's Group App and Ads Manager by the time of the cited technical talk.
The article reports an October 2025 announcement that React, React Native, and JSX would be donated to a React Foundation under the Linux Foundation.
The article says the React Native implementations for Windows and macOS are currently maintained by Microsoft.

semantic_distinctions.distinction: React supplies the component/declarative programming model; React Native applies it to native platform UI and APIs rather than browser DOM UI.
semantic_distinctions.why_it_matters: Prevents treating the native framework as merely React DOM inside a mobile web page.

semantic_distinctions.distinction: The source says React Native does not manipulate the DOM through the Virtual DOM and instead messages native views.
semantic_distinctions.why_it_matters: Clarifies the rendering target and platform boundary.

semantic_distinctions.distinction: The syntax is similar, but the source explicitly says React Native does not use CSS as its stylesheet system.
semantic_distinctions.why_it_matters: Avoids assuming browser CSS support or identical layout behavior.

semantic_distinctions.distinction: The source says React Native does not use HTML; View, Text and Button are framework components mapped to native UI.
semantic_distinctions.why_it_matters: Separates browser document structure from native component composition.

semantic_distinctions.distinction: JavaScript is the runtime language described; TypeScript adds static type annotations and is commonly used for type safety.
semantic_distinctions.why_it_matters: Separates authoring-time type checking from runtime execution.

semantic_distinctions.distinction: Props are component inputs; state is component-owned data updated through setters such as setCount.
semantic_distinctions.why_it_matters: Supports correct data-flow and component design.

semantic_distinctions.distinction: title: string is required; baseNumber?: number is optional in the example interface.
semantic_distinctions.why_it_matters: Clarifies compile-time component contracts.

semantic_distinctions.distinction: The examples use function components; the source also names React class components in its description of React principles.
semantic_distinctions.why_it_matters: Distinguishes component declaration styles without implying only one is supported.

semantic_distinctions.distinction: The source describes an asynchronous serialized bridge boundary between the JavaScript process and native platform code.
semantic_distinctions.why_it_matters: Makes execution boundaries and communication mechanisms explicit.

semantic_distinctions.distinction: Cross-platform development reuses framework logic while still integrating with target-specific APIs and implementations.
semantic_distinctions.why_it_matters: Prevents assuming every platform has identical features or zero native code.

semantic_distinctions.distinction: Tailwind use is described as possible through plugins rather than as proof that React Native directly uses browser CSS.
semantic_distinctions.why_it_matters: Separates extension capability from native styling semantics.

semantic_distinctions.distinction: The article's platform list and its Microsoft maintenance statement are separate claims; platform presence does not establish identical maintenance status.
semantic_distinctions.why_it_matters: Avoids overreading a platform list as a support-level guarantee.

semantic_distinctions.distinction: 2015 is the initial public release date; 0.87.1 is a later stable version as reported by the source.
semantic_distinctions.why_it_matters: Separates project age from current-version metadata.

semantic_distinctions.distinction: The article describes a serialized asynchronous batched bridge. This graph preserves that description without asserting that every version's internal architecture is identical.
semantic_distinctions.why_it_matters: Prevents historical architecture descriptions from being generalized beyond source scope.

semantic_distinctions.distinction: Claims quoted from the article are marked as source-reported; architectural abstractions and potential trade-offs are labeled as derived explanatory models.
semantic_distinctions.why_it_matters: Maintains provenance and avoids presenting interpretation as citation.

semantic_distinctions.distinction: The source describes the project as open-source and separately lists the MIT License.
semantic_distinctions.why_it_matters: Separates governance/distribution model from a specific license field.

semantic_distinctions.distinction: Platform support and examples of companies using React Native are distinct kinds of evidence.
semantic_distinctions.why_it_matters: A platform target does not prove adoption by every named organization.

semantic_distinctions.distinction: The example uses baseNumber || 0, which falls back for any falsy value; the graph records the exact code rather than rewriting it as a nullish check.
semantic_distinctions.why_it_matters: Preserves example semantics and the source's exact implementation.

misconceptions.misconception: React Native renders the application by manipulating browser DOM nodes through React's Virtual DOM.
misconceptions.correction: The supplied article explicitly contrasts React Native with DOM manipulation and describes messages updating native views.

misconceptions.misconception: React Native directly uses standard browser CSS.
misconceptions.correction: The article says the styling syntax resembles CSS but React Native does not use CSS itself; styles affect native views.

misconceptions.misconception: A React Native screen is an HTML document.
misconceptions.correction: The source says React Native does not use HTML and presents View, Text and Button as framework components.

misconceptions.misconception: Cross-platform means no native platform code or APIs are involved.
misconceptions.correction: The article says React components wrap native code and interact with native APIs.

misconceptions.misconception: Every platform listed has identical support and maintenance.
misconceptions.correction: The source lists many targets and separately identifies Microsoft as maintainer of Windows/macOS implementations; it does not claim equal support across all targets.

misconceptions.misconception: TypeScript replaces JavaScript as the runtime described by the article.
misconceptions.correction: The source describes JavaScript interpretation on device and TypeScript as a commonly used typed authoring option.

misconceptions.misconception: Props and state are interchangeable.
misconceptions.correction: Props are component inputs; state is updated by a setter such as setCount.

misconceptions.misconception: baseNumber is required in the TypeScript example.
misconceptions.correction: The question mark marks baseNumber as optional; title has no question mark and is required.

misconceptions.misconception: The article describes the JavaScript/native bridge as synchronous and unbatched.
misconceptions.correction: The source explicitly describes serialized data over an asynchronous and batched bridge.

misconceptions.misconception: The described bridge details necessarily apply identically to every React Native version and platform.
misconceptions.correction: This graph preserves the article's architecture description with a version/scope qualification; it does not assert universal implementation identity.

misconceptions.misconception: React Native is only for Android and iOS.
misconceptions.correction: The supplied article lists additional targets including desktop, TV, web, UWP, Vega OS, OpenHarmony and visionOS.

misconceptions.misconception: React and React Native are identical products.
misconceptions.correction: React provides the component/declarative model, while React Native integrates it with native platform views and APIs.

misconceptions.misconception: Open-source status and MIT license are the same type of fact.
misconceptions.correction: The article states the project is open-source and separately lists MIT as the license.

misconceptions.misconception: Version 0.87.1 was the initial React Native release.
misconceptions.correction: The article gives 2015 as the initial release date and 0.87.1 as a later stable release listed in the infobox.

misconceptions.misconception: Any performance consequence inferred from bridge serialization is a direct measured claim in the article.
misconceptions.correction: The source states serialization, asynchrony and batching; specific performance effects are explanatory hypotheses requiring workload-specific measurement.

misconceptions.misconception: Every organization listed as a user still uses React Native in the same way today.
misconceptions.correction: The article specifically notes Shopify is retiring its use, so adoption statements must preserve their time context.

misconceptions.misconception: The article's 2025 foundation announcement by itself proves every governance or transfer detail is complete.
misconceptions.correction: The supplied text reports an announcement; this graph does not independently verify its implementation status.

misconceptions.misconception: The article's citation warning proves all of its listed references are unreliable.
misconceptions.correction: The notice says some sources may be unreliable, not that every citation is invalid.

value.name: Router versus switch
value.router: Uses Layer-3 destination IP/prefix to forward between IP networks
value.switch: Uses Layer-2 MAC addresses to bridge frames
value.overlap: Multilayer switches can also perform Layer-3 routing

value.distinction: Routing computes/maintains route choices; forwarding applies a selected FIB entry to a packet.
Routing table holds route information; FIB is a forwarding-optimized structure derived from it.
Router primarily uses Layer-3 destination IP; switch bridges using Layer-2 MAC addresses.
Multilayer switches can route between subnets, so capabilities overlap.
Basic forwarding does not guarantee delivery; endpoints provide reliability where needed.
NAT maps addressing/connection information; the source says it is not universally regarded as a security feature.
Control plane computes route state/FIB; forwarding plane applies FIB to packets.
Static route is manually configured; dynamic route is learned through a protocol.
Default route is used when no more-specific destination entry matches.
Access serves customer/site connectivity; distribution aggregates traffic and may enforce WAN QoS.
Distribution aggregates/policies traffic; core provides high-bandwidth backbone transit.
Edge peers at network boundaries; core carries traffic between edge routers within an AS.
P is provider transit; PE connects CE and provides VPN services.
PE is provider-side; CE is customer-side edge.
Tail drop waits for a full buffer; RED/WRED can drop earlier, with WRED differentiating traffic types.
ASIC accelerates common operations; CPU handles packets/functions requiring special attention.
Wi-Fi router integrates routing, switching, and AP; a residential gateway may also integrate a modem.
Interfaces, processors, buffers, and accelerators execute work; OS/routing code supplies behavior/configuration.
Basic IP forwarding uses header addressing and usually not payload.
AS is a routing/policy domain; physical interfaces/links are the transmission substrate.

value.misconception: A router guarantees packets reach the final destination.
value.correction: A router forwards hop by hop; basic connectionless routing does not guarantee delivery.

value.misconception: Routing and forwarding are the same operation.
value.correction: Routing maintains/selects routes and builds the FIB; forwarding uses the FIB for each packet.

value.misconception: A router normally chooses routes by reading the application payload.
value.correction: Pure IP forwarding primarily uses destination IP and optional header hints, not payload.

value.misconception: The routing table and FIB are identical.
value.correction: The FIB is derived from route information and optimized for forwarding.

value.misconception: NAT is a complete security control.
value.correction: NAT is not universally recognized as a security feature; firewalling and policy are distinct.

value.misconception: All routers are ASIC appliances.
value.correction: Routers range from software/CPU systems to network processors and ASIC-assisted devices.

value.misconception: Every router needs separate Wi-Fi AP and switch hardware.
value.correction: Home Wi-Fi routers commonly integrate router, switch, and AP functions, sometimes with modem.

value.misconception: The default route is the only route in a router.
value.correction: Route tables can contain specific static/dynamic routes and a default route for unmatched destinations.

value.misconception: A router and Layer-3 switch are wholly separate capabilities.
value.correction: Multilayer switches can route between subnets.

value.misconception: More buffering removes congestion.
value.correction: Buffers are finite; queues can increase latency and queue-management policies may drop packets.

value.misconception: QoS creates additional bandwidth.
value.correction: QoS prioritizes traffic but does not create capacity.

value.misconception: The Internet has one centrally controlled router backbone.
value.correction: Major ISP systems collectively form a distributed backbone core; there is no single central backbone router.

value.misconception: Open-source router software is automatically more secure.
value.correction: The article reports a debated argument about visibility of flaws, not a universal proof.

value.misconception: Control plane and forwarding plane must be separate physical boxes.
value.correction: The article describes functional units operating simultaneously; physical separation is not required by that statement.

value.misconception: A route entry guarantees end-to-end reachability.
value.correction: A route informs a local forwarding decision; downstream failures and congestion can still interrupt delivery.

source_claims.claim: A router forwards packets between computer networks using network-layer destination information and routing information/policy.
A router is a Layer-3 device because its primary forwarding decision is based on the destination IP address.
The control plane maintains routing information and builds a FIB; the forwarding plane consults the FIB to forward packets.
Routing tables may include static, dynamic, and default routes; a default route may also be obtained by DHCP.
Connectionless router/gateway design does not assure reliable delivery; reliability is left to hosts.
Tail drop, RED, and WRED are queue-management policies used when packets arrive faster than a router can process/transmit them.
QoS classifies traffic and affects processing priority; it is important for latency-sensitive VoIP traffic.
Router implementations range from CPU/software forwarding to network processors and ASIC-accelerated hardware.
Router roles include access, distribution, core, edge, provider, provider-edge, customer-edge, interior, exterior, and border/gateway.
Routers may integrate firewall, VPN, and NAT features, but NAT is not universally recognized as a security feature.
Wi-Fi routers combine router, switch, and wireless access point functions, and residential gateways may also integrate a modem.
The article traces router precursors from NPL/ARPANET interface computers to CYCLADES, Xerox PARC, DARPA, BBN, and 1981 multiprotocol router programs.
Routers running multiple routing protocols may selectively redistribute routes between them.
Pure IP forwarding usually uses Layer-3 addresses and optional header hints, not payload inspection.
The source does not deeply specify ASIC microarchitecture, MTU/fragmentation mechanics, or specific routing algorithms.

semantic_distinctions.distinction: Routing computes/maintains route choices; forwarding applies a selected FIB entry to a packet.
Routing table holds route information; FIB is a forwarding-optimized structure derived from it.
Router primarily uses Layer-3 destination IP; switch bridges using Layer-2 MAC addresses.
Multilayer switches can route between subnets, so capabilities overlap.
Basic forwarding does not guarantee delivery; endpoints provide reliability where needed.
NAT maps addressing/connection information; the source says it is not universally regarded as a security feature.
Control plane computes route state/FIB; forwarding plane applies FIB to packets.
Static route is manually configured; dynamic route is learned through a protocol.
Default route is used when no more-specific destination entry matches.
Access serves customer/site connectivity; distribution aggregates traffic and may enforce WAN QoS.
Distribution aggregates/policies traffic; core provides high-bandwidth backbone transit.
Edge peers at network boundaries; core carries traffic between edge routers within an AS.
P is provider transit; PE connects CE and provides VPN services.
PE is provider-side; CE is customer-side edge.
Tail drop waits for a full buffer; RED/WRED can drop earlier, with WRED differentiating traffic types.
ASIC accelerates common operations; CPU handles packets/functions requiring special attention.
Wi-Fi router integrates routing, switching, and AP; a residential gateway may also integrate a modem.
Interfaces, processors, buffers, and accelerators execute work; OS/routing code supplies behavior/configuration.
Basic IP forwarding uses header addressing and usually not payload.
AS is a routing/policy domain; physical interfaces/links are the transmission substrate.

misconceptions.misconception: A router guarantees packets reach the final destination.
misconceptions.correction: A router forwards hop by hop; basic connectionless routing does not guarantee delivery.

misconceptions.misconception: Routing and forwarding are the same operation.
misconceptions.correction: Routing maintains/selects routes and builds the FIB; forwarding uses the FIB for each packet.

misconceptions.misconception: A router normally chooses routes by reading the application payload.
misconceptions.correction: Pure IP forwarding primarily uses destination IP and optional header hints, not payload.

misconceptions.misconception: The routing table and FIB are identical.
misconceptions.correction: The FIB is derived from route information and optimized for forwarding.

misconceptions.misconception: NAT is a complete security control.
misconceptions.correction: NAT is not universally recognized as a security feature; firewalling and policy are distinct.

misconceptions.misconception: All routers are ASIC appliances.
misconceptions.correction: Routers range from software/CPU systems to network processors and ASIC-assisted devices.

misconceptions.misconception: Every router needs separate Wi-Fi AP and switch hardware.
misconceptions.correction: Home Wi-Fi routers commonly integrate router, switch, and AP functions, sometimes with modem.

misconceptions.misconception: The default route is the only route in a router.
misconceptions.correction: Route tables can contain specific static/dynamic routes and a default route for unmatched destinations.

misconceptions.misconception: A router and Layer-3 switch are wholly separate capabilities.
misconceptions.correction: Multilayer switches can route between subnets.

misconceptions.misconception: More buffering removes congestion.
misconceptions.correction: Buffers are finite; queues can increase latency and queue-management policies may drop packets.

misconceptions.misconception: QoS creates additional bandwidth.
misconceptions.correction: QoS prioritizes traffic but does not create capacity.

misconceptions.misconception: The Internet has one centrally controlled router backbone.
misconceptions.correction: Major ISP systems collectively form a distributed backbone core; there is no single central backbone router.

misconceptions.misconception: Open-source router software is automatically more secure.
misconceptions.correction: The article reports a debated argument about visibility of flaws, not a universal proof.

misconceptions.misconception: Control plane and forwarding plane must be separate physical boxes.
misconceptions.correction: The article describes functional units operating simultaneously; physical separation is not required by that statement.

misconceptions.misconception: A route entry guarantees end-to-end reachability.
misconceptions.correction: A route informs a local forwarding decision; downstream failures and congestion can still interrupt delivery.

value.distinction: Routing selects a path/next hop; forwarding transits each packet between interfaces.
IP routing uses structured network-layer addresses; bridging is Layer-2 forwarding.
Static routes are configured manually; dynamic routes are learned/updated through protocols.
Distance vector exchanges destination costs with neighbors; link state floods topology information and computes paths locally.
Path vector advertises domain/path descriptions; distance vector advertises destination costs.
Intra-domain routing operates within an AS; inter-domain routing connects ASs.
Unicast targets one receiver; broadcast targets all nodes in scope.
Multicast targets an interested subset; broadcast targets all nodes within scope.
Anycast chooses one of several receivers sharing an address; unicast targets a specific receiver.
The routing table holds route information; the FIB is optimized for forwarding lookups.
Metrics compare routes under a protocol; administrative distance can compare sources in an implementation-specific way.
ECMP uses multiple equal-cost paths instead of only one route.
Hot-potato routing minimizes an ISP’s internal distance to exit, potentially increasing end-to-end latency.
Centralized routing can optimize global state; distributed protocols exchange local route/topology information.
Deterministic routing repeats a preferred path until information changes; randomized routing can choose an intermediate destination.
Tail drop waits for buffer exhaustion; RED begins probabilistic drops earlier.
WRED varies drop behavior by traffic type.
An AS sequence can map to multiple concrete router-level paths.
Metrics quantify path attributes; policies can override a metric-optimal path for business or administrative reasons.
Convergence is the network settling after updates; route selection chooses among candidates at a given moment.

value.misconception: Routing and forwarding are the same operation.
value.correction: Routing selects path/next-hop state; forwarding applies the FIB to individual packets.

value.misconception: Every router computes the entire end-to-end path for each packet.
value.correction: Large networks generally use next-hop routing; each node forwards toward the next hop.

value.misconception: The lowest latency route is always selected.
value.correction: Metrics and policies vary; BGP decisions may reflect business relationships or hot-potato routing.

value.misconception: A routing metric can be compared directly across all protocols.
value.correction: The source says metrics cannot be compared across routes learned from different protocols; implementations may use administrative distance.

value.misconception: Multicast is the same as broadcast.
value.correction: Multicast targets an interested subset; broadcast targets all nodes within its scope.

value.misconception: Anycast delivers to every node sharing an address.
value.correction: Anycast selects one member of the group, usually based on routing distance/cost.

value.misconception: Static routing is suitable for any rapidly changing large topology.
value.correction: The source notes manual table construction becomes infeasible for large, rapidly changing networks.

value.misconception: Link-state routing simply shares a single final route.
value.correction: Nodes flood link-state information, construct topology maps, and independently compute shortest-path trees.

value.misconception: Path-vector routing advertises only a scalar distance.
value.correction: Path-vector announcements include destination reachability and path/domain descriptions.

value.misconception: Adding a network link always improves every user’s route.
value.correction: Under selfish multi-agent route choices, Braess’s paradox shows an added road can increase travel time.

value.misconception: A full buffer is the only way to manage congestion.
value.correction: The source describes RED/WRED early drop behavior in addition to tail drop.

value.misconception: A shortest AS-level path uniquely determines the router-level path.
value.correction: Multiple router-level paths may correspond to a selected AS-level path.

value.misconception: Centralized routing is limited to a single small network.
value.correction: The source describes centralized optimization across geographically distributed private data-center WANs.

value.misconception: Dynamic routing prevents all routing failures.
value.correction: Dynamic routing adapts to failures, but incorrect routing, flapping, degradation, and downtime remain possible.

value.misconception: A router must inspect application payloads to choose an IP route.
value.correction: Pure IP forwarding typically uses Layer-3 addresses and optional header hints, not packet payload content.

source_claims.claim: Routing selects a path; forwarding moves packets between interfaces.
Routing decisions usually rely on routing tables populated manually or with protocol assistance.
Structured IP addresses allow route aggregation and scale better than unstructured bridging in large networks.
Unicast, broadcast, multicast, and anycast represent distinct delivery semantics.
Dynamic routing updates route tables using protocol information and dominates the Internet.
Distance-vector routing uses Bellman–Ford-style iterative neighbor cost exchange.
Link-state routers flood topology information and independently calculate least-cost paths.

Inter-AS route choices can reflect commercial relationships and hot-potato policies rather than global latency.
Centralized routing can optimize network-wide performance objectives in private WANs.
Incorrect routing and route flapping can cause performance degradation or downtime.
Early router concepts emerged from NPL, ARPANET, CYCLADES, Xerox PARC, and DARPA-related work.

misconceptions.correction: The source notes manual table construction becomes infeasible for large, rapidly changing networks.

misconceptions.misconception: Link-state routing simply shares a single final route.
misconceptions.correction: Nodes flood link-state information, construct topology maps, and independently compute shortest-path trees.

misconceptions.misconception: Path-vector routing advertises only a scalar distance.
misconceptions.correction: Path-vector announcements include destination reachability and path/domain descriptions.

misconceptions.misconception: Adding a network link always improves every user’s route.
misconceptions.correction: Under selfish multi-agent route choices, Braess’s paradox shows an added road can increase travel time.

misconceptions.misconception: A full buffer is the only way to manage congestion.
misconceptions.correction: The source describes RED/WRED early drop behavior in addition to tail drop.

misconceptions.misconception: A shortest AS-level path uniquely determines the router-level path.
misconceptions.correction: Multiple router-level paths may correspond to a selected AS-level path.

misconceptions.misconception: Centralized routing is limited to a single small network.
misconceptions.correction: The source describes centralized optimization across geographically distributed private data-center WANs.

misconceptions.misconception: Dynamic routing prevents all routing failures.
misconceptions.correction: Dynamic routing adapts to failures, but incorrect routing, flapping, degradation, and downtime remain possible.

misconceptions.misconception: A router must inspect application payloads to choose an IP route.
misconceptions.correction: Pure IP forwarding typically uses Layer-3 addresses and optional header hints, not packet payload content.

value.name: Four-layer model
value.expression: Application → Transport → Internet → Link
value.meaning: Functional TCP/IP decomposition.

value.name: Encapsulation
value.expression: application data → transport unit → IP datagram → link frame → medium
value.meaning: Data gains protocol context while descending the stack.

value.name: Decapsulation
value.expression: medium → frame → IP datagram → transport data → application
value.meaning: Receiver reverses encapsulation.

value.name: IP forwarding
value.expression: destination IP → routing decision → next hop → repeated forwarding → destination
value.meaning: IP moves datagrams across networks.

value.name: TCP reliability
value.expression: connection + ordering + retransmission + flow control + congestion control
value.meaning: TCP supplies reliable transport over IP.

value.name: UDP service
value.expression: application data → UDP datagram → IP → link
value.meaning: UDP provides connectionless best-effort transport.

value.name: Endpoint addressing
value.expression: IP address + transport port → application endpoint
value.meaning: Host location plus service/channel identity.

value.name: IPv4 to IPv6
value.expression: 32-bit IPv4 → exhaustion → 128-bit IPv6
value.meaning: Address-space expansion.

value.name: End-to-end architecture
value.expression: simple forwarding core + intelligent endpoints
value.meaning: Core forwards; endpoints provide broader intelligence/reliability.

value.name: TCP/IP and OSI mapping
value.expression: TCP/IP application≈OSI session+presentation+application; transport≈transport; internet≈network; link≈data-link/physical boundary
value.meaning: Approximate cross-model correspondence.

value.name: HTTP/3 stack
value.expression: HTTP/3 → QUIC → UDP → IP → Link
value.meaning: Modern HTTP/3 transport chain.

value.name: NFS example stack
value.expression: NFS → XDR → RPC → UDP → IP → Link
value.meaning: Source example demonstrating cross-layer composition.

value.name: Implementation stack
value.expression: application → transport → IP → link driver/firmware/chipset → medium
value.meaning: Abstract protocol layers connect to concrete network hardware.

value.name: Historical convergence
value.expression: ARPANET/NCP → internetworking research → TCP/IP → 1983 migration → adoption
value.meaning: Research and deployment produced the dominant Internet suite.

value.distinction: TCP/IP is an Internet architecture; OSI is a seven-layer general reference model.
IP provides internetworking; TCP provides reliable transport.
TCP is connection-oriented/reliable; UDP is connectionless/best-effort.
IP addresses identify hosts/locations; ports identify service channels.
IP packets are carried inside local link frames.
Layering defines scopes; encapsulation wraps data across those scopes.
End-to-end concerns endpoint intelligence; layering concerns functional separation.
IPv6 expands addresses from 32 to 128 bits.
Gateway was an earlier term for router.
QUIC is a transport protocol carried by UDP.
HTTP/3 uses QUIC exclusively.
User protocols serve applications; support protocols serve infrastructure.
IP/UDP provide best-effort while TCP/SCTP can provide reliability.
TCP/IP link/physical correspondence varies by representation.
IETF routing protocols carried over IP can be categorized as application-layer protocols in the cited TCP/IP treatment.

value.misconception: TCP/IP has seven layers exactly like OSI.
value.correction: TCP/IP's standard four-layer representation differs from OSI.

value.misconception: IP guarantees reliable delivery.
value.correction: IP is best-effort; reliability can be added above it.

value.misconception: TCP and IP are the same protocol.
value.correction: TCP is transport; IP is internetworking.

value.misconception: UDP has no error detection.
value.correction: UDP uses a checksum for error detection.

value.misconception: A port is another IP address.
value.correction: A port identifies a logical communication channel/service.

value.misconception: Routers normally interpret application payloads.
value.correction: Routers generally forward encapsulated traffic without application interpretation.

formal_models.name: Encapsulation
formal_models.expression: application data → transport unit → IP datagram → link frame → medium
formal_models.meaning: Data gains protocol context while descending the stack.

formal_models.name: Decapsulation
formal_models.expression: medium → frame → IP datagram → transport data → application
formal_models.meaning: Receiver reverses encapsulation.

formal_models.name: IP forwarding
formal_models.expression: destination IP → routing decision → next hop → repeated forwarding → destination
formal_models.meaning: IP moves datagrams across networks.

formal_models.name: TCP reliability
formal_models.expression: connection + ordering + retransmission + flow control + congestion control
formal_models.meaning: TCP supplies reliable transport over IP.

formal_models.name: UDP service
formal_models.expression: application data → UDP datagram → IP → link
formal_models.meaning: UDP provides connectionless best-effort transport.

formal_models.expression: IP address + transport port → application endpoint
formal_models.meaning: Host location plus service/channel identity.

formal_models.name: IPv4 to IPv6

formal_models.name: End-to-end architecture

source_claims.claim: TCP/IP organizes communication into four functional layers and specifies packetization, addressing, transmission, routing and reception.
IETF maintains the suite's technical standards and the suite predates OSI.
DARPA-sponsored ARPANET research and BBN IMPs formed early infrastructure.
Kahn and Cerf hid differences among local networks and delegated reliability to hosts.
The 1978 reformulation separated TCP and IP into distinct transport and internetwork functions.
End-to-end design, encapsulation and layering are central architectural principles.
IPv4/TCP-IP became active on ARPANET in 1983 and DoD standardized TCP/IP for military networking.
Transport provides channels, ports, reliability, segmentation, flow/congestion control and multiple protocol choices.
Application protocols include both user and support protocols and usually treat lower layers as abstractions.
TCP/IP and OSI use different layer representations and IETF does not require strict OSI compliance.
TCP/IP is hardware independent and has implementations across essentially every computing platform.
Minimal implementations include IP, ARP, ICMP, TCP, UDP and IGMP; IPv6 adds NDP and ICMPv6 among its support protocols.

semantic_distinctions.distinction: TCP/IP is an Internet architecture; OSI is a seven-layer general reference model.
IP provides internetworking; TCP provides reliable transport.
TCP is connection-oriented/reliable; UDP is connectionless/best-effort.
IP addresses identify hosts/locations; ports identify service channels.
IP packets are carried inside local link frames.
Layering defines scopes; encapsulation wraps data across those scopes.
End-to-end concerns endpoint intelligence; layering concerns functional separation.
IPv6 expands addresses from 32 to 128 bits.
Gateway was an earlier term for router.
QUIC is a transport protocol carried by UDP.
HTTP/3 uses QUIC exclusively.
User protocols serve applications; support protocols serve infrastructure.
IP/UDP provide best-effort while TCP/SCTP can provide reliability.
TCP/IP link/physical correspondence varies by representation.
IETF routing protocols carried over IP can be categorized as application-layer protocols in the cited TCP/IP treatment.

misconceptions.misconception: IP guarantees reliable delivery.
misconceptions.correction: IP is best-effort; reliability can be added above it.

misconceptions.misconception: TCP and IP are the same protocol.
misconceptions.correction: TCP is transport; IP is internetworking.

misconceptions.misconception: UDP has no error detection.
misconceptions.correction: UDP uses a checksum for error detection.

misconceptions.misconception: A port is another IP address.
misconceptions.correction: A port identifies a logical communication channel/service.

misconceptions.misconception: Routers normally interpret application payloads.
misconceptions.correction: Routers generally forward encapsulated traffic without application interpretation.

value.misconception: A framework is just a library.
value.correction: The article emphasizes framework-controlled flow and hooks as inversion of control.

value.misconception: MVC and three-tier architecture are the same.
value.correction: MVC separates software responsibilities; three-tier separates client, application and database.

value.misconception: Frameworks only work for dynamic sites.
value.correction: The article says frameworks can also apply to static sites.

value.misconception: All frameworks render only on the server.
value.correction: The article distinguishes server-side and client-side approaches and says mixed approaches are common.

value.misconception: An SPA is a framework.
value.correction: An SPA is an application architecture that often uses a client-side framework.

value.misconception: HTTP automatically maintains session state.
value.correction: The article describes HTTP as stateless and session management as a separate framework capability.

value.misconception: A cache always serves the request.
value.correction: Cached copies satisfy requests only when cache conditions are met.

value.misconception: Authentication and authorization are identical.
value.correction: Authentication verifies identity; authorization controls access.

value.misconception: ORM and unified DB API are interchangeable.
value.correction: ORM maps objects to records; unified API abstracts database backends.

value.misconception: All routing uses regular expressions.
value.correction: The article describes pattern matching, rewriting and graph traversal.

value.misconception: Ajax requires a full page reload.
value.correction: Ajax exchanges data in the background and updates page regions.

value.misconception: Frameworks always improve runtime performance.
value.correction: Abstractions can add overhead, bundle size and complexity; outcomes depend on context.

value.misconception: Modern standards make all frameworks unnecessary.
value.correction: The article says frameworks remain useful for productivity, structure and edge cases.

value.misconception: Every frontend framework uses a virtual DOM.
value.correction: Svelte is described as compiling components and eliminating the virtual DOM.

value.misconception: Fresh zero-runtime-overhead is an independently verified benchmark.
value.correction: It is a source characterization, not a measurement verified here.

value.misconception: A framework guarantees security.
value.correction: Some provide authentication and authorization; the article does not claim all are secure by default.

value.misconception: The citation warning proves every claim is false.
value.correction: The notice asks for more citations; each claim requires individual assessment.

misconceptions.misconception: A framework is just a library.
misconceptions.correction: The article emphasizes framework-controlled flow and hooks as inversion of control.

misconceptions.misconception: MVC and three-tier architecture are the same.
misconceptions.correction: MVC separates software responsibilities; three-tier separates client, application and database.

misconceptions.misconception: Frameworks only work for dynamic sites.
misconceptions.correction: The article says frameworks can also apply to static sites.

misconceptions.misconception: All frameworks render only on the server.
misconceptions.correction: The article distinguishes server-side and client-side approaches and says mixed approaches are common.

misconceptions.misconception: An SPA is a framework.
misconceptions.correction: An SPA is an application architecture that often uses a client-side framework.

misconceptions.misconception: HTTP automatically maintains session state.
misconceptions.correction: The article describes HTTP as stateless and session management as a separate framework capability.

misconceptions.misconception: A cache always serves the request.
misconceptions.correction: Cached copies satisfy requests only when cache conditions are met.

misconceptions.misconception: Authentication and authorization are identical.
misconceptions.correction: Authentication verifies identity; authorization controls access.

misconceptions.misconception: ORM and unified DB API are interchangeable.
misconceptions.correction: ORM maps objects to records; unified API abstracts database backends.

misconceptions.misconception: All routing uses regular expressions.
misconceptions.correction: The article describes pattern matching, rewriting and graph traversal.

misconceptions.misconception: Ajax requires a full page reload.
misconceptions.correction: Ajax exchanges data in the background and updates page regions.

misconceptions.misconception: Frameworks always improve runtime performance.
misconceptions.correction: Abstractions can add overhead, bundle size and complexity; outcomes depend on context.

misconceptions.misconception: Modern standards make all frameworks unnecessary.
misconceptions.correction: The article says frameworks remain useful for productivity, structure and edge cases.

misconceptions.misconception: Every frontend framework uses a virtual DOM.
misconceptions.correction: Svelte is described as compiling components and eliminating the virtual DOM.

misconceptions.misconception: Fresh zero-runtime-overhead is an independently verified benchmark.
misconceptions.correction: It is a source characterization, not a measurement verified here.

misconceptions.misconception: A framework guarantees security.
misconceptions.correction: Some provide authentication and authorization; the article does not claim all are secure by default.

misconceptions.misconception: The citation warning proves every claim is false.
misconceptions.correction: The notice asks for more citations; each claim requires individual assessment.
