value.name: Cryptographic hash function
value.definition: A deterministic algorithm that maps an arbitrary-length binary input to a fixed-length digest, with security goals including preimage resistance, second-preimage resistance, and collision resistance.

value.primary_source: User-supplied Wikipedia article text: Cryptographic hash function
value.scope_note: The graph follows the supplied article's terminology and coverage, while adding explicit relationship structure, schema, patterns, and cautious engineering rules for machine use.
source_derived_content: Merkle–Damgård, wide-pipe, sponge, and HAIFA constructions
value.editorial_caveat: Algorithm status and parameter recommendations change. Use current standards and expert review for production decisions; the graph is not a substitute for a cryptographic design review.

value.name: Secure file verification
value.purpose: Detect modification or substitution of downloaded content.
steps: Obtain the expected digest from an authenticated/trusted source.
Compute the digest of the received file with a suitable modern algorithm.
Compare values using the correct algorithm and encoding.
If a mismatch occurs, reject or investigate the file; if it matches, interpret the result only within the trust model.
caveats: A digest posted beside a file on the same unauthenticated channel may be replaced together with the file.
A matching hash does not prove that software is benign or that the publisher is trustworthy.

value.name: Password storage with a password KDF
value.purpose: Reduce the rate of offline password guessing after a verifier database is exposed.
steps: Generate a unique random salt per password.
Derive a verifier using a password KDF such as Argon2, scrypt, bcrypt, or PBKDF2 with appropriate parameters.
Store the algorithm identifier, parameters, salt, and verifier.
On login, recompute and compare; upgrade parameters as policy changes.
caveats: Do not store plaintext passwords.
Do not use a fast hash such as raw SHA-256 or SHA-1 alone for password storage.
Parameter choices should follow current platform and standards guidance.

value.name: HMAC message authentication
value.purpose: Authenticate messages using a shared secret and a standardized keyed construction.
steps: Agree on a secure hash and shared secret key.
Compute the HMAC over the canonical message representation.
Transmit the message and authentication tag.
Receiver recomputes the HMAC and compares tags using an appropriate constant-time comparison.
caveats: Do not substitute naive hash(secret || message) constructions for HMAC.
Key management and message canonicalization remain important.

value.name: Content-addressed storage
value.purpose: Address and deduplicate objects based on content.
steps: Select a collision-resistant hash and a canonical byte representation.
Hash the content to derive a content address.
Store the object and index its address to physical storage.
On retrieval, recompute the hash to verify content integrity.
caveats: Collision handling and algorithm migration should be part of the design.
The content address is not automatically a claim of publisher authenticity.

value.name: Merkle-tree verification
value.purpose: Commit to a large data set and verify components using a root digest and authentication path.
steps: Hash each leaf using an unambiguous encoding.
Hash internal nodes from their child hashes.
Publish or authenticate the root digest.
Verify a selected leaf by recomputing its path to the root.
caveats: Tree layout, leaf/node domain separation, and encoding must be specified to avoid ambiguity.

value.name: Hash-based proof of work
value.purpose: Make request creation moderately costly while allowing cheap validation.
steps: Define a target predicate over a hash output.
Vary a nonce or candidate header and compute hashes until the predicate passes.
Verifier performs one or a small number of hash computations and checks the predicate.
caveats: Difficulty must be calibrated; proof of work does not itself establish the truth or legitimacy of the submitted content.

value.name: Cryptographic hash algorithm migration
value.purpose: Retire weak digest algorithms while maintaining interoperability.
steps: Inventory every algorithm use and stored identifier format.
Choose a modern algorithm appropriate to the use case and threat model.
Version formats and APIs so algorithm identity is explicit.
Where feasible, verify old objects and add new digests; plan dual-read or staged migration.
Monitor standards and cryptanalysis and retire obsolete formats.
caveats: A digest's byte length alone does not uniquely identify the algorithm.
Do not assume legacy digests become secure because they are combined with a modern digest.

value.statement: A cryptographic hash is not encryption and has no decryption key or general inverse operation.
A matching digest proves only a content match relative to the expected digest and trust chain; it does not establish that the content is safe or benign.
For an ideal n-bit hash, generic preimage work is about 2^n and generic collision work about 2^(n/2); real algorithms may be weaker due to cryptanalysis.
Fast general-purpose hashes should not be used alone to store passwords; use a salted password KDF with current recommended parameters.
For hash-based message authentication, use HMAC or another reviewed construction rather than naive secret-prefix/suffix hashing.
MD5 and SHA-1 are unsuitable for new applications that depend on collision resistance.
CRC-32 and similar checksums detect accidental corruption but do not provide cryptographic protection against intentional manipulation.
Persist the algorithm name/version and output parameters alongside a digest; digest bytes alone are not a robust self-describing identifier.

value.title: File digest comparison
value.input: A downloaded archive and a trusted SHA-256 digest string.
steps: Compute SHA-256 over the exact downloaded bytes.
Encode the result consistently, commonly as hexadecimal.
Compare with the authenticated expected digest.
value.output: Equal digests provide strong evidence of byte-for-byte identity under SHA-256's security assumptions and the trust model.

value.title: Leading-zero proof of work
value.input: A candidate message/header plus a nonce.
steps: Check whether the digest begins with the required number of zero bits.
If not, vary the nonce and repeat.
value.output: A valid candidate is relatively cheap to verify; expected search effort grows exponentially with the number of required leading zero bits.

value.title: Digest commitment
value.input: A secret solution m held by Alice.
steps: Alice computes H(m) and publishes the digest before revealing m.
Bob later computes H(m) over the revealed solution.
They compare the result to the earlier commitment.
value.output: The matching digest supports the claim that the revealed solution matches the committed value, assuming the hash and protocol are appropriate.

value.title: Salted password verifier
value.input: Password candidate, unique random salt, KDF name and parameters.
steps: Derive a verifier with the selected password KDF.
Store the salt, algorithm parameters and verifier, not the plaintext password.
At login, derive again and compare.
value.output: Unique salts reduce cross-account precomputation and KDF cost slows each password guess.

value.title: Local commits are repository-local until published
value.statement: A successful local commit does not automatically update a remote repository; use push or an explicit hosting workflow to publish changes.

value.title: Review the index before committing
value.statement: git commit records staged content, so inspect staged diffs and status to avoid committing unintended changes.

value.title: A content hash is not publisher authentication
value.statement: Object hashes support content identity and integrity checks, but signed tags/commits or a trusted release process are needed to authenticate who published content.

value.title: Do not assume SHA-1 collision resistance
value.statement: The source documents the SHAttered demonstration and Git's hash-transition work; deployments should follow current Git guidance on hash compatibility and security.

value.title: Do not treat .gitignore as secret removal
value.statement: Ignoring a file prevents matching untracked files from being added by ordinary workflows; it does not erase already committed secrets from history or other clones.

value.title: Rotate exposed credentials before history cleanup
value.statement: If a credential was committed, revoke/rotate it first; history rewriting alone cannot ensure every clone or cache has discarded the value.

value.title: Prefer revert for changes already shared
value.statement: A new revert commit is generally safer for shared published history than rewriting commits on which others may depend.

value.title: Enforce permissions outside core Git
value.statement: Git's core does not provide access control; enforce read/write authorization at the server, SSH, hosting or authorization-tool layer.

value.title: Treat untrusted repositories as executable-risk inputs
value.statement: Inspect repository configuration, hooks, submodule URLs and scripts before running commands or tools from untrusted repositories.

value.title: Use authenticated protected transports for remotes
value.statement: Prefer appropriately configured SSH or HTTPS and verify host identity; an unencrypted or untrusted transport can expose users to redirection or interception.

value.title: Keep Git clients and servers patched
value.statement: Historical vulnerabilities were fixed in later releases; update supported clients, servers and hosting services to receive security fixes.

value.title: Do not rely on unreachable objects as durable backups
value.statement: Unreachable objects may be removed by automatic or explicit garbage collection; preserve important commits with refs or backups.

value.title: Rename history is inferred, not stored as permanent file identity
value.statement: Git detects renames heuristically while viewing history; a rename with substantial simultaneous edits may appear as deletion plus addition.

value.title: Pull requests belong to hosting/workflow layers
value.statement: A pull request is not a native Git object or command; Git transports commits and refs while hosting services manage review records and merge UI.

value.title: Validate merges that require manual conflict resolution
value.statement: A successful merge operation can still require human judgment; test the integrated result and review staged resolutions before finalizing.

value.title: Limit unnecessary ref advertisement in large repositories
value.statement: Where supported, protocol v2 allows clients to request relevant refs, reducing overhead for fetches that need only a subset of repository state.

value.title: Verify signatures for security-sensitive releases
value.statement: When a release uses signed tags, verify the signature and trust in the signing key before relying on the tag as publisher-authenticated.

value.title: Distinguish working tree, index and object database
value.statement: Working-tree edits are not staged; staged content is not committed; committed objects are local history until pushed.

value.title: Do not assume every repository uses the same default branch name
value.statement: Repositories may use main, master or a configured alternative; inspect local and remote refs rather than hard-coding a branch name.

value.title: Create and commit a local change
value.scenario: A developer changes a file and wants a recorded snapshot.
value.outcome: The index contents become a new commit in local history; nothing is published remotely unless pushed.

value.title: Collaborate on a feature branch
value.scenario: A developer contributes a feature to a shared repository.
steps: open a pull/merge request on the hosting service
value.outcome: Commits remain locally available offline, then are published to a remote branch and optionally reviewed using a hosting-layer pull request.

value.title: Resolve conflicting edits
value.scenario: Two branches modify overlapping lines and Git cannot automatically choose a result.
steps: edit files to desired combined result
value.outcome: The resulting history records the integrated state; tests and review are needed to validate semantic correctness.

value.title: Authenticate a release tag
value.scenario: A maintainer wants consumers to verify that a release tag was signed by an expected key.
value.outcome: Signature verification checks the tag signature; consumers must also trust the signer/key and verify release provenance.

value.title: Respond to a committed credential
value.scenario: A password or API token accidentally enters a commit and may have been pushed.
steps: Revoke or rotate the credential immediately
Check access logs and downstream use
Coordinate removal/rewriting of affected history if required
Notify collaborators and clean relevant clones/caches where feasible
Add preventive scanning and appropriate ignore rules
value.outcome: The credential is invalidated first; history cleanup reduces future exposure but cannot guarantee every copy is erased.

value.title: Inspect repository integrity and storage
value.scenario: A maintainer wants to check object connectivity and reduce loose-object overhead.
value.outcome: Integrity checks and object packing can reveal repository issues and improve storage efficiency; garbage collection can prune unreachable objects.

effects: commit references root tree and parent commits

steps.action: Store new objects loosely
effects: fast object creation, more filesystem entries

steps.action: Run maintenance and pack objects
effects: packfiles and indexes improve storage/transfer efficiency

steps.action: Check repository integrity
effects: integrity/connectivity checks run

architecture_patterns.name: Release authentication pattern
architecture_patterns.description: Use an annotated signed tag to identify and authenticate a release point.

steps.action: Prepare a reviewed release commit
effects: release state exists in history

steps.action: Create annotated signed tag
effects: tag object contains metadata and signature

steps.action: Publish tag and history
effects: remote receives tag subject to policy

steps.action: Verify signer and tag before consuming release
effects: signature verification supports publisher authentication

architecture_patterns.name: Prevent and remediate secret exposure
architecture_patterns.description: Reduce the chance that credentials are committed and define remediation if a secret enters history.

steps.action: Ignore local secret/config files where appropriate
effects: untracked matching files are excluded

steps.action: Use secret scanning and pre-commit checks
effects: credentials can be detected before publication

steps.action: If a secret was committed, revoke or rotate it immediately
effects: exposed credential is no longer trusted

steps.action: Coordinate history cleanup and remote cleanup
effects: sensitive content may be removed by history rewrite, but clones/caches may retain copies

steps.action: Use revert rather than rewriting ordinary shared history
effects: published shared history remains stable for routine changes

architecture_patterns.name: Secure repository transport and authorization
architecture_patterns.description: Separate transport security from repository authorization and signed-history verification.

steps.action: Choose an authenticated transport
effects: protects transport and/or authenticates remote depending on configuration

steps.action: Enforce repository permissions at server/hosting layer
effects: read/write access constrained by policy

steps.action: Review untrusted clone URLs, submodule URLs and hooks
effects: reduces malicious repository/config execution risk

steps.action: Verify signed release tags or commits when provided
effects: authenticates signer for signed content; hashes alone do not prove identity

steps.action: Keep Git client updated
effects: receives security fixes for known vulnerabilities

architecture_patterns.name: Fork-and-review workflow
architecture_patterns.description: Uses an independent repository and hosting-service pull request for collaboration.

steps.action: Fork or clone the upstream repository
effects: independent development copy created

steps.action: Develop commits on a topic branch
effects: change history isolated from upstream default branch

steps.action: Push branch to a writable remote
effects: branch becomes available for review

steps.action: Open pull/merge request on hosting service
effects: review metadata and discussion tracked by forge

steps.action: Review, test and merge through configured process
effects: approved commits integrated into target branch

architecture_patterns.name: Large repository optimization
architecture_patterns.description: Use packing, selective transfer and virtualization/extensions when repository size becomes expensive.

steps.action: Pack objects and run maintenance
effects: reduced loose-object overhead and delta-compressed storage

steps.action: Use protocol v2-capable clients/servers
effects: fetch can request only relevant refs

steps.action: Use Git LFS for appropriate large binary assets
effects: large payloads handled through LFS workflows

steps.action: Consider VFS for Git for huge working trees
effects: placeholder files downloaded when accessed

steps.action: Measure repository history and clone costs
effects: choose optimization based on workload

derived_rules.title: Local commits are repository-local until published
derived_rules.statement: A successful local commit does not automatically update a remote repository; use push or an explicit hosting workflow to publish changes.

derived_rules.title: Review the index before committing
derived_rules.statement: git commit records staged content, so inspect staged diffs and status to avoid committing unintended changes.

derived_rules.title: A content hash is not publisher authentication
derived_rules.statement: Object hashes support content identity and integrity checks, but signed tags/commits or a trusted release process are needed to authenticate who published content.

derived_rules.title: Do not assume SHA-1 collision resistance
derived_rules.statement: The source documents the SHAttered demonstration and Git's hash-transition work; deployments should follow current Git guidance on hash compatibility and security.

derived_rules.title: Do not treat .gitignore as secret removal
derived_rules.statement: Ignoring a file prevents matching untracked files from being added by ordinary workflows; it does not erase already committed secrets from history or other clones.

derived_rules.title: Rotate exposed credentials before history cleanup
derived_rules.statement: If a credential was committed, revoke/rotate it first; history rewriting alone cannot ensure every clone or cache has discarded the value.

derived_rules.title: Prefer revert for changes already shared
derived_rules.statement: A new revert commit is generally safer for shared published history than rewriting commits on which others may depend.

derived_rules.title: Enforce permissions outside core Git
derived_rules.statement: Git's core does not provide access control; enforce read/write authorization at the server, SSH, hosting or authorization-tool layer.

derived_rules.title: Treat untrusted repositories as executable-risk inputs
derived_rules.statement: Inspect repository configuration, hooks, submodule URLs and scripts before running commands or tools from untrusted repositories.

derived_rules.title: Use authenticated protected transports for remotes
derived_rules.statement: Prefer appropriately configured SSH or HTTPS and verify host identity; an unencrypted or untrusted transport can expose users to redirection or interception.

derived_rules.title: Keep Git clients and servers patched
derived_rules.statement: Historical vulnerabilities were fixed in later releases; update supported clients, servers and hosting services to receive security fixes.

derived_rules.title: Do not rely on unreachable objects as durable backups
derived_rules.statement: Unreachable objects may be removed by automatic or explicit garbage collection; preserve important commits with refs or backups.

derived_rules.title: Rename history is inferred, not stored as permanent file identity
derived_rules.statement: Git detects renames heuristically while viewing history; a rename with substantial simultaneous edits may appear as deletion plus addition.

derived_rules.title: Pull requests belong to hosting/workflow layers
derived_rules.statement: A pull request is not a native Git object or command; Git transports commits and refs while hosting services manage review records and merge UI.

derived_rules.title: Validate merges that require manual conflict resolution
derived_rules.statement: A successful merge operation can still require human judgment; test the integrated result and review staged resolutions before finalizing.

derived_rules.title: Limit unnecessary ref advertisement in large repositories
derived_rules.statement: Where supported, protocol v2 allows clients to request relevant refs, reducing overhead for fetches that need only a subset of repository state.

derived_rules.title: Verify signatures for security-sensitive releases
derived_rules.statement: When a release uses signed tags, verify the signature and trust in the signing key before relying on the tag as publisher-authenticated.

derived_rules.title: Distinguish working tree, index and object database
derived_rules.statement: Working-tree edits are not staged; staged content is not committed; committed objects are local history until pushed.

derived_rules.title: Do not assume every repository uses the same default branch name
derived_rules.statement: Repositories may use main, master or a configured alternative; inspect local and remote refs rather than hard-coding a branch name.

examples.title: Create and commit a local change
examples.scenario: A developer changes a file and wants a recorded snapshot.
examples.outcome: The index contents become a new commit in local history; nothing is published remotely unless pushed.

examples.title: Collaborate on a feature branch
examples.scenario: A developer contributes a feature to a shared repository.
steps: open a pull/merge request on the hosting service
examples.outcome: Commits remain locally available offline, then are published to a remote branch and optionally reviewed using a hosting-layer pull request.

examples.title: Resolve conflicting edits
examples.scenario: Two branches modify overlapping lines and Git cannot automatically choose a result.
steps: edit files to desired combined result
examples.outcome: The resulting history records the integrated state; tests and review are needed to validate semantic correctness.

examples.title: Authenticate a release tag
examples.scenario: A maintainer wants consumers to verify that a release tag was signed by an expected key.
examples.outcome: Signature verification checks the tag signature; consumers must also trust the signer/key and verify release provenance.

examples.title: Respond to a committed credential
examples.scenario: A password or API token accidentally enters a commit and may have been pushed.
steps: Revoke or rotate the credential immediately
Check access logs and downstream use
Coordinate removal/rewriting of affected history if required
Notify collaborators and clean relevant clones/caches where feasible
Add preventive scanning and appropriate ignore rules
examples.outcome: The credential is invalidated first; history cleanup reduces future exposure but cannot guarantee every copy is erased.

examples.title: Inspect repository integrity and storage
examples.scenario: A maintainer wants to check object connectivity and reduce loose-object overhead.
examples.outcome: Integrity checks and object packing can reveal repository issues and improve storage efficiency; garbage collection can prune unreachable objects.

value.title: Mirai (malware) — Full Detail Knowledge Graph
value.created_for: Machine-readable knowledge graph preserving concepts, people, variants, incidents, architecture, and defensive connections
value.source_basis: User-provided Wikipedia article text; source-derived claims are distinguished from defensive synthesis.
value.safety_scope: Educational and defensive. No executable attack commands, exploit instructions, credential lists, target-selection guidance, or traffic-generation instructions are included.

value.name: Mirai botnet lifecycle (conceptual)
value.description: High-level lifecycle from exposed device discovery through compromise, reporting, C2 tasking, DDoS participation, and defender containment.
steps: Internet-exposed or reachable IoT asset has a weakness
Malware discovers a potentially vulnerable device
Weak credentials or an exploitable software flaw permits unauthorized access
Compromised device is recruited into the botnet
Bots generate distributed traffic against a target
Defenders detect, contain, remediate, and recover
security_notes: Conceptual model only; not an operational attack recipe.
Break the chain through secure defaults, patching, management-plane isolation, monitoring, and upstream DDoS controls.

value.name: IoT device hardening baseline
value.description: Reduce the likelihood that an embedded device can be recruited into a botnet.
steps: Inventory device models, firmware, owners, and exposure
Replace default credentials with unique credentials
Disable unnecessary remote administration and Telnet
Restrict management access to trusted networks
Segment IoT devices and monitor outbound behavior
Replace devices that cannot be supported securely
security_notes: A reboot or factory reset alone is not durable remediation if defaults and vulnerabilities remain.

value.name: Layered DDoS resilience
value.description: Combine application, edge, network-provider, and incident-response measures.
steps: Baseline normal traffic and service health
Detect abnormal volume, protocol patterns, and application pressure
Engage provider or scrubbing services for upstream traffic
Use CDN/Anycast and rate limits where appropriate
Preserve allowlisted legitimate traffic and critical functions
Communicate status and review telemetry after mitigation
security_notes: No single control prevents every DDoS class; controls should be layered and rehearsed.

value.name: Variant and threat-intelligence workflow
value.description: Track the Mirai-derived ecosystem without assuming every family has identical behavior.
steps: Record observed behavior, timestamps, confidence, and provenance
Map variant lineage while distinguishing confirmed from suspected links
Translate indicators into defensive detections and patch priorities
security_notes: The source article mixes reported, suspected, and attributed claims; preserve uncertainty.

value.name: Response to a suspected infected IoT device
value.description: A defensive containment and recovery workflow for suspected Mirai infection.
steps: Confirm symptoms with logs and network telemetry
Isolate the device from external access and outbound abuse
Update firmware or restore a trusted image
Change all default and exposed credentials
Disable unnecessary services and restrict management access
Validate traffic and monitor for reinfection
security_notes: Coordinate with the ISP, vendor, and incident-response team when service disruption or widespread compromise is suspected.

value.name: Public malware code reuse and variant evolution
value.description: Public release of malware source can lower the barrier to derivative variants and new targeting.
steps: Other actors reuse or modify it
Variants add target architectures, exploits, or capabilities
Defenders update asset coverage and detection
Patching and secure configuration reduce exploitable surface
security_notes: The same release can aid analysis while also enabling harmful reuse; analysis should remain defensive and authorized.

value.name: Evidence-based incident attribution
value.description: Distinguish technical observations from claims about people or organizations.
steps: Collect verifiable logs and forensic evidence
Correlate infrastructure, samples, timelines, and victim reports
Refer legal conclusions to competent authorities
Update assessments when new evidence appears
security_notes: An alias, public claim, or shared codebase alone does not prove authorship or operational control.

value.rule: Never leave factory-default credentials enabled on Internet-reachable IoT devices.
Disable Telnet and other unnecessary cleartext remote administration services.
Expose device administration only to explicitly trusted management networks.
Track and apply vendor firmware updates for supported devices.
Replace unsupported devices that cannot be secured to an acceptable standard.
Place IoT devices in appropriately restricted network segments.
Monitor and restrict unnecessary outbound connections from embedded devices.
Maintain an inventory of device models, firmware, owners, and exposure.
Do not treat rebooting as full remediation when the original weakness remains.
After factory reset, patch the device and change credentials before reconnecting it.
Alert on unusual outbound volume, unexpected remote access, and abnormal device resource use.
Use layered DDoS protection across application, edge, network, and provider boundaries.
Prepare provider escalation and scrubbing procedures before a major DDoS incident.
Use suitable rate limits and service-level protection without blocking legitimate clients indiscriminately.
Preserve logs and relevant telemetry during incident response where lawful and feasible.
Isolate suspected compromised IoT assets when needed to stop further abuse.
Verify clean firmware, credential changes, and expected traffic before restoring network access.
Record whether a variant, incident, or attribution is confirmed, reported, or suspected.
Keep source provenance and publication dates attached to threat-intelligence claims.

architecture_patterns.name: Mirai botnet lifecycle (conceptual)

Defenders detect, contain, remediate, and recover
security_notes: Conceptual model only; not an operational attack recipe.
Break the chain through secure defaults, patching, management-plane isolation, monitoring, and upstream DDoS controls.

Update firmware or restore a trusted image

value.title: nginx — Full-detail knowledge graph
value.description: A source-grounded, machine-readable graph of nginx, its features, protocols, architecture, ecosystem, history, licensing, comparative notes and implementation considerations.
value.scope: Based on the user-provided Wikipedia article text. Inferences are explicitly labeled.

value.name: Edge reverse proxy
value.description: Clients connect to nginx, which terminates or handles HTTP-level traffic and forwards requests to upstream application services.
value.source_basis: Core reverse-proxy role is explicit; detailed deployment flow is a generalized architecture interpretation.

value.name: Static content delivery
value.description: nginx serves static files, index files and optionally auto-indexed directory listings.
value.source_basis: Explicitly supported by the article.

value.name: Load-balanced application
value.description: nginx distributes incoming requests across backend servers and can use in-band health checks.
value.source_basis: Load balancing and in-band health checks are explicitly listed.

value.name: Reverse proxy with HTTP caching
value.description: nginx caches eligible responses so repeated requests can be served without always querying the backend.
value.source_basis: Caching is explicit; exact cache policy and bypass rules are not covered in the supplied article.

value.name: Dynamic application integration
value.description: nginx serves as a front end for dynamic content through FastCGI, SCGI, uWSGI, WSGI application servers or Phusion Passenger.
value.source_basis: Integrations are explicitly listed.

value.name: TLS-enabled frontend
value.description: nginx supports TLS/SSL features such as SNI, OCSP stapling and TLS protocol integrations; a frontend TLS termination topology is a common inference.
value.source_basis: TLS/SSL features are explicit; exact termination topology is inferred.

value.name: Mail protocol proxy
value.description: nginx can proxy SMTP, POP3 and IMAP, with TLS/SSL and STARTTLS; authentication is delegated to an external HTTP server or script.
value.source_basis: Protocol and authentication features are explicit.

value.name: Graceful configuration or executable upgrade
value.description: The article states nginx can upgrade its executable and configuration without losing client connections.
value.source_basis: Explicitly listed feature; operational procedure is not detailed in the supplied article.

value.name: Containerized web frontend
value.description: nginx is commonly deployed in Docker containers according to a 2018 usage survey; container orchestration details are outside the source.
value.source_basis: The source reports a historical survey finding, not a current universal deployment statistic.

value.name: Commercial API gateway and management
value.description: NGINX Plus API gateway functionality was associated with NGINX Controller, announced as an API management tool in 2017.
value.source_basis: Commercial product relationship is explicit; flow is conceptual.

value.rule: For high numbers of concurrent connections, nginx's asynchronous event-driven approach is a core architectural choice.
value.rationale: The article contrasts its event-driven model with thread-based handling and connects it to predictable performance under high load.

value.rule: Do not assume nginx natively supports Apache-style .htaccess per-file overrides.
value.rationale: The article explicitly identifies this as a flexibility difference.

value.rule: Verify third-party module compatibility and build requirements before deploying modules.
value.rationale: The article notes modules may need to be compiled alongside nginx, may not all support dynamic loading, and some still require static linking.

value.rule: Treat the article's HTTP/3 status as experimental from nginx 1.25.0, not as a blanket statement about every build or later release.
value.rationale: The source specifically characterizes HTTP/3 as experimental starting with version 1.25.0.

value.rule: Encrypted Client Hello support depends on using a compatible OpenSSL branch and the relevant nginx build/configuration.
value.rationale: The source conditions ECH support on nginx 1.29.4 and an OpenSSL branch implementing ECH.

value.rule: Plan an external HTTP service or authentication script for nginx mail-proxy authentication.
value.rationale: The source says mail proxy authentication requires an external HTTP server or script.

value.rule: Do not assume NGINX Unit receives upstream maintenance after October 2025.
value.rationale: The article says it was archived by maintainers and is no longer receiving updates.

value.rule: Distinguish the BSD-licensed nginx project from proprietary NGINX Plus.
value.rationale: The source lists different license models.

value.rule: When relying on native ACME automation, verify the deployed nginx version and certificate lifecycle configuration.
value.rationale: The article reports native ACME issuance and renewal support, but does not provide a complete configuration procedure.

value.rule: Keep popularity figures tied to the survey and date rather than treating them as timeless market share.
value.rationale: The article cites different survey dates and populations, including all websites versus the busiest sites.

value.rule: Define cacheability, invalidation, and bypass rules explicitly when using nginx HTTP caching.
value.rationale: The source confirms reverse-proxy caching but does not describe policy details; this is an implementation recommendation inferred from the capability.

value.rule: Consider upstream health checks when deploying nginx as a load balancer.
value.rationale: In-band health checks are listed as a load-balancing feature.

value.rule: Describe the 2019 Rambler matter as a reported copyright claim/dispute, not as a settled determination of ownership.
value.rationale: The supplied article describes allegations and subsequent events but does not establish a court finding that resolves ownership.

value.rule: Validate protocol features against the exact nginx version and build in use.
value.rationale: The article ties multiple capabilities to particular versions and build dependencies.

value.rule: Treat versions, adoption statistics, and project status as claims from the supplied article snapshot, not independently verified current facts.
value.rationale: The article contains dated and potentially time-sensitive claims.

steps: Install an nginx build appropriate for the target operating system.
Configure a server block/virtual server for the intended host name.
Set the content root and index file behavior.
Validate the configuration and test requests.
value.caveat: Operational commands and configuration syntax are not included in the source article; these steps are generalized guidance.

value.title: Reverse proxy to an application
value.purpose: Forward client HTTP requests to an upstream application server.
steps: Configure a virtual server for the public hostname.
Define a location/routing rule for application traffic.
Configure proxy forwarding to the upstream/backend.
Test request routing, headers, error handling and logs.
value.caveat: The source confirms reverse proxy capability but does not provide exact directives.

value.title: Load balance multiple backends
value.purpose: Distribute requests across upstream servers.
steps: Configure the frontend server to route requests to the pool.
Choose a suitable load-balancing policy for the workload.
Configure or verify health checks and test backend failure behavior.
value.caveat: The source mentions load balancing and in-band health checks but does not enumerate algorithms.

value.title: Enable HTTPS and certificate lifecycle
value.purpose: Use nginx TLS support and, where suitable, ACME certificate issuance/renewal.
steps: Verify nginx version and TLS library/build capabilities.
Configure certificates and TLS settings for the hostname.
If using native ACME, configure issuance and renewal according to version-specific documentation.
Test certificate validity, renewal behavior and protocol compatibility.
value.caveat: The supplied article does not provide a working configuration example; verify current official documentation before production deployment.

value.title: Serve a dynamic application
value.purpose: Integrate nginx with a supported application handler/server.
steps: Identify the application runtime and supported integration (FastCGI, SCGI, uWSGI, WSGI application server, Passenger or gRPC).
Enable caching only when correct for the application semantics.
Test application errors, concurrency and deployment behavior.
value.caveat: The source lists integrations but not app-specific configuration.

value.title: Proxy mail protocols
value.purpose: Use nginx mail proxy for SMTP, POP3 or IMAP.
steps: Select the mail protocols and TLS/STARTTLS requirements.
Configure the mail proxy and upstream mail servers.
Provide an external HTTP authentication service or script.
Test authentication failures and secure transport.
value.caveat: The source states external authentication is required but does not provide configuration.

value.title: Evaluate a third-party module
value.purpose: Add a module while accounting for build and compatibility constraints.
steps: Check the module's maintenance status and license.
Verify compatibility with the exact nginx version and build.
Determine whether dynamic loading is supported or static linking is required.
Build and test in staging before production rollout.
value.caveat: Derived from the article's module-loading discussion.

value.label: ISO image vs raw disc image
value.description: ISO stores logical-sector user data and omits control/error-correction information; raw images can retain complete disc information.

value.label: Filesystem vs physical track
value.description: A filesystem can reside inside a physical track, but ISO does not model physical tracks as track containers.

value.label: Data optical disc vs audio CD
value.description: Data discs use filesystem-bearing sectors; audio CDs use continuous encoded audio streams and track addressing.

value.label: Single-track vs multi-track
value.description: A single-track data disc can be represented as an ISO; a multi-track disc cannot be fully represented by one ISO.

value.label: ISO semantics vs .img extension
value.description: .img may be used for ISO images but can also denote images with different contents.

value.label: ISO 9660 vs UDF
value.description: Both filesystem structures can occur in optical-disc images; UDF is commonly associated with DVD/Blu-ray in the source.

value.label: Image vs physical disc
value.description: Image is a transferable binary artifact; physical disc is the optical medium it represents.

value.label: Mount vs burn
value.description: Mount exposes image through an OS interface; burning creates physical optical media.

value.label: Archival vs emulation
value.description: The same image artifact can preserve disc contents or provide input to an emulator.

value.label: ISO vs virtual CD-ROM
value.description: ISO is the stored image; virtual CD-ROM is the runtime interface exposing it as optical media.

value.label: Filesystem binary copy vs raw media copy
value.description: ISO preserves filesystem/user data rather than every physical-media control/error structure.

value.label: Track addressing vs file addressing
value.description: Audio CD content is addressed through track/index/time structures rather than filesystem files.

value.label: ISO is always a raw copy of every physical disc byte
value.correction: False: source says ISO omits control headers and error-correction data.

value.label: Every optical disc can be stored in one ISO
value.correction: False: multi-track and audio-disc structures exceed the ISO filesystem model.

value.label: An ISO contains physical tracks
value.correction: False: source explicitly says there is no concept of a track inside an ISO.

value.label: Audio CD tracks are files
value.correction: False: source describes continuous encoded audio rather than a filesystem.

value.label: .img always means exactly the same thing as .iso
value.correction: False: .img can contain different kinds of image data.

value.label: UDF cannot occur in an ISO image
value.correction: False: source explicitly says an ISO image may contain UDF.

value.label: Mounting an ISO burns it to a disc
value.correction: False: mounting exposes it virtually; burning creates physical media.

value.label: ISO cannot be transferred because it represents physical media
value.correction: False: image is a binary file and can move over links/removable storage.

value.label: USB limitations are inherent to ISO format
value.correction: False: source attributes historical limitation to software-tool availability.

value.label: ISO and virtual CD-ROM are identical concepts
value.correction: False: ISO is stored representation; virtual CD-ROM is runtime interface.

source_claims.text: Optical disc image is a sector-by-sector disk image containing disc filesystem and data.
Images can be created from optical discs, file collections, or other image files.
ISO stores user data, not control headers/error correction; logical data sectors are 2,048 bytes.
An image can be transferred over data links/removable media unlike a physical optical disc.
Suitable driver software can expose ISO to the OS as though it were a physical optical disc.
ISO has no physical track concept and cannot fully represent multi-track discs.
Audio CDs cannot be represented as ISO because audio tracks contain continuous encoded audio rather than filesystems.
CUE/BIN, CCD/IMG, and MDS/MDF can store complete multi-track images with companion track metadata.
Historically, writing ISO to flash drives was limited by software tooling; raw-image writers later existed.
ISO is used for emulation, virtual CD-ROMs for hypervisors, and OS installation media.

fields.value: A detailed machine-readable knowledge graph derived from the user-provided Wikipedia article text on overlay networks, with explicit entities, relationships, examples, architectural patterns, trade-offs, and source provenance. Model-expanded illustrations are marked separately from article-stated claims.

limitations: The input is a Wikipedia article excerpt, not a full technical standard.

Examples and architecture patterns added beyond the article are explicitly labeled as model expansion.

value.id_policy: Stable namespace-prefixed IDs; relationship endpoints must refer to an entity or an architecture pattern ID.
value.source_policy: Source references point to the user-provided article and its bibliography records. Article claims are not treated as independently verified.

value.name: Data-center VXLAN overlay pattern
steps: VM or cluster endpoint emits packet
VXLAN encapsulates the inner Ethernet frame
destination VM or cluster receives frame
value.grounding: General technical illustration consistent with the article's VXLAN/data-center discussion; exact implementation details are model-expanded.

value.name: Provider BGP VPN WAN pattern
steps: Enterprise sites connect to provider edge
Provider uses BGP VPN mechanisms to maintain isolated routing context
Provider infrastructure transports traffic across WAN
Remote site receives traffic in its enterprise routing context
value.grounding: Illustrative generalization of the article's BGP VPN use case; specific control-plane details vary by implementation.

value.name: Resilient overlay path recovery pattern
steps: RON nodes measure path quality among participating nodes
A direct path degrades or disconnects
Overlay compares direct and relay paths against application-specific metrics
Traffic is rerouted directly or through another RON node
Node continues monitoring for future path changes
value.grounding: Based on the article's RON section.

value.name: End-system multicast delivery pattern
steps: Peers form an overlay distribution topology
Each overlay edge uses an underlying unicast path
Peers forward data to downstream peers
Topology is maintained as participants or paths change
value.grounding: Based on the article's overlay multicast section.

value.name: Logical-address DHT lookup pattern
steps: Application has a logical key or destination identifier
DHT routes lookup across overlay nodes
Responsible node is discovered without requester knowing its IP beforehand
Application sends message using discovered overlay route
value.grounding: Based on the article's DHT discussion; exact lookup procedure depends on the DHT algorithm.

overlay_families.description: Encapsulation/tunnel-based approaches that create logical connectivity over an underlay.
Provider and enterprise WAN overlays, including VPN and programmable SD-WAN approaches.
Overlays that organize peers or route using logical identifiers rather than only destination IP addresses.
Application-layer path monitoring and rerouting.
Peer-based distribution over underlying unicast paths.
Systems named by the article among overlay networks; this grouping is a taxonomy aid and does not imply identical designs or guarantees.

value.benefit: Can identify and route to destinations independently of their currently known IP address.
value.cost_or_limit: Requires overlay-level naming, lookup, or routing mechanisms.

value.benefit: Can select overlay-node sequence and apply application/site/user-specific policies.
value.cost_or_limit: Cannot directly control the underlay's route between two overlay nodes.

value.benefit: Can detect path degradation and reroute at the overlay layer.
value.cost_or_limit: Still depends on lower-layer availability and may choose a longer path.

value.benefit: Can provide logical isolation and optionally encryption.
value.cost_or_limit: An overlay by itself does not guarantee confidentiality, authentication, or secure endpoint behavior.

value.benefit: Enables logical networks and tunnels over shared infrastructure.
value.cost_or_limit: Additional headers consume capacity and can affect MTU/fragmentation behavior (MTU note is model-expanded).

value.benefit: Can prioritize traffic by application, user, or site.
value.cost_or_limit: DiffServ prioritization does not itself guarantee end-to-end throughput.

value.benefit: Can distribute data among peers without relying on router-level IP multicast.
value.cost_or_limit: Requires maintaining an overlay topology and may create redundant transmissions.

value.title: Proof of Work — Full Detail Knowledge Graph
value.description: Machine-readable knowledge graph covering proof-of-work fundamentals, history, algorithms, consensus, mining, security, economics, environmental considerations, useful-work variants, people and publications from the supplied article.
value.source_basis: User-supplied Wikipedia article text

value.name: Hashcash anti-spam stamp
value.description: Require a sender to generate a hash satisfying a recipient- or message-bound difficulty target, then verify it cheaply before accepting the request.

steps.action: Construct a stamp from version, difficulty, date, resource identifier and trial value.
effects: stamp binds work to the request context

steps.action: Search candidate values until the stamp hash meets the leading-zero target.
effects: computational work is expended

steps.action: Attach the stamp to the request or email.
effects: recipient receives proof material

steps.action: Verify the stamp hash and target with a small number of computations.
effects: request can be accepted or rejected based on policy

value.name: Bitcoin-style proof-of-work mining loop
value.description: Miners search over candidate block data and trial values until a digest satisfies the network difficulty target; nodes independently validate the result.

steps.action: Assemble a candidate block template.
effects: candidate transactions and metadata are selected

steps.action: Vary nonce or other candidate data and compute SHA-256-based hashes.
effects: repeated hashing consumes computational resources

steps.action: Check each digest against the difficulty target.
effects: invalid candidates are discarded

steps.action: Broadcast a candidate block when a valid proof is found.
effects: other nodes can inspect the candidate

steps.action: Nodes validate proof, transactions and consensus rules.
effects: valid block may extend the canonical chain

steps.action: Miner may receive the block reward if the block is accepted.
effects: economic incentives support mining

value.name: Merchant confirmation risk management
value.description: Use increasing confirmation depth as a practical way to increase the computational burden of reversing a payment, while recognizing that confirmations are not absolute finality.

steps.action: Observe the block containing the payment transaction.
effects: initial confirmation exists

steps.action: Wait for additional blocks to build on that block.
effects: confirmation depth increases

steps.action: Evaluate transaction value and network risk before releasing goods or services.
effects: risk tolerance informs operational policy

steps.action: Avoid treating a fixed number of confirmations as a mathematical guarantee against all attacks.
effects: residual reorganization risk remains explicit

value.name: Difficulty adjustment to target block interval
value.description: Periodically change the proof threshold based on observed block production to keep average production near a target interval.

steps.action: Measure block production over the protocol's adjustment window.
effects: observed timing is collected

steps.action: Compare observed timing with the target interval.
effects: direction and magnitude of adjustment are determined

steps.action: Update the difficulty parameter under consensus rules.
effects: future proof acceptance threshold changes

steps.action: Nodes enforce the same adjustment rules.
effects: consensus remains deterministic across compliant nodes

value.name: Coordinated mining pool
value.description: Miners coordinate work through a pool to smooth reward variance and divide payouts, while creating concentration and coordination considerations.

steps.action: Miners contribute hash power to a pool.
effects: pool coordinates multiple participants

steps.action: Pool distributes candidate work or assignments.
effects: participants search for valid proof candidates

steps.action: Pool accounts for submitted work and accepted blocks.
effects: contribution and reward shares can be calculated

steps.action: Monitor pool concentration and operational control.
effects: centralization risks are visible

value.name: Proof of useful work optimization loop
value.description: Combine a consensus protocol with a computational task whose output can solve an optimization problem beyond producing a proof.

steps.action: Define a useful optimization problem and verifiable solution criteria.
effects: work has external computational value

steps.action: Run the selected local-search or optimization algorithm.
effects: candidate solutions are produced

steps.action: Verify solution validity and protocol eligibility.
effects: valid work can contribute to consensus

steps.action: Apply the protocol's consensus and reward rules.
effects: participants are incentivized for useful computation

value.name: Optimisable proof-of-work algorithm market
value.description: Reward both problem solvers and contributors of improved algorithms according to adoption and a proportional influence mechanism.

steps.action: Specify a family of computational challenges.
effects: multiple problem classes can be used

steps.action: Contributors submit improved algorithms.
effects: algorithm candidates become available

steps.action: Miners select and run algorithms to solve challenge instances.
effects: algorithm adoption and performance become observable

steps.action: Calculate influence and distribute rewards under protocol rules.
effects: solvers and algorithm contributors can be compensated

value.name: Proof-of-work security-budget review
value.description: Assess whether the resources securing a network remain adequate relative to plausible attack resources and economic incentives.

steps.action: Estimate honest network hash rate and its concentration.
effects: defensive resource baseline is established

steps.action: Estimate the cost and availability of acquiring attack hash power.
effects: attacker resource assumptions are explicit

steps.action: Review subsidy, fees, energy costs, hardware access and pool concentration.
effects: economic security drivers are identified

steps.action: Model reorganization, censorship and double-spend consequences.
effects: threat impact is considered

steps.action: Reassess after reward changes, halvings or market shifts.

value.title: Proof generation should be costly relative to verification
value.statement: A PoW design should document the prover's expected work factor and verifier's validation cost; a high prover cost without cheap reliable verification defeats the core asymmetry.

value.title: Difficulty controls expected work, not the meaning of the result
value.statement: Difficulty should be selected for the threat model and service context; satisfying a target proves compliance with that target, not that arbitrary useful work was performed.

value.title: Interactive challenges can adapt to service load
value.statement: Where challenge-response is used, adapt difficulty carefully so abuse becomes expensive without making legitimate requests impractical.

value.title: Bind anti-spam work to the request context
value.statement: A Hashcash-style stamp should be checked against its specified fields and policy to reduce trivial replay or cross-context reuse.

value.title: Nodes must independently validate candidate blocks
value.statement: A miner's claim is not sufficient; nodes must verify proof validity, transactions and consensus rules before accepting a block.

value.title: Confirmations increase confidence but are not absolute finality
value.statement: Operational payment policies should account for value and reorganization risk rather than treating any fixed confirmation count as impossible to reverse.

value.title: Majority hash power can reorganize history
value.statement: Threat models should include reorganization, double spending and censorship when an attacker controls a majority of relevant mining power.

value.title: Monitor miner revenue as a security input
value.statement: Track subsidy and fees alongside hash rate, energy and hardware economics; lower rewards can alter the cost of attacking the network.

value.title: Measure mining concentration, not only total hash rate
value.statement: Total network hash rate does not by itself reveal how mining power is coordinated or controlled; monitor pools and ownership concentration.

value.title: ASIC resistance is not equivalent to attack resistance
value.statement: Commodity-hardware designs may lower specialization advantages while making large amounts of rentable general-purpose compute relevant to attack analysis.

value.title: Report energy consumption with context
value.statement: Energy assessments should state the measurement period, energy mix, system boundary and assumptions; electricity use alone does not settle all environmental or grid questions.

value.title: Useful-work consensus requires verifiable task outputs

value.title: Specify reward attribution for algorithm contributions

value.title: Memory-bound work shifts rather than eliminates hardware economics

value.name: Hybrid encryption and session protection
value.description: Use public-key key establishment or encapsulation to derive a shared secret, then derive a symmetric session key and protect bulk traffic symmetrically.

value.name: PKI-authenticated TLS
value.description: A client validates a certificate chain and identity, authenticates the server public key, performs key establishment, and uses symmetric traffic protection.

value.name: Web-of-trust public-key authentication
value.description: Users use endorsements and key identity checks rather than relying solely on a centralized certificate hierarchy.

value.name: Signed software update
value.description: Publisher signs release metadata or package; client verifies the signature with an authenticated publisher public key before installation.

value.name: Ephemeral key agreement with forward secrecy
value.description: A protocol uses fresh ephemeral key material and erases it appropriately so later compromise of a long-term key need not reveal prior session secrets.

value.name: Public-key trust and revocation lifecycle
value.description: Generate keys securely, bind public keys to identities, validate certificates and status, rotate or revoke compromised credentials, and maintain trust anchors.

value.name: Encrypted content with metadata exposure
value.description: Public-key encryption protects message body content but headers and traffic patterns can remain observable; metadata protection requires additional design.

value.rule: Never treat a received public key as authentic solely because it is available; bind it to the intended identity through a trusted validation method.
value.rationale: Key substitution can enable man-in-the-middle attacks.

value.rule: Protect private keys against disclosure, unauthorized use, backup exposure, and weak custody arrangements.
value.rationale: Anyone with the private key may impersonate its owner or decrypt data depending on the key's role.

value.rule: Use public-key operations for key establishment or encapsulation and symmetric authenticated encryption for bulk data when appropriate.
value.rationale: Public-key operations are generally more computationally expensive than symmetric protection.

value.rule: Validate certificate chain, intended identity, validity period, and revocation status before relying on a certified key.
value.rationale: A compromised or mis-issued certificate authority can undermine the trust hierarchy.

value.rule: Use well-designed ephemeral key agreement and erase ephemeral secrets when forward secrecy is required.
value.rationale: Ephemeral session keys can limit the consequences of later long-term key compromise.

value.rule: Choose algorithms and parameters based on current cryptographic guidance, threat models, and required security lifetime.
value.rationale: Long keys do not repair every algorithmic weakness; some schemes have structural attacks or quantum-related risks.

value.rule: Use constant-time operations and implementation-specific mitigations where relevant; assess side-channel exposure.
value.rationale: Information leakage can compromise keys even when the mathematical algorithm is sound.

value.rule: Do not assume encryption hides sender, recipient, timing, size, subject, or traffic relationships; add metadata protection when required.
value.rationale: Traffic analysis can infer sensitive relationships from unencrypted metadata.

value.rule: Do not confuse digital signatures with encryption: signatures support authenticity/integrity, while encryption protects confidentiality.
value.rationale: A signature does not inherently conceal message content and encryption alone does not authenticate the sender.

value.rule: Use role-appropriate keys and lifecycle policies; consider separating signing keys from encryption/key-agreement keys.
value.rationale: Different operations have different legal, recovery, revocation and forward-secrecy implications.

value.rule: Generate keys and cryptographic randomness with a suitable cryptographically secure random-number generator.
value.rationale: Predictable key material can defeat otherwise sound algorithms.

value.rule: Treat forward secrecy as a protocol property with assumptions, not as a universal guarantee; endpoint compromise and poor ephemeral-secret handling remain risks.
value.rationale: Security depends on protocol implementation and secret erasure.

value.rule: Treat encrypted-header designs as specialized and deployment-dependent rather than assuming metadata privacy is provided by ordinary public-key encryption.
value.rationale: The source describes encrypted metadata as experimental and not broadly deployed at the time of the article.

value.name: Alice signs a message for Bob
steps: Alice signs message data using her private signing key.
Bob obtains an authentic copy of Alice's public key.
Bob verifies the signature against the message.
A valid signature supports integrity and key-possession-based attribution, but does not encrypt the message.

value.name: Source sends an encrypted message to a journalist
steps: The journalist publishes an authentic encryption public key.
The source encrypts the message using that public key.
The journalist decrypts using the paired private key.
Message content is concealed, but ordinary encryption may leave communication metadata visible and does not by itself authenticate the sender.

value.name: Publisher-signed software update
steps: Publisher creates a signing key pair and distributes the public key through a trusted channel or software installation.
Publisher signs an update or its authenticated digest/manifest.
Client verifies the signature before applying the update.
Compromise of the signing key or trust bootstrap can undermine the workflow.

value.name: TLS hybrid cryptosystem
steps: Client authenticates the server certificate and public-key identity.
Protocol establishes or derives shared traffic secrets using public-key cryptographic mechanisms.
Symmetric cryptography protects application data; suitable ephemeral key exchange can provide forward secrecy.

value.name: Public-key substitution attack
steps: Attacker intercepts a public-key distribution exchange.
Attacker substitutes a key they control and relays traffic between parties.
Without authenticated key binding, each party may encrypt to or trust the attacker's key.
Certificate validation, web-of-trust checks, or another authenticated channel can prevent or detect substitution.

architecture_patterns.name: Hybrid encryption and session protection
architecture_patterns.description: Use public-key key establishment or encapsulation to derive a shared secret, then derive a symmetric session key and protect bulk traffic symmetrically.

architecture_patterns.name: PKI-authenticated TLS
architecture_patterns.description: A client validates a certificate chain and identity, authenticates the server public key, performs key establishment, and uses symmetric traffic protection.

architecture_patterns.name: Web-of-trust public-key authentication
architecture_patterns.description: Users use endorsements and key identity checks rather than relying solely on a centralized certificate hierarchy.

architecture_patterns.name: Signed software update
architecture_patterns.description: Publisher signs release metadata or package; client verifies the signature with an authenticated publisher public key before installation.

architecture_patterns.name: Ephemeral key agreement with forward secrecy
architecture_patterns.description: A protocol uses fresh ephemeral key material and erases it appropriately so later compromise of a long-term key need not reveal prior session secrets.

architecture_patterns.name: Public-key trust and revocation lifecycle
architecture_patterns.description: Generate keys securely, bind public keys to identities, validate certificates and status, rotate or revoke compromised credentials, and maintain trust anchors.

architecture_patterns.name: Encrypted content with metadata exposure
architecture_patterns.description: Public-key encryption protects message body content but headers and traffic patterns can remain observable; metadata protection requires additional design.

derived_security_rules.rule: Never treat a received public key as authentic solely because it is available; bind it to the intended identity through a trusted validation method.
derived_security_rules.rationale: Key substitution can enable man-in-the-middle attacks.

derived_security_rules.rule: Protect private keys against disclosure, unauthorized use, backup exposure, and weak custody arrangements.
derived_security_rules.rationale: Anyone with the private key may impersonate its owner or decrypt data depending on the key's role.

derived_security_rules.rule: Use public-key operations for key establishment or encapsulation and symmetric authenticated encryption for bulk data when appropriate.
derived_security_rules.rationale: Public-key operations are generally more computationally expensive than symmetric protection.

derived_security_rules.rule: Validate certificate chain, intended identity, validity period, and revocation status before relying on a certified key.
derived_security_rules.rationale: A compromised or mis-issued certificate authority can undermine the trust hierarchy.

derived_security_rules.rule: Use well-designed ephemeral key agreement and erase ephemeral secrets when forward secrecy is required.
derived_security_rules.rationale: Ephemeral session keys can limit the consequences of later long-term key compromise.

derived_security_rules.rule: Choose algorithms and parameters based on current cryptographic guidance, threat models, and required security lifetime.
derived_security_rules.rationale: Long keys do not repair every algorithmic weakness; some schemes have structural attacks or quantum-related risks.

derived_security_rules.rule: Use constant-time operations and implementation-specific mitigations where relevant; assess side-channel exposure.
derived_security_rules.rationale: Information leakage can compromise keys even when the mathematical algorithm is sound.

derived_security_rules.rule: Do not assume encryption hides sender, recipient, timing, size, subject, or traffic relationships; add metadata protection when required.
derived_security_rules.rationale: Traffic analysis can infer sensitive relationships from unencrypted metadata.

derived_security_rules.rule: Do not confuse digital signatures with encryption: signatures support authenticity/integrity, while encryption protects confidentiality.
derived_security_rules.rationale: A signature does not inherently conceal message content and encryption alone does not authenticate the sender.

derived_security_rules.rule: Use role-appropriate keys and lifecycle policies; consider separating signing keys from encryption/key-agreement keys.
derived_security_rules.rationale: Different operations have different legal, recovery, revocation and forward-secrecy implications.

derived_security_rules.rule: Generate keys and cryptographic randomness with a suitable cryptographically secure random-number generator.
derived_security_rules.rationale: Predictable key material can defeat otherwise sound algorithms.

derived_security_rules.rule: Treat forward secrecy as a protocol property with assumptions, not as a universal guarantee; endpoint compromise and poor ephemeral-secret handling remain risks.
derived_security_rules.rationale: Security depends on protocol implementation and secret erasure.

derived_security_rules.rule: Treat encrypted-header designs as specialized and deployment-dependent rather than assuming metadata privacy is provided by ordinary public-key encryption.
derived_security_rules.rationale: The source describes encrypted metadata as experimental and not broadly deployed at the time of the article.

examples.name: Alice signs a message for Bob
steps: Alice signs message data using her private signing key.
Bob obtains an authentic copy of Alice's public key.
Bob verifies the signature against the message.
A valid signature supports integrity and key-possession-based attribution, but does not encrypt the message.

examples.name: Source sends an encrypted message to a journalist
steps: The journalist publishes an authentic encryption public key.
The source encrypts the message using that public key.
The journalist decrypts using the paired private key.
Message content is concealed, but ordinary encryption may leave communication metadata visible and does not by itself authenticate the sender.

examples.name: Publisher-signed software update
steps: Publisher creates a signing key pair and distributes the public key through a trusted channel or software installation.
Publisher signs an update or its authenticated digest/manifest.
Client verifies the signature before applying the update.
Compromise of the signing key or trust bootstrap can undermine the workflow.

examples.name: TLS hybrid cryptosystem
steps: Client authenticates the server certificate and public-key identity.
Protocol establishes or derives shared traffic secrets using public-key cryptographic mechanisms.
Symmetric cryptography protects application data; suitable ephemeral key exchange can provide forward secrecy.

examples.name: Public-key substitution attack
steps: Attacker intercepts a public-key distribution exchange.
Attacker substitutes a key they control and relays traffic between parties.
Without authenticated key binding, each party may encrypt to or trust the attacker's key.
Certificate validation, web-of-trust checks, or another authenticated channel can prevent or detect substitution.

value.core_thesis: A sandbox separates running programs inside a restricted environment and controls their available resources and host access to contain failures and vulnerabilities.
value.relationship_semantics: Directed relationships preserve mechanism, effect, conditions, scope, implementation, containment, restriction, comparison, use, historical association and provenance.

value.mechanism: Execution occurs inside a restricted environment with controlled resources and host-facing operations.
value.effect: Reduces the ability of failures and vulnerabilities to spread.
value.conditions: Strength depends on enforcement of the sandbox boundary.
value.inverse_or_converse: Broader host access weakens separation.

value.mechanism: Network, host inspection, input devices and other resources are disallowed or heavily restricted.
value.effect: Limits the guest's ability to harm the host.
value.conditions: Requires effective resource/access enforcement.
value.inverse_or_converse: Unrestricted host access weakens containment.

value.mechanism: System-call filtering is one of the Linux kernel mechanisms used for application sandboxing.
value.effect: Reduces the kernel interface exposed to a sandboxed application.
value.conditions: The source explicitly combines it with cgroups and namespaces.
value.inverse_or_converse: A broader syscall surface increases available operations.

value.mechanism: cgroups are a Linux kernel feature used as part of application sandboxing.
value.effect: Contributes resource control.
value.conditions: Source does not specify a complete cgroup policy.
value.inverse_or_converse: Broader resource allowance weakens containment.

value.mechanism: Linux namespaces are a kernel feature used as part of application sandboxing.
value.effect: Contributes process/environment separation.
value.conditions: Used with seccomp and cgroups.
value.inverse_or_converse: Broader namespace visibility weakens isolation.

value.mechanism: Each application receives its own Linux user ID.
value.effect: Creates application-level OS identity separation.
value.conditions: Mechanism stated directly by source.
value.inverse_or_converse: Shared identity would broaden permissions.

value.mechanism: Adds hardening to Android app sandboxing and permits sandboxing every app as described.
value.effect: Increases sandbox scope/hardening.
value.conditions: Source contrasts this with stock Android.

value.mechanism: A virtual machine emulates a complete host computer so a conventional guest OS can boot and run.
value.effect: Guest execution is separated from native host execution.
value.conditions: Host-resource access is mediated through the emulator.
value.inverse_or_converse: Direct native host access bypasses the described mediation.

value.mechanism: Host resources are accessed through the emulator rather than natively.
value.effect: Creates a mediated host/guest boundary.
value.conditions: Depends on the emulator/VM layer.
value.inverse_or_converse: Direct access bypasses mediation.

value.mechanism: Network-access restrictions and a restricted filesystem namespace define the jail boundary.
value.effect: Limits network and filesystem reach.
value.conditions: Source notes common use in virtual hosting.
value.inverse_or_converse: Removing restrictions expands reach.

value.mechanism: Predetermined rules govern process spawning, code injection, network use and file/registry access.
value.effect: Programs receive constrained access levels.
value.conditions: SELinux and AppArmor are cited implementations.
value.inverse_or_converse: More permissive rules increase authority.

value.mechanism: A sandbox mimics or replicates a target desktop and contains malware execution.
value.effect: Researchers can evaluate malware behavior without exposing the real target host.
value.conditions: A nonrepresentative environment may not reproduce target behavior.

value.mechanism: Opaque tokens/capabilities confer specific rights.
value.effect: Enables fine-grained authority.
value.conditions: Can operate at kernel or user-space levels.
value.inverse_or_converse: Fewer capabilities reduce permitted actions.

value.mechanism: Only read(), write(), exit(), and sigreturn() are permitted.
value.effect: Dramatically reduces the system-call surface.
value.conditions: The allowlist is exactly as stated in the source.
value.inverse_or_converse: Operations requiring other calls cannot execute.

value.mechanism: The HTML5 sandbox attribute restricts iframe content.
value.effect: Embedded content runs under a constrained browser context.
value.conditions: Scope is embedded content.
value.inverse_or_converse: Removing the attribute removes those restrictions.

value.mechanism: Store, read and jump assembly instructions are sandboxed into isolated memory segments.
value.effect: Constrains untrusted native code to designated memory regions.
value.conditions: Mechanism described as Software Fault Isolation.
value.inverse_or_converse: Broader instruction reach weakens the isolation.

value.mechanism: Contest programs execute in a constrained server environment.
value.effect: Submitted programs can be tested while limiting impact on the judge host.
value.conditions: Source explicitly lists online judges as a use case.
value.inverse_or_converse: Unrestricted execution increases server risk.

value.mechanism: Pasted code snippets execute on a server inside a sandbox.
value.effect: User-supplied code can run while limiting server impact.
value.conditions: Source explicitly lists executable pastebins.
value.inverse_or_converse: Unrestricted execution increases server risk.
