value.label: 1996 — Secure Environment for Untrusted Helper Applications
Sandbox vs virtualization
value.description: Sandboxing is a security mechanism; virtualization can provide a highly controlled environment but is broader.

value.label: Restricted OS vs full VM
value.description: A restricted process environment is distinct from a VM emulating a complete host computer.

value.label: Kernel mechanism vs policy
value.description: seccomp/cgroups/namespaces are listed Linux building blocks; rule-based frameworks impose access policy.

value.label: Android UID isolation
value.description: The described Android sandbox uses per-application Linux user IDs.

value.label: Jail vs VM
value.description: A jail is characterized by network and filesystem namespace restrictions rather than full hardware emulation.

value.label: Capabilities vs rules
value.description: Capabilities grant rights through tokens; rule-based systems assign access levels through rules.

value.label: OS vs instruction isolation
value.description: SFI constrains native instructions to memory segments.

value.label: Defense vs analysis
value.description: Sandboxing can contain threats and provide a controlled observation environment.

value.label: Restriction vs absolute denial
value.description: Resources may be disallowed or heavily restricted; sandboxing is not necessarily total denial.

value.label: Guest vs host
value.description: The sandbox boundary separates guest execution from host resources.

value.label: Security mechanism vs application container
value.description: The source presents sandboxing as a security mechanism and does not equate it with application containerization.

value.label: Trusted vs untrusted code
value.description: Sandboxing is especially useful for unverified/untrusted code.

value.label: Browser active code vs unrestricted code
value.description: Native Client and iframe sandboxing show active browser code can execute under restrictions.

value.label: Strict vs normal syscall surface
value.description: Strict seccomp exposes only four named system calls.

value.label: Embedded vs top-level content
value.description: HTML5 sandbox specifically constrains iframe content.

value.label: Platform-specific mechanisms
value.description: Linux, Android, Apple, Windows, browser and language runtimes use different mechanisms.

value.label: Virtual-hosting jail
value.description: Jails are noted as common in virtual hosting.

value.label: Fine-grained capability control
value.description: Capability systems are explicitly described as fine-grained sandboxing.

value.statement: Sandbox means full VM
value.correction: The source treats VMs as one implementation and lists many non-VM mechanisms.

value.statement: Sandbox blocks everything
value.correction: The source describes controlled, disallowed, or heavily restricted resources.

value.statement: Sandbox is only for malware
value.correction: Online judges and pastebins are explicit non-malware use cases.

value.statement: Every app sandbox requires a VM
value.correction: Android's described mechanism uses Linux user IDs.

value.statement: Jail equals VM
value.correction: The source characterizes jails through network and filesystem namespace restrictions.

value.statement: Capabilities equal rule policies
value.correction: Tokens/capabilities grant specific rights; rule systems assign access levels.

value.statement: Sandboxing is only OS-level
value.correction: The source includes browser, runtime, capability and instruction-level mechanisms.

value.statement: SFI is just process isolation
value.correction: SFI isolates specified native-code instruction effects into memory segments.

source_claims.statement: Sandbox separates running programs to mitigate spread of system failures and software vulnerabilities.
Sandbox resources include storage and memory scratch space; network access, host inspection and input-device access are usually restricted.
Sandboxing can be comparable to virtualization when providing a highly controlled environment.
Sandboxing is implemented by executing software in a restricted operating-system environment.
Linux application sandboxing uses seccomp, cgroups and namespaces.
Android assigns each application its own Linux user ID for application sandboxing.
GrapheneOS hardens app sandboxing and allows sandboxing every app as described.
Apple App Sandbox is required for specified App Store apps and recommended for other signed apps.
Virtual machines emulate a complete host computer and mediate host-resource access through the emulator.
Jails restrict network access and filesystem namespace and are common in virtual hosting.
Rule-based execution controls process spawning, code injection, network access and file/registry operations.
Security researchers use sandboxing to analyze malware behavior in replicated target environments.
Google Native Client sandboxes compiled C/C++ code in browsers independently of the user's OS.
Capability systems use opaque tokens to grant specific rights and can operate at kernel or user-space levels.
Strict seccomp permits only read, write, exit and sigreturn.
HTML5 iframe sandboxing restricts embedded content.
Java virtual machines sandbox untrusted applets/code.
.NET CLR Code Access Security restricts untrusted code.
SFI isolates store, read and jump assembly instructions into memory segments.
Online judges and executable pastebins are sandbox use cases.

misconceptions.statement: Sandbox means full VM

misconceptions.statement: Sandbox blocks everything
misconceptions.correction: The source describes controlled, disallowed, or heavily restricted resources.

misconceptions.statement: Sandbox is only for malware
misconceptions.correction: Online judges and pastebins are explicit non-malware use cases.

misconceptions.statement: Every app sandbox requires a VM
misconceptions.correction: Android's described mechanism uses Linux user IDs.

misconceptions.statement: Jail equals VM
misconceptions.correction: The source characterizes jails through network and filesystem namespace restrictions.

misconceptions.statement: Capabilities equal rule policies
misconceptions.correction: Tokens/capabilities grant specific rights; rule systems assign access levels.

misconceptions.statement: Sandboxing is only OS-level

misconceptions.statement: SFI is just process isolation
misconceptions.correction: SFI isolates specified native-code instruction effects into memory segments.

source_claims.text: System image is a serialized copy of entire computer-system state in non-volatile form.
Disk cloning can produce a system image only when relevant state is on disk; some state may be outside disks or inaccessible.
Exact shutdown/restoration capability makes system images usable as backups.
Hibernation images the computer's entire RAM.
Process image captures process state and creates persistence.
DBMS can dump database state before closing and restore it after restart.
Emulators may save system images called savestates in video gaming.
Mobile agents can migrate by saving, copying, and restarting state elsewhere.
Smalltalk and Lisp support system images; Lisp can preserve compiled/customized code and loaded data.
Executable images can be distributed to avoid repeated initialization.
Lisp Machines boot from Worlds containing OS, applications, and data; incremental Worlds store changes.
System images resemble core dumps structurally but have different purposes.

limitations: Tor is an anonymity-enhancing system, not a guarantee of absolute anonymity.
Low-latency routing cannot reliably defeat an adversary able to observe and correlate traffic at both ends.
Traffic from applications not routed through Tor Browser or a configured Tor proxy is not automatically protected.

public_internet_circuit.component: client application configured to use Tor
public_internet_circuit.action: The application sends supported TCP traffic to a local Tor SOCKS interface or Tor Browser.
The first relay receives traffic from the client; it can see the client's network address but ordinarily not the final destination.
Forwards the circuit to the next hop without being the public Internet exit.
Removes the final Tor relay layer and connects to the public Internet destination; destination typically sees the exit IP.
Receives the request. If the application protocol lacks end-to-end encryption, traffic between exit and destination may be observable or modifiable.

onion_service_connection.action: Knows or obtains the service's .onion address and uses Tor-capable software.
Client obtains service connection information through Tor's distributed directory mechanisms.
Client chooses a path through Tor, including a rendezvous point.
Onion service independently builds a Tor path and connects to the rendezvous point.
Joins the circuits; communication remains within Tor and does not use a public Internet exit.

value.important_distinction: Tor routes traffic through relays; it is not a replacement for HTTPS, secure endpoint configuration, or sound operational security.

protected_properties: reduce destination visibility of the client's ordinary public IP
reduce any single relay's ability to see both source and destination
support location privacy and censorship circumvention
support onion services without publishing the host's ordinary IP address
out_of_scope_or_limited_properties: perfect anonymity against global or multi-point traffic observation
protection from malware or a compromised operating system
preventing identification when a user logs into a personal account or reveals identifying details
automatically routing every application on a device through Tor
end-to-end encryption between exit relay and public destination when the application does not provide it
preventing a destination from recognizing or blocking Tor exit IP addresses
attacker_capabilities_to_consider: control or observation of one relay
observation by an ISP or local network
simultaneous observation of traffic entering and leaving Tor
operation of multiple malicious relays (Sybil behavior)
blocking public relays or Tor traffic
mitigations_and_hygiene: Use the official Tor Browser or correctly configured applications.
Keep software updated and obtain it from official project sources.
Use HTTPS for public Internet websites.
Do not assume other applications on the device are routed through Tor.
Avoid logging into identifying accounts when identity separation is the goal.
Do not open downloaded documents in an application that can make unprotected network requests while the user is online unless the risks are understood.
Use bridges or supported pluggable transports where appropriate for censorship circumvention.
Use official Tor Project documentation for current configuration advice.

value.subject: BitTorrent .torrent meta-info file format
value.description: Detailed machine-readable graph of torrent-file structure, metadata fields, v1/v2 identity and integrity models, extensions, discovery methods, workflow, examples, limitations, and source references.
value.source_policy: Primary descriptive claims are grounded in the user-provided Torrent file article text. General security implications are explicitly identified as inference where applicable.

value.name: Parse and interpret a v1 .torrent file
value.summary: Decode bencoding, read the info dictionary, interpret single-file or multi-file layout, and use piece hashes to verify payload chunks.

steps.action: Read the .torrent byte stream and decode its bencoded top-level dictionary.
Read announce if present, plus optional extension fields such as announce-list, url-list, httpseeds, nodes, and private.
Read info.name and either info.length for a single file or info.files entries for a multi-file torrent.
Read piece length and split the logical content stream into pieces; multi-file v1 content follows files-list order.
Interpret pieces as concatenated 20-byte SHA-1 digests, one digest per piece.
Calculate the v1 infohash over the exact bencoded info dictionary and use it for torrent identity.
Use trackers and/or DHT to discover peers, fetch pieces, verify them, and assemble the payload.

value.name: BitTorrent v2 metadata and Merkle verification
value.summary: Use v2 metadata fields and SHA-256-based Merkle structures to describe files and verify content at block and piece levels.

steps.action: Identify v2 metadata using meta version = 2.
Read file tree to determine the directory and file hierarchy.
Read piece length, which must be a power of two in v2.
For each non-empty file, interpret piece root as the Merkle root built from 16 KiB blocks.
Use piece layers to carry per-piece Merkle root data.
Use SHA-256-based piece hashing and v2 infohashing; use the full hash in btmh magnet links.
When speaking to legacy tracker/DHT message structures, account for the described 20-byte truncated hash.

value.name: Trackerless discovery via DHT
value.summary: Omit the announce tracker field and include optional DHT bootstrap nodes, allowing peer discovery through a distributed hash table.

steps.action: Represent a trackerless torrent without an announce key.
Optionally include nodes as host/port pairs, ideally useful nearby routing-table nodes or a known reliable node.
Client uses Mainline DHT to discover peers for the torrent identity.
Client connects directly to discovered peers and participates in the swarm.

value.name: Combine peers, trackers, and web seeds
value.summary: Use multiple peer-discovery endpoints and optional HTTP(S) web seeds to improve availability and reduce pressure on any single distribution server.

steps.action: Include announce-list with multiple tracker URLs when supported.
Optionally include url-list web-seed URLs.
Client discovers peers through trackers and/or DHT as permitted by torrent policy.
Client fetches pieces from peers and web seeds, combining sources where supported.

value.name: Private torrent discovery policy
value.summary: Use the private flag and a private tracker to enforce a community-controlled peer-discovery convention, while recognizing that the flag is not anonymity.

steps.action: Set info.private to 1.
Use a private tracker that gates peer-list access.
Disable DHT, PEX, and LSD in compliant clients to preserve tracker control.
Do not treat this flag as encryption or anonymity; modifying the info dictionary changes the infohash.

value.name: Hybrid v1/v2 compatibility
value.summary: Carry old and new metadata fields to support both v1 and v2 clients, while managing distinct v1 and v2 infohash identities.

steps.action: Include v1-compatible and v2 metadata structures in the hybrid torrent.
Compute the corresponding v1 and v2 infohashes.
Recognize that distinct identities may produce separate swarms in the respective networks.
Use client logic to associate and merge the corresponding v1 and v2 swarm participation.

value.name: Separate integrity from trust and safety
value.summary: Use metadata hashes to detect corruption or mismatch, but do not infer that a file is safe, lawful, or trustworthy solely because its hashes match.

steps.action: Verify downloaded pieces or blocks against hashes in the torrent metadata.
Treat successful verification as evidence that bytes match the metadata's committed hashes.
Assess source trust, file behavior, and legal authorization separately.

value.statement: For v1, the pieces byte string length is a multiple of 20 bytes because each SHA-1 digest is 160 bits.
Piece count for a non-empty classic content stream is the ceiling of total content bytes divided by piece length.
BitTorrent v2 requires piece length to be a power of two.
Infohash identity is computed from the bencoded info dictionary; changing fields outside info such as announce does not affect it, while changing info does.
The v2 Merkle tree described by the article is constructed from 16 KiB blocks.

fields.label: Caveats

The source article itself notes citation and cleanup issues, including extension status labels that may be outdated.
The source's displayed piece-length expression has formatting corruption; the intended example value is 256 KiB = 262144 bytes.
The graph preserves the article's descriptions of BEP status rather than independently updating each status.
A successful hash check verifies consistency with torrent metadata; it does not prove that content is benign, lawful, or trustworthy.

derived_rules.statement: For v1, the pieces byte string length is a multiple of 20 bytes because each SHA-1 digest is 160 bits.

value.name: Migration model

value.meaning: A VM can be stopped/snapshotted/moved/resumed on another host; synchronized snapshots can reduce interruption.

value.name: Failover model
value.expression: Host failure + last coherent backup state -> VM continuation
value.meaning: Failover continues VM operation from the last-known coherent state available to the backup server.

value.name: Nested virtualization model

value.meaning: Nested virtualization recursively places hypervisors/VMs inside another virtualization layer.

value.event: System and process virtual machines date to the 1960s; system VMs grew from time-sharing.
IBM CP-40 and CP-67 are identified with early/full virtualization.
Hardware-assisted virtualization was introduced on IBM System/370 for VM/370.
Pascal p-code systems popularized process virtual machines.
Smalltalk-80 VM work advanced JIT compilation.
Java HotSpot incorporated successful VM optimization techniques.
Intel and AMD added additional hardware virtualization support.
Intel Haswell-era VMCS shadowing is cited as accelerating nested virtualization.

value.name: System VM vs Process VM
value.description: System VM provides a whole machine/guest OS abstraction; process VM supports a program/process abstraction.

value.name: Host vs Guest
value.description: Host is the physical machine; guest is the virtual environment executing on it.

value.name: Full vs Hardware-Assisted Virtualization
value.description: Full virtualization describes the guest-facing virtualization behavior; hardware-assisted virtualization describes architectural support that facilitates the VMM.

value.name: System VM vs OS-level Virtualization
value.description: System VM can execute a complete guest OS; OS-level environments share the host OS kernel.

value.name: VM vs Virtual Memory
value.description: Virtual memory abstracts memory; system virtualization generalizes machine abstraction and can include privileged instruction handling.

value.name: Snapshot vs Backup
value.description: Snapshot is a point-in-time VM state; failover may use backup-server material representing a last coherent state.

value.name: Migration vs Failover
value.description: Migration deliberately moves a VM to another host; failover continues after host failure using last-known coherent state.

value.name: Namespace-style isolation vs VM isolation
value.description: OS-level virtualization shares a kernel; system VMs isolate through separate guest environments.

value.name: Process VM vs Interpreter
value.description: A process VM is the runtime abstraction; an interpreter is one implementation mechanism.

value.name: JIT vs Interpreter
value.description: JIT is an optimization/compilation technique that can improve process-VM performance; interpreter is an execution mechanism.

value.name: Nested vs ordinary virtualization
value.description: Nested virtualization places a hypervisor inside another hypervisor; ordinary system virtualization does not require recursive layers.

value.name: KSM vs memory overcommitment
value.description: KSM merges identical pages; memory overcommitment is the broader memory-sharing/resource-management context.

value.name: Virtual disk vs snapshot overlay
value.description: Virtual disk is the VM storage abstraction; overlay is a snapshot layer storing subsequent changes.

value.name: Guest OS vs host OS
value.description: Guest OS executes inside VM; host OS is the surrounding OS when applicable.

value.name: Isolation vs Portability
value.description: Isolation separates execution environments; process VMs use abstraction to provide platform independence.

value.misconception: A virtual machine always means a full guest operating system.
value.correction: Process VMs execute a single program/process and can exist entirely as a host-OS application.

value.misconception: System VMs and process VMs are the same abstraction.
value.correction: They operate at different abstraction levels: whole-machine/OS versus program/process.

value.misconception: OS-level virtualization creates a separate kernel for every guest.
value.correction: The source says OS-level guest environments share the host OS kernel.

value.misconception: Full virtualization requires modifying the guest OS.
value.correction: The source defines full virtualization as sufficient simulated hardware for an unmodified guest OS.

value.misconception: Hardware-assisted virtualization is the same thing as full virtualization.
value.correction: Hardware assistance describes architectural support for the VMM; full virtualization describes the guest-visible virtualization model.

value.misconception: A snapshot is just a backup copy of one disk file.
value.correction: Snapshots can include VM storage and other state such as RAM, BIOS and configuration.

value.misconception: Migration and failover are identical.
value.correction: Migration intentionally moves state; failover responds to host failure from last coherent backup state.

value.misconception: Nested virtualization means running containers inside containers.
value.correction: The source defines it as running VMs/hypervisors inside another virtualization layer.

value.misconception: Process VMs cannot use JIT compilation.
value.correction: The source explicitly identifies JIT as an implementation/performance technique for process VMs.

value.misconception: VMs always hide distributed communication in cluster environments.
value.correction: The source states cluster-oriented process VMs do not hide that communication takes place.

value.misconception: KSM and memory overcommitment are identical.
value.correction: KSM is a specific page-merging mechanism within broader memory sharing/overcommitment.

value.misconception: Docker is unrelated to virtualization.
value.correction: The source explicitly classifies Docker as an OS-level virtualization example.

source_claims.claim: A VM virtualizes or emulates a computer system; system VMs execute whole OSs while process VMs execute programs in platform-independent environments.
System VM architecture includes host/guest terminology, historical time-sharing motivations, memory sharing, embedded uses, sandboxing and server consolidation.
Process VMs are host applications supporting one process and provide platform-independent programming environments; cluster-oriented variants abstract communication.
VM history spans 1960s time-sharing, IBM systems, compiler intermediate representations, p-code, Smalltalk, JIT, Self, HotSpot and register-based VMs.
Full virtualization and hardware-assisted virtualization are distinct techniques with IBM, Intel and AMD historical milestones and many implementation examples.
OS-level virtualization partitions resources through the kernel, shares the host OS kernel and includes Docker and container technologies.
Snapshots capture VM state/storage; overlays form a coherent virtual disk; migration moves VM state; failover uses last-known coherent backup state.
Nested virtualization recursively runs hypervisors/VMs and may rely on hardware support such as VMCS shadowing.
VMs are used for security isolation and compartmentalization architectures can limit malware spread.

IBM CP-40 and CP-67 are identified with early/full virtualization.

semantic_distinctions.name: System VM vs Process VM
semantic_distinctions.description: System VM provides a whole machine/guest OS abstraction; process VM supports a program/process abstraction.

semantic_distinctions.name: Host vs Guest
semantic_distinctions.description: Host is the physical machine; guest is the virtual environment executing on it.

semantic_distinctions.name: Full vs Hardware-Assisted Virtualization
semantic_distinctions.description: Full virtualization describes the guest-facing virtualization behavior; hardware-assisted virtualization describes architectural support that facilitates the VMM.

semantic_distinctions.name: System VM vs OS-level Virtualization
semantic_distinctions.description: System VM can execute a complete guest OS; OS-level environments share the host OS kernel.

semantic_distinctions.name: VM vs Virtual Memory
semantic_distinctions.description: Virtual memory abstracts memory; system virtualization generalizes machine abstraction and can include privileged instruction handling.

semantic_distinctions.name: Snapshot vs Backup
semantic_distinctions.description: Snapshot is a point-in-time VM state; failover may use backup-server material representing a last coherent state.

semantic_distinctions.name: Migration vs Failover
semantic_distinctions.description: Migration deliberately moves a VM to another host; failover continues after host failure using last-known coherent state.

semantic_distinctions.name: Namespace-style isolation vs VM isolation
semantic_distinctions.description: OS-level virtualization shares a kernel; system VMs isolate through separate guest environments.

semantic_distinctions.name: Process VM vs Interpreter
semantic_distinctions.description: A process VM is the runtime abstraction; an interpreter is one implementation mechanism.

semantic_distinctions.name: JIT vs Interpreter
semantic_distinctions.description: JIT is an optimization/compilation technique that can improve process-VM performance; interpreter is an execution mechanism.

semantic_distinctions.name: Nested vs ordinary virtualization
semantic_distinctions.description: Nested virtualization places a hypervisor inside another hypervisor; ordinary system virtualization does not require recursive layers.

semantic_distinctions.name: KSM vs memory overcommitment
semantic_distinctions.description: KSM merges identical pages; memory overcommitment is the broader memory-sharing/resource-management context.

semantic_distinctions.name: Virtual disk vs snapshot overlay
semantic_distinctions.description: Virtual disk is the VM storage abstraction; overlay is a snapshot layer storing subsequent changes.

semantic_distinctions.name: Guest OS vs host OS
semantic_distinctions.description: Guest OS executes inside VM; host OS is the surrounding OS when applicable.

semantic_distinctions.name: Isolation vs Portability
semantic_distinctions.description: Isolation separates execution environments; process VMs use abstraction to provide platform independence.

misconceptions.misconception: A virtual machine always means a full guest operating system.
misconceptions.correction: Process VMs execute a single program/process and can exist entirely as a host-OS application.

misconceptions.misconception: System VMs and process VMs are the same abstraction.
misconceptions.correction: They operate at different abstraction levels: whole-machine/OS versus program/process.

misconceptions.misconception: OS-level virtualization creates a separate kernel for every guest.
misconceptions.correction: The source says OS-level guest environments share the host OS kernel.

misconceptions.misconception: Full virtualization requires modifying the guest OS.
misconceptions.correction: The source defines full virtualization as sufficient simulated hardware for an unmodified guest OS.

misconceptions.misconception: Hardware-assisted virtualization is the same thing as full virtualization.
misconceptions.correction: Hardware assistance describes architectural support for the VMM; full virtualization describes the guest-visible virtualization model.

misconceptions.misconception: A snapshot is just a backup copy of one disk file.
misconceptions.correction: Snapshots can include VM storage and other state such as RAM, BIOS and configuration.

misconceptions.misconception: Migration and failover are identical.
misconceptions.correction: Migration intentionally moves state; failover responds to host failure from last coherent backup state.

misconceptions.misconception: Nested virtualization means running containers inside containers.
misconceptions.correction: The source defines it as running VMs/hypervisors inside another virtualization layer.

misconceptions.misconception: Process VMs cannot use JIT compilation.
misconceptions.correction: The source explicitly identifies JIT as an implementation/performance technique for process VMs.

misconceptions.misconception: VMs always hide distributed communication in cluster environments.
misconceptions.correction: The source states cluster-oriented process VMs do not hide that communication takes place.

misconceptions.misconception: KSM and memory overcommitment are identical.
misconceptions.correction: KSM is a specific page-merging mechanism within broader memory sharing/overcommitment.

misconceptions.misconception: Docker is unrelated to virtualization.
misconceptions.correction: The source explicitly classifies Docker as an OS-level virtualization example.

source_claims.title: Definition
source_claims.statement: A volume or logical drive is a distinctly-addressable storage area with a single file system.

source_claims.title: Storage topology
source_claims.statement: Mass storage is commonly divided into partitions used as volumes; volumes may span multiple media for redundancy, while simple volumes use one medium without redundancy or striping.

source_claims.title: Windows example
source_claims.statement: The source's two-drive example maps D0/P0 to NTFS C:, D0/P1 to FAT32 D:, and D1/P0 to FAT32 E:.

source_claims.title: Partition versus volume recognition
source_claims.statement: An OS may recognize a partition without recognizing its volume when it is unformatted or uses an unsupported filesystem such as ext4 in the Windows example.

source_claims.title: File-packed volume
source_claims.statement: A volume can be packed in one file, such as an ISO9660 disc image or Apple Disk Image; because it is a file inside a host volume, it is not a partition.

source_claims.title: Windows mounting
source_claims.statement: Windows handles volumes in the kernel and configures volumes/mount points through Disk Management or diskpart; mounted volumes receive paths via drive letters or NTFS mount points.

source_claims.title: Unix mounting
source_claims.statement: Unix-like systems commonly use volume managers and mount; non-boot volumes are grafted into the filesystem tree at a mount point.

source_claims.title: Cross-volume performance
source_claims.statement: Moving a file within a volume can change metadata without copying content, while moving across volumes requires copying content and deleting the source.

source_claims.title: Identifiers
source_claims.statement: Volumes can use human-readable labels and more fixed identifiers; serial numbers historically originated on mainframes and later supported media-change detection.

source_claims.title: FAT/NTFS labels and serials
source_claims.statement: FAT, NTFS, and exFAT impose different volume-label constraints; FAT/NTFS serial numbers support detection of volume replacement and formatting changes the serial.

review_questions.question: What is Wi-Fi?
review_questions.answer: Wireless networking using radio waves rather than wires.

review_questions.question: What does IEEE 802.11 specify?
review_questions.answer: Protocols and behavior for wireless local-area networking.

review_questions.question: How do Wi-Fi and IEEE 802.11 differ?
review_questions.answer: IEEE 802.11 is the standards family; Wi-Fi is the common ecosystem term.

review_questions.question: Does Wi-Fi guarantee Internet access?
review_questions.answer: No; upstream connectivity is separate.

review_questions.question: Which frequency bands are emphasized in the supplied articles?
review_questions.answer: 2.4 GHz and 5 GHz.

review_questions.question: Why can 2.4 GHz be crowded?
review_questions.answer: Multiple wireless technologies and Wi-Fi networks share the band.

review_questions.question: What is a channel?
review_questions.answer: A specific frequency allocation within a broader band.

review_questions.question: What is transmit power control?
review_questions.answer: Adjusting transmit power to what is needed, where required.

review_questions.question: Why does bit rate differ from throughput?
review_questions.answer: Protocol overhead, contention, interference, and retries reduce useful delivered data.

review_questions.question: What year does the article give for the first 802.11 standard?
What rate does the source give for the original standard?
review_questions.answer: 1–2 Mbit/s.

review_questions.question: Which standards does the source say were widely used in 2007?
What introduction date appears in the Wi-Fi infobox?
review_questions.answer: September 1998.

review_questions.question: Which hardware categories are listed?
review_questions.answer: Personal computers, gaming consoles, televisions, printers, mobile phones, and tablets.

review_questions.question: What is an access point?
review_questions.answer: A device that provides wireless connectivity and connects stations to a network.

review_questions.question: What is a Wi-Fi station?
review_questions.answer: A device with a compatible 802.11 interface participating in a WLAN.

review_questions.question: Why may 5 GHz have less congestion?
review_questions.answer: The source says it is less used overall and has more channels; local conditions vary.

review_questions.question: Why does 5 GHz have additional restrictions?
review_questions.answer: Radio regulations constrain channels and operating conditions.

review_questions.question: What is interference?
review_questions.answer: Unwanted or competing radio energy that reduces communication performance.

review_questions.question: What is medium contention?
review_questions.answer: Competition among devices for transmission opportunities on shared airtime.

review_questions.question: Why is global compatibility conditional?
review_questions.answer: Device capabilities, bands, channels, regulations, and configurations differ.

review_questions.question: What does the source say about the Wi-Fi name?
review_questions.answer: It is wordplay on hi-fi and replaced a longer technical label.

review_questions.question: What health statement does the source report?
review_questions.answer: It attributes to WHO the statement that Wi-Fi is not dangerous; this graph does not independently verify it.

review_questions.question: What is a hotspot?
review_questions.answer: A location or device offering wireless network access.

review_questions.question: Which possible interferers are named?
review_questions.answer: Microwave ovens, Bluetooth devices, and DECT telephones.

review_questions.question: Why are 2007 and 2013 claims historical?
review_questions.answer: They are dated snapshots, not current prevalence measurements.

review_questions.question: What is the difference between a band and a channel?
review_questions.answer: A band is a range; a channel is a specific allocation within it.

review_questions.question: What does the MAC layer do?
review_questions.answer: Coordinates access to the shared wireless medium.

review_questions.question: What does the PHY layer do?
review_questions.answer: Handles radio signaling and transmission/reception.

review_questions.question: Why separate source claims from synthesis?
review_questions.answer: To preserve what the article says while making explanatory connections transparent.

fields.value: BitTorrent v2 metadata and Merkle verification

fields.label: Summary
fields.value: Use v2 metadata fields and SHA-256-based Merkle structures to describe files and verify content at block and piece levels.

value.action: Identify v2 metadata using meta version = 2.
Read file tree to determine the directory and file hierarchy.
Read piece length, which must be a power of two in v2.
For each non-empty file, interpret piece root as the Merkle root built from 16 KiB blocks.
Use piece layers to carry per-piece Merkle root data.
Use SHA-256-based piece hashing and v2 infohashing; use the full hash in btmh magnet links.
When speaking to legacy tracker/DHT message structures, account for the described 20-byte truncated hash.

fields.label: Name
fields.value: Parse and interpret a v1 .torrent file

fields.label: Summary
fields.value: Decode bencoding, read the info dictionary, interpret single-file or multi-file layout, and use piece hashes to verify payload chunks.

value.action: Read the .torrent byte stream and decode its bencoded top-level dictionary.
Read announce if present, plus optional extension fields such as announce-list, url-list, httpseeds, nodes, and private.
Read info.name and either info.length for a single file or info.files entries for a multi-file torrent.
Read piece length and split the logical content stream into pieces; multi-file v1 content follows files-list order.
Interpret pieces as concatenated 20-byte SHA-1 digests, one digest per piece.
Calculate the v1 infohash over the exact bencoded info dictionary and use it for torrent identity.
Use trackers and/or DHT to discover peers, fetch pieces, verify them, and assemble the payload.

record.name: Parse and interpret a v1 .torrent file
record.summary: Decode bencoding, read the info dictionary, interpret single-file or multi-file layout, and use piece hashes to verify payload chunks.

steps.action: Read the .torrent byte stream and decode its bencoded top-level dictionary.
Read announce if present, plus optional extension fields such as announce-list, url-list, httpseeds, nodes, and private.
Read info.name and either info.length for a single file or info.files entries for a multi-file torrent.
Read piece length and split the logical content stream into pieces; multi-file v1 content follows files-list order.
Interpret pieces as concatenated 20-byte SHA-1 digests, one digest per piece.
Calculate the v1 infohash over the exact bencoded info dictionary and use it for torrent identity.
Use trackers and/or DHT to discover peers, fetch pieces, verify them, and assemble the payload.

fields.value: Password storage with a password KDF

fields.label: Purpose
fields.value: Reduce the rate of offline password guessing after a verifier database is exposed.

fields.label: Steps
value: Generate a unique random salt per password.
Derive a verifier using a password KDF such as Argon2, scrypt, bcrypt, or PBKDF2 with appropriate parameters.
Store the algorithm identifier, parameters, salt, and verifier.
On login, recompute and compare; upgrade parameters as policy changes.

fields.label: Caveats
value: Do not use a fast hash such as raw SHA-256 or SHA-1 alone for password storage.
Parameter choices should follow current platform and standards guidance.

fields.label: Core problem

value.because: Controllers turn desired-state declarations into repeatable reconciliation loops.
Failure-induced divergence can trigger replacement/recovery actions.

fields.label: Purpose
fields.value: Reduce the rate of offline password guessing after a verifier database is exposed.

fields.label: Steps
value: Generate a unique random salt per password.
Derive a verifier using a password KDF such as Argon2, scrypt, bcrypt, or PBKDF2 with appropriate parameters.
Store the algorithm identifier, parameters, salt, and verifier.
On login, recompute and compare; upgrade parameters as policy changes.

Parameter choices should follow current platform and standards guidance.

fields.value: Use v2 metadata fields and SHA-256-based Merkle structures to describe files and verify content at block and piece levels.

value.action: Identify v2 metadata using meta version = 2.
Read file tree to determine the directory and file hierarchy.
Read piece length, which must be a power of two in v2.
For each non-empty file, interpret piece root as the Merkle root built from 16 KiB blocks.
Use piece layers to carry per-piece Merkle root data.
Use SHA-256-based piece hashing and v2 infohashing; use the full hash in btmh magnet links.
When speaking to legacy tracker/DHT message structures, account for the described 20-byte truncated hash.

fields.label: Purpose
fields.value: Detect modification or substitution of downloaded content.

fields.label: Steps
value: Obtain the expected digest from an authenticated/trusted source.
Compute the digest of the received file with a suitable modern algorithm.
Compare values using the correct algorithm and encoding.
If a mismatch occurs, reject or investigate the file; if it matches, interpret the result only within the trust model.

fields.label: Caveats
value: A digest posted beside a file on the same unauthenticated channel may be replaced together with the file.
A matching hash does not prove that software is benign or that the publisher is trustworthy.

contrasted_with.dark_web: A subset of the deep web intentionally hidden and generally reachable through specialized software or networks rather than standard browsers and methods.

definitions.terminology_warning: Deep web and dark web are not synonyms. Media usage has sometimes conflated them, which has created persistent confusion.

historical_term_attribution.claim: Credited with establishing the term 'deep web' as a search-indexing term.

possible_access_requirements: Specialized software for certain intentionally hidden services

examples.name: Restricted social-media pages and profiles
examples.access_pattern: Privacy settings, account permissions, or login

examples.name: Paywalled video, magazine, and newspaper services
Web archives
examples.access_pattern: Archive interface and historical snapshot selection

non_indexing_mechanisms.name: Contextual web
non_indexing_mechanisms.description: Pages vary according to access context, such as client IP range or prior navigation sequence.
non_indexing_mechanisms.crawler_challenge: A crawler may not reproduce the context needed to obtain the same page.

non_indexing_mechanisms.name: Dynamic content
non_indexing_mechanisms.description: Pages are generated in response to submitted queries or forms and may not exist as stable, discoverable URLs before the query.
non_indexing_mechanisms.crawler_challenge: The query space may be too large or indeterminate to enumerate.

non_indexing_mechanisms.name: Limited-access content
non_indexing_mechanisms.description: Technical or policy controls limit crawling, indexing, or caching.
non_indexing_mechanisms.crawler_challenge: Access controls or directives can prevent crawling or cached copies.

non_indexing_mechanisms.name: Non-HTML or non-text content
non_indexing_mechanisms.description: Information is embedded in multimedia or file formats that a search engine may not recognize or extract.
non_indexing_mechanisms.crawler_challenge: Text extraction, format recognition, or semantic interpretation may be limited.

non_indexing_mechanisms.name: Private web
non_indexing_mechanisms.crawler_challenge: The crawler cannot retrieve the protected content without authorized access.

non_indexing_mechanisms.name: Scripted content
non_indexing_mechanisms.description: Pages or data are exposed through links created by JavaScript or content fetched dynamically by client-side scripts.
non_indexing_mechanisms.crawler_challenge: A crawler that does not execute the relevant scripts or reproduce application behavior may miss content.

non_indexing_mechanisms.name: Special-software-accessible content
non_indexing_mechanisms.description: Some intentionally hidden services are accessible through specialized software or networks.
non_indexing_mechanisms.crawler_challenge: Ordinary browsers and conventional crawlers do not directly access all such services.

non_indexing_mechanisms.name: Unlinked content
non_indexing_mechanisms.description: Pages with few or no links from known pages may remain undiscovered by link-following crawlers.
non_indexing_mechanisms.crawler_challenge: A crawler generally needs a known URL, link, sitemap, submission, or other discovery route.

non_indexing_mechanisms.name: Archived web content
non_indexing_mechanisms.description: Historical snapshots may be accessible through archival interfaces but may not be indexed as ordinary current pages.
non_indexing_mechanisms.classification_note: The supplied article describes archives as a possible deep-web case; classification can depend on the search engine and the particular archive resource.

conventional_search_engine_model.typical_method: Follow hyperlinks from known URLs and process retrievable pages.
limitations: Cannot enumerate every possible database query.
May not access authenticated resources.
May not execute all client-side application behavior.
May not interpret all multimedia or specialized file formats.
May not discover unlinked pages.
May avoid content restricted by site policy or technical controls.

deep_web_crawling_methods.name: Form-interface discovery
deep_web_crawling_methods.description: Identify web forms and query interfaces, then submit selected queries to obtain otherwise undiscovered result pages.

deep_web_crawling_methods.name: User-supplied or learned query terms
deep_web_crawling_methods.description: Use important terms provided by users or collected from query interfaces to generate searches against hidden-web databases.

deep_web_crawling_methods.name: Automatic query generation
deep_web_crawling_methods.description: Generate meaningful queries for search forms and extract structured data from resulting pages.

deep_web_crawling_methods.name: Sitemaps
deep_web_crawling_methods.description: A site can advertise discoverable URLs through the Sitemap Protocol.

deep_web_crawling_methods.name: OAI-PMH
deep_web_crawling_methods.description: A metadata-harvesting protocol that can help expose records or resources from participating repositories.

deep_web_crawling_methods.name: Search-engine form surfacing
deep_web_crawling_methods.description: Search engines may select representative form values and combinations to generate URLs that can be indexed.

form_surfacing_strategies: Select input values for keyword-search fields.
Identify fields constrained to specific data types, such as dates.
Select a limited number of input combinations likely to produce useful indexable URLs.
tradeoffs: Crawling forms can expose useful pages that ordinary link traversal misses.
The number of possible queries can be enormous.
Poorly chosen submissions may create low-value pages or inflate apparent popularity.
Access permission, privacy, rate limits, and site policies remain important constraints.

historical_development.event: Used the term 'Invisible Web' for websites not registered with search engines, as reported by the cited historical account.
An early published use described websites that were not registered with search engines and therefore were difficult to find.
A December press release described the No. 1 Deep Web program.
Published 'The Deep Web: Surfacing Hidden Value' in The Journal of Electronic Publishing and is credited with the now-common term.
Presented an architectural model for a hidden-web crawler that used important terms and query interfaces.

historical_development.entity: Alexandros Ntoulas, Petros Zerfos, and Junghoo Cho
historical_development.event: Published work on automatically generating meaningful queries and downloading hidden-web content.
Research explored query languages and extraction of structured data from result pages; terminology varies across references.
The supplied article notes the Sitemap Protocol was first developed and introduced in 2005 as a mechanism for advertising URLs.
Research described form submission selection and methods for surfacing some query-generated pages into search indexes.
Designed Tor2web, a proxy application intended to make access to Tor hidden-service links possible through ordinary web browsers.
The terms deep web and dark web were increasingly conflated in coverage that discussed search terminology alongside illegal activity on darknet networks.

use_cases: Accessing personal email and account dashboards
Searching databases whose results are generated only after a query
Finding scholarly, government, library, or repository records not fully represented in general search indexes
Researching hidden-web crawling and information retrieval

principles: Not indexed does not mean illegal.
Deep web is not synonymous with dark web.
Authentication and authorization must be respected.
Do not bypass access controls, CAPTCHAs, paywalls, or rate limits without authorization.
Crawler designs should respect robots directives, terms of service, privacy, data minimization, and rate limits.
Specialized anonymity networks and proxy services have distinct trust and privacy properties.
risk_categories: Malicious or deceptive content on some hidden services
False assumptions that a proxy or hidden service guarantees anonymity
security_privacy_and_ethics.classification_caution: The deep web is a broad indexing category containing routine private services as well as other forms of non-indexed content; it should not be classified as inherently illicit.

limitations_and_uncertainties: The exact boundary of the deep web depends on the search engine, index, crawl policy, and time.
A page may be indexed by one service and not another.
Some categories, especially web archives and dynamically rendered pages, can be classified differently depending on the definition used.
The article contains historical descriptions of systems; listed statuses should not be treated as current operational status without fresh verification.
A relationship edge indicates a conceptual association and does not necessarily mean a direct technical dependency.

fields.label: Core problem
fields.value: Coordinate desired software state across changing distributed compute infrastructure without requiring humans to manually orchestrate every machine and recovery action.

value.because: Controllers turn desired-state declarations into repeatable reconciliation loops.
Failure-induced divergence can trigger replacement/recovery actions.
Schedulers and workload controllers coordinate resource supply with workload demand.
A common API/object model abstracts workload management across machines, distributions and cloud environments.
CRDs, controllers, operators, scheduler extensions and CSI allow the platform to be adapted without changing the entire core.
The same declarative state model applies across workloads, networking, storage, configuration and infrastructure.

fields.label: Purpose
fields.value: Detect modification or substitution of downloaded content.

fields.label: Steps
value: Obtain the expected digest from an authenticated/trusted source.
Compute the digest of the received file with a suitable modern algorithm.
Compare values using the correct algorithm and encoding.
If a mismatch occurs, reject or investigate the file; if it matches, interpret the result only within the trust model.

fields.label: Caveats
value: A digest posted beside a file on the same unauthenticated channel may be replaced together with the file.
A matching hash does not prove that software is benign or that the publisher is trustworthy.

fields.label: Purpose
fields.value: Address and deduplicate objects based on content.

fields.label: Steps
value: Select a collision-resistant hash and a canonical byte representation.
Hash the content to derive a content address.
Store the object and index its address to physical storage.
On retrieval, recompute the hash to verify content integrity.

fields.label: Caveats
value: Collision handling and algorithm migration should be part of the design.
The content address is not automatically a claim of publisher authenticity.

fields.label: Steps
value: Define a target predicate over a hash output.
Vary a nonce or candidate header and compute hashes until the predicate passes.
Verifier performs one or a small number of hash computations and checks the predicate.

fields.label: Caveats
value: Difficulty must be calibrated; proof of work does not itself establish the truth or legitimacy of the submitted content.

record.statement: A Hashcash-style stamp should be checked against its specified fields and policy to reduce trivial replay or cross-context reuse.

fields.label: Scenario
fields.value: A service wants to impose a computational cost on high-volume requests.

fields.label: Steps
value: Select a difficulty policy appropriate to the service and request context.
Have the client search for a stamp whose SHA-1 digest satisfies the stated leading-zero requirement, if reproducing the historical example.
Verify the supplied stamp and its bound fields.
Reject invalid or policy-expired stamps and apply ordinary abuse controls as well.

fields.label: Outcome
fields.value: The service can impose asymmetric computational cost, while recognizing that PoW is only one abuse-control mechanism.

record.name: HMAC

record.label: HMAC

fields.label: Purpose
fields.value: Authenticate messages using a shared secret and a standardized keyed construction.

fields.label: Steps
value: Agree on a secure hash and shared secret key.
Compute the HMAC over the canonical message representation.
Transmit the message and authentication tag.
Receiver recomputes the HMAC and compares tags using an appropriate constant-time comparison.

fields.label: Caveats
value: Do not substitute naive hash(secret || message) constructions for HMAC.
Key management and message canonicalization remain important.

fields.value: Defensive triage for a sudden website outage

fields.value: A public website becomes slow and intermittently unreachable. The team must determine whether the cause is a traffic flood, an application bottleneck, or an ordinary traffic surge.

fields.label: Steps
value: Check service health, latency, error rates, and provider telemetry
Compare bit rate, packet rate, request rate, and connection counts with baseline
Review application-path completion and expensive endpoint metrics
Coordinate with the hosting provider or upstream DDoS service if links are saturated
Apply proportionate mitigation and monitor false positives

fields.label: Title
fields.value: Defensive triage for a sudden website outage

fields.label: Scenario
fields.value: A public website becomes slow and intermittently unreachable. The team must determine whether the cause is a traffic flood, an application bottleneck, or an ordinary traffic surge.

fields.label: Steps
value: Check service health, latency, error rates, and provider telemetry
Compare bit rate, packet rate, request rate, and connection counts with baseline
Review application-path completion and expensive endpoint metrics
Coordinate with the hosting provider or upstream DDoS service if links are saturated
Apply proportionate mitigation and monitor false positives
Confirm recovery and document the incident

fields.label: Caveats
value: Symptoms alone do not prove an attack.
Do not indiscriminately block all traffic to a production web port.

fields.label: Name
fields.value: BitTorrent v2 metadata and Merkle verification

fields.label: Summary
fields.value: Use v2 metadata fields and SHA-256-based Merkle structures to describe files and verify content at block and piece levels.

value.action: Identify v2 metadata using meta version = 2.
Read file tree to determine the directory and file hierarchy.
Read piece length, which must be a power of two in v2.
For each non-empty file, interpret piece root as the Merkle root built from 16 KiB blocks.
Use piece layers to carry per-piece Merkle root data.
Use SHA-256-based piece hashing and v2 infohashing; use the full hash in btmh magnet links.
When speaking to legacy tracker/DHT message structures, account for the described 20-byte truncated hash.

value.action: Read the .torrent byte stream and decode its bencoded top-level dictionary.
Read announce if present, plus optional extension fields such as announce-list, url-list, httpseeds, nodes, and private.
Read info.name and either info.length for a single file or info.files entries for a multi-file torrent.
Read piece length and split the logical content stream into pieces; multi-file v1 content follows files-list order.
Interpret pieces as concatenated 20-byte SHA-1 digests, one digest per piece.
Calculate the v1 infohash over the exact bencoded info dictionary and use it for torrent identity.
Use trackers and/or DHT to discover peers, fetch pieces, verify them, and assemble the payload.

fields.label: Purpose
fields.value: Detect modification or substitution of downloaded content.

fields.label: Steps
value: Obtain the expected digest from an authenticated/trusted source.
Compute the digest of the received file with a suitable modern algorithm.
Compare values using the correct algorithm and encoding.
If a mismatch occurs, reject or investigate the file; if it matches, interpret the result only within the trust model.

fields.label: Caveats
value: A digest posted beside a file on the same unauthenticated channel may be replaced together with the file.
A matching hash does not prove that software is benign or that the publisher is trustworthy.

fields.label: Title
fields.value: Defensive triage for a sudden website outage

fields.label: Scenario
fields.value: A public website becomes slow and intermittently unreachable. The team must determine whether the cause is a traffic flood, an application bottleneck, or an ordinary traffic surge.

fields.label: Steps
value: Check service health, latency, error rates, and provider telemetry
Compare bit rate, packet rate, request rate, and connection counts with baseline
Review application-path completion and expensive endpoint metrics
Coordinate with the hosting provider or upstream DDoS service if links are saturated
Apply proportionate mitigation and monitor false positives
Confirm recovery and document the incident

fields.label: Caveats
value: Symptoms alone do not prove an attack.
Do not indiscriminately block all traffic to a production web port.

fields.value: Detect modification or substitution of downloaded content.

fields.label: Steps
value: Obtain the expected digest from an authenticated/trusted source.
Compute the digest of the received file with a suitable modern algorithm.
Compare values using the correct algorithm and encoding.
If a mismatch occurs, reject or investigate the file; if it matches, interpret the result only within the trust model.

value: A digest posted beside a file on the same unauthenticated channel may be replaced together with the file.
A matching hash does not prove that software is benign or that the publisher is trustworthy.

fields.label: Title
fields.value: Defensive triage for a sudden website outage

fields.label: Scenario
fields.value: A public website becomes slow and intermittently unreachable. The team must determine whether the cause is a traffic flood, an application bottleneck, or an ordinary traffic surge.

fields.label: Steps
value: Check service health, latency, error rates, and provider telemetry
Compare bit rate, packet rate, request rate, and connection counts with baseline
Review application-path completion and expensive endpoint metrics
Coordinate with the hosting provider or upstream DDoS service if links are saturated
Apply proportionate mitigation and monitor false positives
Confirm recovery and document the incident

fields.label: Caveats
value: Symptoms alone do not prove an attack.
Do not indiscriminately block all traffic to a production web port.

Escalate to upstream filtering if the access link is saturated

Use only authorized monitoring and configuration changes.

browser.definition: A software user agent for retrieving, interpreting, and presenting Web resources.

timeline.name: World Wide Web Wanderer and Wandex
timeline.significance: A web robot and index initially used to measure the size of the Web.

timeline.name: ALIWEB
timeline.significance: Relied on site administrators to submit index files instead of using a web robot.

timeline.name: JumpStation
timeline.significance: Combined crawling, indexing, and searching in one web resource-discovery tool.

timeline.name: WebCrawler
timeline.significance: Among the first crawler-based engines to search the full text of web pages.

timeline.name: Lycos
timeline.significance: Launched from work at Carnegie Mellon University and became a major commercial endeavor.

timeline.name: Yahoo! Search
timeline.significance: Search was added to Yahoo!'s human-curated directory.

timeline.name: RankDex
timeline.significance: Used hyperlinks to assess website quality.

timeline.name: Netscape search distribution deal
timeline.significance: Netscape rotated five major search providers on its search page under commercial agreements.

timeline.name: Google Search and PageRank
timeline.significance: Google launched and later rose to prominence through ranking and interface choices.

timeline.name: MSN Search
timeline.significance: Initially relied on third-party results before Microsoft moved toward its own search technology.

timeline.name: Baidu
timeline.significance: Launched using technology associated with Robin Li's work.

timeline.name: Google becomes dominant
timeline.significance: The article attributes this to ranking quality, link analysis, and a minimalist interface.

timeline.name: Yahoo! search technology consolidation
timeline.significance: Yahoo! acquired Inktomi in 2002 and Overture-owned search assets in 2003, then launched its own technology in 2004.

timeline.name: Microsoft transitions to its own search technology
timeline.significance: Microsoft moved toward its own crawler and search infrastructure.

timeline.name: Bing launches
timeline.significance: Microsoft rebranded Live Search as Bing.

timeline.name: Yahoo!-Microsoft search agreement finalized
timeline.significance: Yahoo! Search was to be powered by Bing technology.

timeline.name: YaCy
timeline.significance: A peer-to-peer search engine listed in the article's timeline.

timeline.name: Qwant, Swisscows, Kagi and others appear in timeline
timeline.significance: The article's timeline records continuing diversity in search providers.

timeline.name: Brave Search and You.com
timeline.significance: Newer search services appear in the article's chronology.

timeline.name: Perplexity
timeline.significance: The article lists Perplexity as an AI-era search product.

timeline.name: AI-powered search integration
timeline.significance: Search increasingly combines indexing with language models for conversational answers, summaries, and contextual recommendations.
